lessons.title: What Is Artificial Intelligence?
lessons.content:
Imagine your phone's map app on a Friday evening in Dhaka. You type "Bashundhara City" and within a second it shows a route that avoids the jam at Farmgate, tells you it will take 35 minutes, and even suggests going by metro rail instead. Nobody sat inside your phone drawing that route by hand. A program looked at the roads, the traffic and the goal, and chose a smart plan. That ability, a machine choosing smart actions to reach a goal, is the heart of Artificial Intelligence, or AI.

What it is: Artificial Intelligence is the part of computer science that studies how to build programs and machines that behave intelligently. "Intelligently" here means things like solving problems, making plans, understanding language, recognising pictures, learning from experience and making good decisions when the world is uncertain. AI is not one single algorithm. It is a big toolbox: search algorithms, logic, probability, learning methods and more. This course opens that toolbox one tool at a time.

Why the word is tricky: People argue about what "intelligence" even means. Is a calculator intelligent because it multiplies faster than you? Most people say no. Is a chess program intelligent because it beats world champions? Many say "sort of". Because of this confusion, AI researchers usually describe AI by what the program should do, not by a magic definition of intelligence. The most famous way of organising those descriptions comes from the textbook by Stuart Russell and Peter Norvig, used in most universities, including in Bangladesh.

The four views of AI: Russell and Norvig sort definitions along two questions. First, do we care about thinking or about acting? Second, do we measure success against humans or against an ideal standard called rationality? That gives four boxes. Thinking humanly: build programs that think the way people think, which needs psychology and brain science. Acting humanly: build programs that act so much like people that you cannot tell the difference. Thinking rationally: build programs that reason correctly using logic, the "laws of thought". Acting rationally: build programs that do the best possible thing to reach their goals, given what they know.

Acting humanly and the Turing test: In 1950 the British mathematician Alan Turing wrote a paper asking "Can machines think?". Instead of answering directly, he proposed a game, now called the Turing test. A human judge chats by typing with two hidden partners: one is a person, the other is a machine. If the judge cannot reliably tell which is the machine, the machine passes. To pass, a machine would need natural language processing, knowledge representation, reasoning and learning, which are exactly the big areas of AI. The test is famous, but researchers rarely try to pass it directly, the same way aeroplane designers did not try to build machines that fly exactly like pigeons.

Thinking humanly: This view is about copying the actual steps a human mind uses. If a program solves a puzzle correctly but in a totally different way than people do, it fails this view. This approach mixes AI with cognitive science, the study of how minds work. It is useful for understanding people, but it is hard, because we still do not fully know how the brain does most things.

Thinking rationally: The Greek philosopher Aristotle tried to write down patterns of correct reasoning, like "All humans are mortal. Socrates is a human. So Socrates is mortal." Logic grew from this. The logic approach in AI says: write facts about the world in logic, and let the computer derive new true facts. You already met propositional logic and quantifiers in Discrete Mathematics; in lessons 16 to 19 we use them to build reasoning agents. The problems: real knowledge is often uncertain, and pure logical reasoning can be extremely slow.

Acting rationally, the view this course uses: A rational agent is something that acts to get the best expected outcome, given what it knows. This view includes logic when logic helps, but it also allows quick reflex actions (pulling your hand from a hot pan is rational even without deep thought) and decisions under uncertainty using probability. It is also easy to measure: we can define a performance score and check if the agent does well. That is why modern AI, and this course, is built around rational agents. Lesson 2 defines agents carefully.

Narrow AI and general AI: Almost every AI system that exists today is narrow AI, sometimes called weak AI. It is good at one kind of task: a spam filter only filters email, a chess engine only plays chess, a face unlock system only checks faces. Artificial general intelligence (AGI), sometimes linked with the term strong AI, means a system that could learn and do almost any intellectual task a human can, across many areas. Modern large language models can handle many different text tasks, which has made the AGI debate much more active, but experts strongly disagree about how close we are. In exams, the safe statement is: today's systems are specialised and have clear weaknesses, and general human-level AI has not been demonstrated.

A short history, the beginning: In 1956 a summer workshop was held at Dartmouth College in the USA, organised by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon and Nathaniel Rochester. The name "artificial intelligence" comes from McCarthy's proposal for this workshop, and 1956 is usually called the birth year of AI as a field. Early programs proved logic theorems, played checkers and solved algebra word problems. Researchers were very optimistic and predicted human-level AI within a generation.

AI winters: The early methods worked on toy problems but failed on real ones, mainly because the number of possibilities explodes (we will see this "combinatorial explosion" in the search lessons) and because computers were slow. Funding dropped in the 1970s, a period called an AI winter. In the 1980s, expert systems became popular: programs that stored hundreds of "IF this THEN that" rules from human experts, such as MYCIN for diagnosing blood infections. They were useful in narrow areas but expensive to build and fragile, and another winter came in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

The modern era: From the 1990s, AI became more mathematical, using probability and statistics to handle uncertainty. In 1997 IBM's Deep Blue defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a match, mostly through very fast search. From around 2012, deep learning (large neural networks trained on huge data using powerful graphics processors) produced big jumps in image recognition and speech recognition. In 2016 DeepMind's AlphaGo beat top Go player Lee Sedol. In the 2020s, large language models made chat assistants widely used. Notice the pattern: progress came in waves, and each wave combined new ideas with more data and faster computers.

The big sub-fields: AI today has several main areas. Search and planning find sequences of actions to reach goals. Knowledge representation and reasoning store facts and draw conclusions. Reasoning under uncertainty uses probability. Machine learning lets programs improve from data. Natural language processing deals with human language. Computer vision deals with images and video. Robotics connects all of this to physical bodies with sensors and motors. This course gives you the foundations of the first three in depth and an overview of the rest.

How AI differs from normal programming: In normal programming, you write exact steps: "add these numbers, print the total". In classic AI, you often describe the problem instead (the start, the goal, the allowed moves, the rules), and a general algorithm finds the steps by itself. In machine learning, you go one step further: you give examples, and the program builds its own rules from them. A good AI engineer knows when plain programming is enough and when an AI method is really needed.

Real life example 1, ride sharing in Dhaka: When you book a Pathao or Uber ride, several AI-style problems are solved quickly. The app must match you with a nearby driver (a decision problem), find a good route through changing traffic (a search problem with costs), estimate arrival time from past trips (a learning problem) and set prices that may change with demand. None of these needs a human-like mind. They need good formulations and good algorithms, exactly what this course teaches.

Real life example 2, agriculture and phones: Some phone apps used by farmers, in Bangladesh and elsewhere, let a farmer photograph a sick rice or potato leaf and get a guess of the disease. Behind this is computer vision: a model trained on many labelled leaf photos. Another example is Bangla speech or text tools, like voice typing in Bangla on your phone, which rely on speech recognition and language processing. These systems can be wrong, so good apps show their confidence and suggest asking an expert.

What AI is not: AI is not magic and it is not a living mind with its own wishes. A search program does not "want" to find the route; it simply follows its algorithm. AI systems can also fail in silly-looking ways: a vision model might misread an image if lighting is unusual, and a chatbot can state false things confidently. Knowing how each method works lets you predict where it will fail, which is one of the most valuable skills you will get from this course.

The course map: We begin with agents and environments (lessons 2 and 3). Then problem formulation and search: uninformed search like BFS and DFS, informed search like A*, local search like hill climbing and genetic algorithms (lessons 4 to 11). Then games with minimax and alpha-beta (12 and 13), constraint satisfaction (14 and 15), logic and reasoning (16 to 20), planning (21), probability and Bayesian networks (22 and 23), and finally an overview of machine learning, language, vision and ethics (24 and 25).

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often write "AI means making computers think like humans" and stop. Exams usually want the four approaches with one line each, and they often ask which approach this course follows (acting rationally) and why. Another favourite is the Turing test: describe its setup and name the abilities needed to pass it. Also, do not mix up AI, machine learning and deep learning. Machine learning is one part of AI, and deep learning is one part of machine learning. Short history questions ask for the Dartmouth workshop (1956) and the meaning of an AI winter.

Recap: AI builds programs that act intelligently. There are four classic views: thinking humanly, acting humanly, thinking rationally and acting rationally, and we follow the rational agent view. The Turing test checks acting humanly. Today's AI is mostly narrow. The field started at Dartmouth in 1956, went through winters and booms, and grew strong with probability, data and fast hardware. Next lesson, we meet the main character of the whole course: the intelligent agent.
key_points: AI is the study of building programs and machines that act intelligently: solving problems, planning, reasoning, learning and deciding.
Russell and Norvig's four views: thinking humanly, acting humanly, thinking rationally, acting rationally.
This course follows the rational agent view: act to get the best expected outcome given what you know.
The Turing test (1950) checks whether a judge can tell a machine from a human by text chat alone.
Almost all real systems are narrow AI; general human-level AI has not been demonstrated.
The term AI comes from the 1956 Dartmouth workshop; the field went through booms and AI winters.
Machine learning is a part of AI, and deep learning is a part of machine learning.
lessons.tip: Keep a small notebook page called "AI around me". Every time you meet an app that searches, plans, recognises or predicts, write which AI area it uses. By the end of the course this page becomes your own revision map.
lessons.task: Pick three apps on your phone (for example a map, a camera, a keyboard). For each, write one line on what "smart" thing it does, and decide which of the four views of AI it fits best and whether it is narrow AI.

quiz.q: Which view of AI does this course (and most modern AI) follow?
quiz.explain: Modern AI is built around rational agents that act to get the best expected outcome given what they know.

options: Whether a program can prove logic theorems
Whether a program runs faster than a human
Whether a program copies human brain steps exactly
Whether a judge chatting by text can tell the machine from a human
quiz.explain: Turing's imitation game: if the judge cannot reliably tell which partner is the machine, it passes.

quiz.q: The name "artificial intelligence" is linked to which event?
quiz.explain: John McCarthy's proposal for the 1956 Dartmouth workshop gave the field its name.

quiz.q: A spam filter that only sorts email is an example of:
quiz.explain: It is good at one specific task only, which is narrow (weak) AI.

quiz.q: Which statement about AI, machine learning and deep learning is correct?
options: They are three names for the same thing
AI is a part of machine learning
Deep learning contains all of AI
Deep learning is part of machine learning, which is part of AI

lessons.title: Intelligent Agents and Rationality
lessons.content:
Think about the security guard at the gate of your apartment building in Dhanmondi. He looks at who is coming (he sees and hears), he checks his register and his memory of residents, and then he acts: he opens the gate, asks a question, or calls the flat on the intercom. He senses, he decides, he acts, again and again all day. In AI language, that guard is an agent. This whole course is about designing good agents, so in this lesson we define exactly what an agent is and what it means for an agent to be "good".

What an agent is: An agent is anything that perceives its environment through sensors and acts upon that environment through actuators. A human is an agent: eyes and ears are sensors, hands, legs and voice are actuators. A robot is an agent: cameras and distance sensors in, motors and grippers out. A software agent, such as a spam filter, also counts: its "sensors" read incoming email text, and its "actuators" move the email to inbox or spam folder. The word "environment" means the part of the world the agent lives in and affects.

Percepts and the percept sequence: A percept is what the agent senses at one moment, for example "the camera sees a red light". The percept sequence is the complete history of everything the agent has ever perceived, from the moment it was switched on until now. An agent's choice of action can depend on that entire history, but never on something it has not perceived. This simple rule is important: an agent cannot react to information it never received.

The agent function: Mathematically, an agent's behaviour is described by an agent function that maps every possible percept sequence to an action. Think of it as a giant, imaginary table: on the left, every possible history; on the right, what the agent does. This is an abstract description, like saying "this person always says sorry after bumping into someone". It tells us what the agent does, not how.

The agent program: The agent program is the real code that runs on the agent's hardware (its "architecture") and implements the agent function. So agent = architecture + program. The function is the mathematical idea; the program is the concrete implementation that receives the current percept and returns an action. Exams love this difference: the agent function is an abstract mapping, the agent program is a concrete program that runs on a physical machine.

Why not just store the table: A naive agent program could literally store the giant table and look up the answer: append the new percept to the history, find that history in the table, return the action. This is called a table-driven agent. It is correct in theory but impossible in practice. If an agent can receive P different percepts and lives for T steps, the table needs P + P^2 + ... + P^T entries. Even with only 10 possible percepts and 20 steps, that is more than 10^20 rows. A camera has billions of possible images per frame. The challenge of AI is to write small programs that produce rational behaviour without such tables.

The vacuum-cleaner world: The textbook's favourite tiny example has just two squares, A and B. Each square can be clean or dirty. A robot vacuum is in one of the squares. Its percept is a pair: [location, status], for example [A, Dirty]. Its actions are Left, Right and Suck. A simple agent program is: if the current square is dirty, then Suck; else if location is A, then go Right; else go Left. Trace it: start [A, Dirty], Suck; now [A, Clean], move Right; [B, Dirty], Suck; [B, Clean], move Left; and so on. Four lines of code replace a huge table.

Rationality: A rational agent is one that does the right thing. But "right" needs a measuring stick, called the performance measure: a score that evaluates the sequence of environment states the agent caused. For the vacuum world, one sensible measure is "one point for each clean square at each time step, over 1000 steps". Then the definition: for each possible percept sequence, a rational agent selects an action that is expected to maximise its performance measure, given the evidence from the percept sequence and whatever built-in knowledge it has.

Four things decide rationality: What is rational at a given time depends on four things. First, the performance measure that defines success. Second, the agent's prior knowledge of the environment. Third, the actions the agent can perform. Fourth, the agent's percept sequence so far. If you change any of these, the rational action may change. For example, if moving costs one point per step, then a vacuum that keeps moving back and forth on clean squares is no longer rational; it should stop when everything is clean.

Is the simple vacuum agent rational: The answer depends on the assumptions, which is exactly the point. Suppose the performance measure gives one point per clean square per time step over 1000 steps, the map is known (two squares, A to the left of B), dirt does not come back once sucked, the only actions are Left, Right and Suck, and the agent always perceives its location and whether that square is dirty. Under these assumptions, the four-line agent is rational: no other agent can expect a higher score. Now change one assumption. If dirt can reappear at random, the agent should keep checking both squares. If the map were unknown and bigger, it would need to explore. Same code, different environment, different verdict.

Is a thermostat an agent: Students sometimes ask whether something as simple as a room thermostat or an automatic street light counts. By the definition, yes: a street light senses darkness (sensor) and switches the lamp on (actuator). It is a very simple agent. The agent idea is not a way of dividing the world into "agents" and "non-agents"; it is a tool for analysing systems. Calling a calculator an agent is allowed, but it does not help much, because its behaviour is fully fixed. The concept becomes useful when the agent must choose among actions in a rich environment.

Design the measure carefully: A classic warning: design the performance measure according to what you actually want in the environment, not according to how you think the agent should behave. If you reward the vacuum "one point per unit of dirt sucked up", a clever agent might suck up dirt, dump it back, and suck it again forever, scoring high while the floor never stays clean. Real-life versions of this problem appear whenever a system is rewarded by a number that does not truly capture the goal.

Rational is not omniscient: An omniscient agent would know the actual outcome of its actions in advance, which is impossible in reality. Rationality only asks for the best expected outcome. Suppose you check both sides of the road and cross Mirpur Road safely, but a loose billboard falls and hits you. Your crossing was still rational; you could not have known. So rationality maximises expected performance, while perfection would maximise actual performance. We judge agents by the first.

Information gathering and learning: Rationality does include doing things to get better information. Looking both ways before crossing is an information gathering action, and a rational agent must do it if it is cheap and useful. A rational agent should also learn from what it perceives. If the agent's designer gave it some prior knowledge, experience should be able to correct or extend that knowledge. An agent that ignores obvious lessons, like a dung beetle that keeps "plugging" its nest even after the ball has been removed, is following a fixed habit, not acting rationally in a changing world.

Autonomy: An agent is autonomous to the extent that it relies on its own percepts and learning rather than only on knowledge built in by its designer. A newborn calf has some built-in reflexes, and then learns the rest. Likewise, a good AI agent should start with useful built-in knowledge but become more independent as it gains experience. Full autonomy from the first second is neither possible nor wise.

PEAS, describing the task environment: Before designing an agent, we specify its task environment with PEAS: Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, Sensors. Writing PEAS first forces you to think clearly about what success means and what the agent can actually sense and do. Almost every university exam has at least one "write the PEAS description" question.

PEAS example 1, an automated taxi: Performance: safe, fast, legal, comfortable trip, low fuel use, maximise profit. Environment: roads, other traffic, pedestrians, customers, weather, police. Actuators: steering, accelerator, brake, indicator lights, horn, a screen or speaker to talk to passengers. Sensors: cameras, radar or lidar, speedometer, GPS, odometer, engine sensors, and a touch screen or microphone for the passenger's destination. Notice that some goals conflict: fastest and safest are not always the same, so the performance measure must balance them.

PEAS example 2, a medical diagnosis system: Performance: healthy patient, lower costs, fewer lawsuits. Environment: patient, hospital, staff. Actuators: display of questions, tests, diagnoses, treatments, referrals. Sensors: keyboard entry of symptoms, findings, test results and patient answers. This shows a software-only agent: no wheels or arms, yet still an agent.

Real life example 1, a smart irrigation pump: Imagine a farmer in Rajshahi with a pump that runs automatically. Performance: crops get enough water, little electricity and water wasted. Environment: the field, soil, weather, the canal or tube-well. Actuators: switching the pump on and off, opening valves. Sensors: soil moisture sensor, rain sensor, a clock. A simple rule like "if soil is dry and no rain is expected, run the pump for 20 minutes" already gives sensible, rational-looking behaviour.

Real life example 2, a bank's Bangla chatbot: Many banks in Bangladesh now offer a chat assistant on their app or Facebook page. Performance: questions answered correctly, quick replies, customers not misled, private data protected. Environment: customers, their messages, the bank's database. Actuators: sending text replies, opening a ticket, handing over to a human officer. Sensors: incoming text messages, account information it is allowed to read. Notice how "hand over to a human" is a rational action when the agent is unsure.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students mix up the agent function and agent program, so remember: function is the abstract mapping from percept sequences to actions; program is the code that runs on an architecture. Many also say "rational means always successful", which is wrong; rational means best expected outcome given the percepts and knowledge. In PEAS questions, students often forget conflicting goals in the performance measure or list sensors under actuators. Typical questions: define an agent and a rational agent, explain the four factors of rationality, write PEAS for a taxi, a vacuum, a part-picking robot or an English tutor app, and explain why table-driven agents are impractical.

Recap: An agent perceives through sensors and acts through actuators. Its behaviour is an agent function from percept sequences to actions, implemented by an agent program running on an architecture. A rational agent picks the action expected to maximise its performance measure, given its percepts and knowledge. Rational is not omniscient, and it includes gathering information and learning. PEAS describes a task environment. Next lesson, we classify environments and look at the main kinds of agent programs.
key_points: An agent perceives its environment through sensors and acts on it through actuators.
The percept sequence is everything the agent has perceived so far; actions may depend on all of it.
The agent function is the abstract mapping from percept sequences to actions; the agent program is the code that implements it.
Table-driven agents are correct in theory but need astronomically large tables.
A rational agent chooses the action expected to maximise its performance measure, given its percepts and built-in knowledge.
Rationality depends on the performance measure, prior knowledge, available actions and the percept sequence.
Rational is not omniscient: it maximises expected, not actual, performance, and includes information gathering and learning.
PEAS (Performance, Environment, Actuators, Sensors) specifies a task environment.
lessons.tip: Whenever you meet a new AI system, force yourself to write its PEAS in four short lines before anything else. It takes one minute and clears up half of the confusion in agent-design questions.
lessons.task: Write the PEAS description for two agents of your choice, for example a rickshaw-hailing app, a robot that sorts mangoes by size, or a quiz app that adapts to your level. Mark any two goals in the performance measure that conflict with each other.

quiz.q: What is the difference between the agent function and the agent program?
options: The function is an abstract mapping from percept sequences to actions; the program is concrete code that implements it
The program is a mathematical table; the function is the hardware
The function only exists for robots, the program only for software agents
quiz.explain: The agent function describes what the agent does; the agent program is how it is implemented on an architecture.

quiz.q: In PEAS, what does the letter A stand for?
quiz.explain: PEAS means Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, Sensors.

quiz.q: A pedestrian checks both sides, crosses carefully, but is hit by a falling billboard. Which is true?
options: The crossing was irrational because the outcome was bad
The pedestrian should have been omniscient
The crossing was still rational, since rationality is about the best expected outcome
quiz.explain: Rationality maximises expected performance given what the agent could know, not the actual outcome.

quiz.q: Why is a table-driven agent impractical?
options: It cannot be rational even in theory
The table needs an entry for every possible percept sequence, which is astronomically large
quiz.explain: The number of possible percept sequences grows like P^T, far too many to store.

quiz.q: Why is "one point per unit of dirt sucked up" a poor performance measure for a vacuum agent?
options: The agent could dump dirt back and suck it again to score points without keeping the floor clean
It is too easy to compute
It makes the environment fully observable
quiz.explain: Measure what you want in the environment (clean floors), not a behaviour that can be gamed.

lessons.title: Environments and Kinds of Agents
lessons.content:
Playing Ludo on your phone and driving a CNG auto-rickshaw through Gulistan are both tasks for an agent, but they feel completely different. In Ludo you see the whole board, the rules never change, and nothing moves while you think. On the road you cannot see behind the bus, other drivers do surprising things, and the scene changes every second. The difficulty of an AI problem depends heavily on the kind of world the agent lives in. In this lesson we learn how to classify environments, and then the five main designs of agent programs, from the simplest reflex to the learning agent.

Why classify environments: If you know the type of environment, you immediately know which techniques will work. A fully visible, rule-fixed puzzle can be solved by the search methods of lessons 4 to 9. A world full of uncertainty needs probability (lessons 22 and 23). A world with opponents needs game methods (lessons 12 and 13). So the first step in any AI design is to describe the environment along a standard set of dimensions. There are seven of them.

Fully vs partially observable: An environment is fully observable if the agent's sensors give it the complete relevant state of the world at each moment. Chess is fully observable: you see every piece. Poker is partially observable: you cannot see the other players' cards. Driving is partially observable: buildings, other vehicles and fog block the view, and sensors are noisy. If the agent has no sensors at all, the environment is unobservable for it. Partial observability is the main reason agents need memory.

Single-agent vs multi-agent: Solving a crossword alone is single-agent. Chess is multi-agent, and competitive: what is good for one player is bad for the other. Driving is multi-agent and partly cooperative: everyone wants to avoid crashes, but drivers also compete for space. A key test: should another entity be treated as an agent? If its behaviour is best described as trying to maximise its own performance measure that depends on what our agent does, then yes. A bus driver is an agent; a falling leaf is just part of the environment.

Deterministic vs nondeterministic (stochastic): If the next state is completely determined by the current state and the agent's action, the environment is deterministic. An 8-puzzle is deterministic: sliding a tile always gives the same result. If outcomes are uncertain, it is nondeterministic; when the uncertainty is described with probabilities, we call it stochastic. Rolling the dice in Ludo is stochastic. Driving is stochastic: tyres can slip and other drivers are unpredictable. Many partially observable environments look stochastic to the agent even if the underlying world is deterministic.

Episodic vs sequential: In an episodic environment, the agent's experience is split into independent episodes; in each, it perceives and then does one action, and that choice does not affect future episodes. A machine that checks each biscuit on a factory belt for cracks is episodic: rejecting one biscuit does not change the next. In a sequential environment, current decisions affect all future decisions. Chess and driving are sequential: one bad move can decide the game. Episodic environments are much simpler because the agent need not think ahead.

Static vs dynamic: A static environment does not change while the agent is deciding. A crossword stays the same while you think. A dynamic environment keeps changing: while the taxi agent thinks, the cars move. If the world itself does not change but the agent's score does with time, it is called semidynamic. Chess played with a clock is the standard example: the board waits, but your clock runs.

Discrete vs continuous: This applies to the state, to time, and to percepts and actions. Chess has a finite number of distinct board positions and moves, so it is discrete. Driving is continuous: speed, position and steering angle take smooth values and change smoothly over time. Computers often handle continuous worlds by cutting them into fine discrete steps, but this choice affects accuracy and speed.

Known vs unknown: This dimension is about the agent's (or designer's) knowledge of the rules, not about the world itself. In a known environment, the outcomes (or outcome probabilities) of all actions are given. In an unknown environment, the agent must learn how the world works. A known environment can still be partially observable: in solitaire card games you know the rules but cannot see the face-down cards. An unknown environment can be fully observable: a new video game shows the whole screen, but you do not know what the buttons do until you try them.

Putting it together: The easiest case is fully observable, single-agent, deterministic, episodic, static, discrete and known. The hardest is partially observable, multi-agent, stochastic, sequential, dynamic, continuous and unknown, and taxi driving in a real city is almost exactly that. A few examples to remember. Crossword: fully observable, single, deterministic, sequential, static, discrete. Chess with a clock: fully, multi, deterministic, sequential, semidynamic, discrete. Poker: partially, multi, stochastic, sequential, static, discrete. Medical diagnosis: partially, single, stochastic, sequential, dynamic, continuous. Image analysis of one photo: fully, single, deterministic, episodic, semidynamic, continuous.

Now, agent programs: We now ask how the inside of an agent should be built. The textbook describes four basic kinds of agent programs, in increasing power: simple reflex agents, model-based reflex agents, goal-based agents and utility-based agents. Any of them can be turned into a learning agent. All of them share the same skeleton: take the current percept, return an action.

Simple reflex agents: These choose an action based only on the current percept, ignoring history. They use condition-action rules, written like "if car-in-front-is-braking then initiate-braking". The vacuum agent from lesson 2 is a simple reflex agent. Pseudo-code: rule = match(interpret(percept), rules); return rule.action. They are fast and simple but work correctly only if the right decision can be made from the current percept alone, which basically means the environment is fully observable. They can also get stuck in infinite loops; a vacuum with no location sensor might move Left forever at the left wall. Adding a little randomness, such as flipping a coin to choose Left or Right, often escapes such loops.

Model-based reflex agents: To handle partial observability, the agent keeps an internal state that tracks the part of the world it cannot currently see. To update this state it needs two kinds of knowledge. A transition model: how the world changes, both on its own and because of the agent's actions ("if I turn the wheel right, the car turns right"; "a car that was overtaking is probably now closer"). A sensor model: how the state of the world shows up in the percepts ("when it rains, the camera image gets droplets"). Then: state = update(state, last action, percept, models); choose a rule using this state. Your memory that a car is in your blind spot, though you cannot see it now, is exactly this.

Goal-based agents: Knowing the current state is not always enough. At a crossroads in Mohakhali, the taxi can turn left, right or go straight; the correct choice depends on where the passenger wants to go. A goal-based agent has goal information describing desirable situations, and it considers the future: "what will happen if I do this, and will it bring me closer to the goal?". Search (lessons 4 to 9) and planning (lesson 21) are the tools for finding action sequences that reach goals. Goal-based agents are more flexible: change the destination and the same agent behaves correctly, while a reflex agent would need all its rules rewritten.

Utility-based agents: Goals only say "happy" or "unhappy". But there are many ways to reach a goal, some faster, safer, cheaper or more comfortable. A utility function maps a state (or sequence of states) to a number that measures how desirable it is. A utility-based agent chooses the action that maximises expected utility, that is, the utility of each possible outcome weighted by its probability. This handles two cases goals cannot: conflicting goals (speed vs safety, with a trade-off) and uncertain goals (several goals none of which is certain to be reached, weighted by likelihood and importance).

Learning agents: Building every rule by hand is slow, and the designer cannot predict everything. A learning agent has four parts. The performance element is the agent we already know: it chooses actions. The critic watches the results and tells how well the agent is doing against a fixed performance standard. The learning element uses the critic's feedback to improve the performance element. The problem generator suggests new, exploratory actions that may be worse in the short term but teach the agent something useful. A taxi agent that gets angry horns after a sudden lane change has received criticism; its learning element should create a rule "avoid sudden lane changes".

How the world is represented inside: Agents also differ in how they represent states. In an atomic representation, a state is a black box with no internal parts, like a city name "Sylhet" in route finding. In a factored representation, a state is a set of variables with values, like fuel = 40%, location = Sylhet, raining = true; CSPs, propositional logic and Bayesian networks use this. In a structured representation, a state contains objects and relations between them, like "the truck is behind the cow, which is blocking the lane"; first-order logic and planning use this. More expressive representations are more compact but reasoning with them is harder.

Real life example 1, a smart traffic signal: Imagine an AI controller at a busy Dhaka junction. The environment is partially observable (cameras miss vehicles in some lanes), multi-agent (drivers, rickshaws, pedestrians), stochastic, sequential, dynamic and fairly continuous. A simple reflex controller that just alternates fixed timings performs badly. A model-based controller estimates queue lengths even for lanes it cannot fully see. A utility-based controller balances total waiting time, fairness to side roads and ambulance priority.

Real life example 2, a Ludo bot: A Ludo-playing app is fully observable (the board is visible), multi-agent and competitive, stochastic (dice), sequential, static while waiting for a move, discrete and known. A good Ludo bot is utility-based: it scores each possible move by safety of its pieces, progress toward home and chances of cutting an opponent, weighting outcomes by the dice probabilities.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often confuse "stochastic" with "partially observable"; one is about outcomes of actions, the other about what the sensors show. Another mix-up is "known" versus "observable": known is about knowing the rules. Chess with a clock is semidynamic, not dynamic. Exams typically give a table of tasks (crossword, chess, poker, taxi, medical diagnosis, part-picking robot) and ask you to fill in each dimension, then ask you to draw and explain the diagram of a model-based or utility-based agent, or the four components of a learning agent.

Recap: Environments are classified as fully or partially observable, single or multi-agent, deterministic or stochastic, episodic or sequential, static, semidynamic or dynamic, discrete or continuous, and known or unknown. Agent programs grow in power from simple reflex to model-based reflex, goal-based and utility-based, and any of them can learn through a critic, a learning element and a problem generator. Next we focus on goal-based agents that solve problems by search, starting with how to formulate a problem.
key_points: Seven environment dimensions: observable, agents, deterministic, episodic, static, discrete, known.
Partial observability means the agent needs memory (internal state) to act well.
Chess with a clock is semidynamic; taxi driving is the hardest kind of environment.
Simple reflex agents use only the current percept and condition-action rules; they need full observability.
Model-based reflex agents keep internal state updated with a transition model and a sensor model.
Goal-based agents look ahead with search and planning; utility-based agents maximise expected utility and handle trade-offs.
A learning agent has a performance element, critic, learning element and problem generator.
States can be atomic, factored or structured.
lessons.tip: Make a seven-column table and fill it for every new example you meet in this course. After ten examples, classifying environments in exams becomes automatic.
lessons.task: Classify three tasks along all seven dimensions: playing carrom with friends, a robot that picks ripe tomatoes in a greenhouse, and an app that translates a Bangla sentence into English. Then say which agent type (reflex, model-based, goal-based, utility-based) you would build for each, and why.

quiz.q: Poker is partially observable mainly because:
options: You cannot see the other players' cards
The cards change while you think
quiz.explain: Hidden cards mean the sensors do not show the full state.

quiz.q: Chess played with a clock is best described as:
quiz.explain: The board does not change while you think, but your performance score (time) does.

quiz.q: What does a model-based reflex agent add to a simple reflex agent?
options: An internal state updated using a transition model and a sensor model
quiz.explain: Internal state lets it handle partial observability by tracking what it cannot see now.

quiz.q: Which part of a learning agent suggests exploratory actions?
quiz.explain: The problem generator proposes new actions that may teach the agent something useful.

quiz.q: Why are utility-based agents more powerful than goal-based agents?
options: They do not need any sensors
They can trade off conflicting goals and handle uncertainty by maximising expected utility
They never need a model of the world
quiz.explain: A utility function rates how good a state is, not just goal or not-goal.

lessons.title: Problem Formulation: Turning a Task into a Search Problem
lessons.content:
Your cousin is coming from Sylhet and asks, "How do I reach your house in Chattogram?" Before you can answer, you quietly do several things in your head. You decide what counts as success (reaching your house), you think about where he is starting from, which buses and trains exist, what each option costs in time and money, and then you look for a good sequence of steps. AI does the same thing, but it must be told all of this precisely. This lesson is about that first, most important step: formulating a problem so that a computer can search for a solution.

Problem-solving agents: A problem-solving agent is a goal-based agent that works in four phases. First, goal formulation: decide what it wants, for example "be in Chattogram". Goals limit what the agent needs to think about. Second, problem formulation: decide which states and actions to consider. Third, search: simulate sequences of actions in its head (in its model) until it finds one that reaches the goal; such a sequence is a solution. Fourth, execution: carry out the actions one by one. If the environment is fully observable, deterministic and known, the agent can execute the whole plan without looking at percepts again, which is called an open-loop system. Otherwise it must keep watching (closed-loop).

The five parts of a problem: A search problem is defined formally by five components. The initial state is where the agent starts, for example In(Sylhet). The actions are what the agent can do in a given state s, written ACTIONS(s); from Sylhet the actions might be Go(Moulvibazar), Go(Sunamganj) and so on. The transition model describes what each action does, written RESULT(s, a), the state you get by doing action a in state s; RESULT(In(Sylhet), Go(Moulvibazar)) = In(Moulvibazar). The goal test checks whether a state is a goal; sometimes it is one state, sometimes a set or a property, like "checkmate". The path cost function gives a number to every path, usually the sum of step costs c(s, a, s'), like kilometres or taka.

State space: The initial state, actions and transition model together define the state space: all states reachable from the initial state by any sequence of actions. You can picture it as a graph. Nodes are states, and directed edges are actions. A path is a sequence of states connected by actions. A solution is a path from the initial state to a goal state, and an optimal solution has the lowest path cost among all solutions. Note: the state space is often far too big to draw or store; the search algorithm explores it bit by bit.

Our practice map: For the next lessons we use a small practice map with six towns: Dhaka, Cumilla, Chandpur, Feni, Noakhali and Chattogram. The road lengths are made-up practice numbers, not exact real distances. Roads: Dhaka-Cumilla 100, Dhaka-Chandpur 90, Cumilla-Feni 60, Chandpur-Noakhali 80, Noakhali-Feni 35, Feni-Chattogram 95, and a long river-and-road route Chandpur-Chattogram 200. Formulation: initial state In(Dhaka); actions Go(neighbour); transition model moves you to that neighbour; goal test In(Chattogram); step cost = road length. The two most obvious solutions are Dhaka-Cumilla-Feni-Chattogram (255) and Dhaka-Chandpur-Chattogram (290). We will see how different algorithms choose between them.

Abstraction, the art of leaving things out: The real journey involves the radio on the bus, the tea break, the potholes and the weather. A good formulation removes all details that do not matter for the decision. This is called abstraction. "In(Cumilla)" stands for millions of possible detailed real situations. An abstraction is valid if every abstract solution can be expanded into a real one; it is useful if carrying out each abstract action is easier than the original problem. Choosing the right level of abstraction is a big part of the skill: too detailed and the search explodes, too vague and the solution cannot be executed.

Toy problem 1, the vacuum world: States: the robot is in one of two squares, and each square may or may not contain dirt, so there are 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 states. Initial state: any of them. Actions: Left, Right, Suck. Transition model: Left in the left square does nothing, Suck in a clean square does nothing, and so on. Goal test: both squares clean. Path cost: 1 per action. With n squares there would be n x 2^n states.

Toy problem 2, the 8-puzzle: A 3x3 board has eight numbered tiles and one blank. A tile next to the blank can slide into it. States: the position of each tile and the blank. Actions are easiest to describe as moving the blank Up, Down, Left or Right (not every action is possible at an edge). Goal test: tiles in order, for example 1 2 3 / 4 5 6 / 7 8 blank. Path cost: 1 per move. There are 9! = 362,880 arrangements, but only half of them, 181,440, can be reached from any given start, because tile moves preserve a parity property. The 15-puzzle (4x4) has about 10^13 reachable states, which already shows how fast state spaces grow.

Toy problem 3, the water jug: You have a 4-litre jug and a 3-litre jug, no markings, and a tap. Get exactly 2 litres in the 4-litre jug. State: a pair (x, y), litres in the big and small jug. Initial state (0, 0). Actions: fill a jug, empty a jug, pour one into the other until the source is empty or the target is full. Goal test: x = 2. One solution: (0,0) fill big to (4,0); pour big into small to (1,3); empty small to (1,0); pour big into small to (0,1); fill big to (4,1); pour big into small until full to (2,3). Six actions. The state space is small, at most 5 x 4 = 20 states, so a computer finds this instantly.

Toy problem 4, the 8-queens and why formulation matters: Place eight queens on a chessboard so no two attack each other (same row, column or diagonal). Formulation A: states are any arrangement of 0 to 8 queens; an action adds a queen to any empty square. There are 64 x 63 x ... x 57, about 1.8 x 10^14, sequences to explore. Formulation B: place queens one per column from left to right, and only in a square not attacked by earlier queens. Now the state space shrinks to just 2,057 states, and solutions are easy to find. Same puzzle, huge difference. A smart formulation can matter more than a smart algorithm.

Incremental versus complete-state formulations: The two 8-queens formulations above are both incremental: you start with an empty board and add one queen at a time. There is another style called a complete-state formulation: every state already has all eight queens on the board, one per column, and an action moves one queen to another square in its column. Here the path does not matter at all; only the final arrangement does. This style is the basis of local search, which we study in lessons 10 and 11. Knowing both styles lets you pick the one that suits the problem.

Step costs and their assumptions: Most search algorithms assume that every step cost is positive, or at least not negative, and that there is some smallest step cost greater than zero. These assumptions sound boring but they matter. If a road had a negative cost, an algorithm might keep driving around a loop to make the total smaller forever. If costs could shrink towards zero, an algorithm might take infinitely many tiny steps. In real problems, costs like distance, time and money are naturally positive, so this is usually fine, but always check when you invent your own cost function.

Counting the cost of a bad formulation: Why do these numbers matter? Suppose your computer checks one million states per second. 2,057 states take about two milliseconds. 1.8 x 10^14 states take about 1.8 x 10^8 seconds, which is more than five years. This is the "combinatorial explosion" that froze early AI. Every time you formulate a problem, quickly estimate the size of the state space before choosing an algorithm.

Real-world problems: Real problems use the same five components but are messier. Route finding powers map apps and airline booking: states include location, time and sometimes fare class; costs combine time, money and comfort. Touring problems, like visiting every city at least once, need the state to include which cities are already visited, not just where you are. The travelling salesperson problem (visit each city exactly once with minimum total distance) is NP-hard. VLSI layout places millions of components on a chip. Robot navigation has continuous states. Automatic assembly sequencing finds the order to put parts together.

States versus nodes, a preview: A state is a situation of the world, like In(Feni). A node is a bookkeeping structure in the search algorithm that contains a state plus extra information, like which node it came from and the path cost so far. The same state can appear in several nodes if it can be reached by different paths. The next lesson builds on this difference.

Real life example 1, a delivery rider: A Foodpanda rider in Dhanmondi must pick up three orders and deliver them. Initial state: rider at the restaurant zone, nothing picked up. Actions: go to a restaurant, go to a customer. Transition model: location changes, and picking up or delivering changes the set of orders being carried. Goal test: all three delivered. Path cost: total travel time, maybe with a penalty for late food. Notice the state must include "which orders are on the bike", not just the location; leaving that out would make the formulation wrong.

Real life example 2, an exam routine: A university wants to schedule final exams. One way to formulate: state is a partial routine (some courses assigned to days), actions assign the next course to a free day, goal test says every course is placed and no student has two exams on the same day, path cost might count students with exams on back-to-back days. Later, in lessons 14 and 15, you will see that this kind of problem is even better formulated as a constraint satisfaction problem.

Common mistakes and exam questions: The biggest mistake is leaving information out of the state that the goal test or actions depend on, like the "orders carried" in the delivery problem. Another is confusing the state space (all reachable states) with the search tree (paths explored). Students also forget the path cost, or write "the goal" instead of a goal test. Typical exam questions: formulate the water jug, missionaries and cannibals, 8-puzzle or 8-queens problem with all five components; compute the state-space size; explain abstraction; and explain why one formulation of 8-queens is better than another.

Recap: A problem-solving agent formulates a goal and a problem, searches for a solution, and executes it. A problem has an initial state, actions, a transition model, a goal test and a path cost. These define the state space, a graph of states. Abstraction removes useless details. Good formulations can shrink a problem from impossible to trivial. Next, we see the general machinery that all search algorithms share: search trees, frontiers and the measures we use to compare algorithms.
key_points: A problem-solving agent: formulate goal, formulate problem, search, execute.
A problem has five parts: initial state, actions, transition model, goal test, path cost.
The state space is the graph of all states reachable from the initial state.
A solution is an action sequence from start to goal; an optimal solution has the lowest path cost.
Abstraction removes details that do not matter; it must still allow the solution to be carried out.
The 8-puzzle has 181,440 reachable states; a smart 8-queens formulation has only 2,057 states.
Always include in the state everything that actions and the goal test depend on.
lessons.tip: For every formulation question, write the five headings first (Initial, Actions, Result, Goal test, Cost), then fill them. Examiners give marks per heading, and it stops you forgetting one.
lessons.task: Formulate the "missionaries and cannibals" puzzle (three of each must cross a river in a two-person boat; cannibals may never outnumber missionaries on either bank). Write the state as a triple, list the actions, and try to find a solution on paper.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the five components of a search problem?
quiz.explain: The five are initial state, actions, transition model, goal test and path cost; heuristics come later.

quiz.q: In the water jug problem with a 4-litre and a 3-litre jug, the state (1, 3) means:
options: 1 litre in the big jug and 3 litres in the small jug
Jug 1 is empty and jug 3 is full
quiz.explain: The state is (litres in the 4-litre jug, litres in the 3-litre jug).

quiz.q: Why is placing queens one per column, only on safe squares, a better 8-queens formulation?
options: It makes the puzzle have more solutions
It allows queens to attack each other
It shrinks the state space from about 10^14 sequences to about 2,000 states
quiz.explain: A smarter formulation can turn an impossible search into a tiny one.

quiz.q: What does abstraction mean in problem formulation?
options: Removing details that do not affect the solution
Adding more detail to every state
quiz.explain: Abstraction keeps only what matters, like using In(Cumilla) instead of every detail of the bus ride.

quiz.q: How many reachable states does the 8-puzzle have from a given start?
quiz.explain: There are 9! = 362,880 arrangements, but only half are reachable from any start.

lessons.title: The Search Framework: Trees, Frontiers and Measures
lessons.content:
Your little brother's cat has gone missing somewhere in the lanes of old Dhaka. You stand at your gate with a notebook. You write down the lanes you could check next. You walk to one, look around, cross it off, and write down the new side lanes you discovered there. You also keep a list of lanes already checked, so you do not waste time going back. Without noticing, you are running a search algorithm. Every AI search algorithm in this course works with the same two lists: places waiting to be explored, and places already explored. This lesson builds that common machinery.

From state space to search tree: In lesson 4 we said the state space is a graph of states connected by actions. A search algorithm explores this graph by building a search tree. The root of the tree is the initial state. Expanding a node means applying every legal action to its state and generating a child node for each result. The children become the next level of the tree. A node with no children yet is a leaf. The tree grows step by step until a goal is found or nothing is left to expand.

Tree versus graph, an important difference: The state space and the search tree are not the same thing. On our practice map, Dhaka connects to Cumilla, and Cumilla connects back to Dhaka. So the search tree contains Dhaka, then Cumilla, then Dhaka again, then Cumilla again, forever. A finite state space with only six towns can produce an infinite search tree, because the tree contains every path, including paths that go round in circles. Search algorithms must handle this, or they may never stop.

What a node contains: A node is a data structure with four or five fields. STATE: the state this node stands for, like In(Feni). PARENT: the node that generated it. ACTION: the action applied to the parent to get here. PATH-COST, written g(n): the total cost of the path from the root to this node. DEPTH: the number of steps from the root. When a goal node is found, we follow PARENT pointers back to the root and reverse the list to get the solution path. Two different nodes can contain the same state if that state was reached by two different paths, for example Feni via Cumilla (g = 160) and Feni via Chandpur and Noakhali (g = 205).

Making a child: The helper CHILD-NODE(problem, parent, action) builds a new node: state = RESULT(parent.state, action), parent = the parent node, action = action, path cost = parent.path_cost + step cost of that action. Example: parent is Dhaka with g = 0, action Go(Chandpur), step cost 90; the child has state Chandpur, g = 90, depth 1.

The frontier: The set of all leaf nodes available for expansion is called the frontier (older books call it the open list). Every search algorithm repeatedly picks one node from the frontier, checks it, and expands it, adding its children to the frontier. The only real difference between most search algorithms is which node they pick next. That choice is made by the data structure used for the frontier. A FIFO queue (first in, first out) gives breadth-first search. A LIFO stack (last in, first out) gives depth-first search. A priority queue that pops the node with the smallest key gives uniform-cost search, greedy search or A*, depending on the key.

Tree search, the basic loop: In words: put the root in the frontier. Loop: if the frontier is empty, return failure. Otherwise remove a node from the frontier. If its state is a goal, return the solution. Otherwise expand it and add all children to the frontier. This is called TREE-SEARCH. It is simple but it does not remember where it has been, so it can loop forever on graphs with cycles and can waste huge time on repeated states.

Redundant paths: Loops are one kind of redundant path. Another kind is simply two different paths to the same state, where one is worse. Think of a city grid where you can move up, down, left or right. A search tree of depth d has about 4^d nodes. But within d steps of the start there are only about 2d^2 different squares. For d = 20, that is about a trillion tree nodes (4^20 is about 1.1 x 10^12) but only around 800 distinct squares. Without detecting repeated states, a search would do over a billion times more work than needed.

Graph search with an explored set: The fix is to remember every expanded state in an explored set (older books call it the closed list). GRAPH-SEARCH works like TREE-SEARCH with two extra rules: after a node is expanded, add its state to the explored set; when generating children, discard any child whose state is already in the explored set or already in the frontier (with some algorithms, we instead replace the frontier node if the new path is cheaper). Now each state is expanded at most once. The explored set is usually a hash table, so checking "have I seen this state?" takes roughly constant time.

The separation property: Graph search has a neat property. The frontier always separates the explored region of the state space from the unexplored region. Every path from the initial state to an unexplored state must pass through some node on the frontier. You can picture an ink blot spreading out from the start: the explored part is inside, the frontier is the edge, and the rest of the world is outside. This picture helps when you try to reason about why an algorithm finds the best path.

A small trace of graph search: Use the practice map and, for now, simply expand nodes in the order they were added (FIFO). Frontier: [Dhaka]. Pop Dhaka; not a goal; explored = {Dhaka}; children Cumilla and Chandpur; frontier [Cumilla, Chandpur]. Pop Cumilla; explored adds Cumilla; its neighbours are Dhaka (explored, discard) and Feni (new); frontier [Chandpur, Feni]. Pop Chandpur; explored adds Chandpur; neighbours Dhaka (discard), Noakhali (new), Chattogram (new); frontier [Feni, Noakhali, Chattogram]. Pop Feni; neighbours Cumilla (discard), Noakhali (already in frontier, discard), Chattogram (already in frontier, discard). Pop Noakhali; nothing new. Pop Chattogram: goal! Path by parent pointers: Chattogram, Chandpur, Dhaka; reversed: Dhaka, Chandpur, Chattogram, cost 290. Notice this is not the cheapest path (255). FIFO order found the path with the fewest steps, not the lowest cost.

When to test the goal: An algorithm can test whether a node is a goal when it is generated (early goal test) or when it is popped for expansion (late goal test). Early testing saves time for breadth-first search. But for algorithms that care about cost, like uniform-cost search and A*, the goal must be tested when the node is popped, because a cheaper path to the goal might still be discovered later. We will see this carefully in lessons 6 and 9.

Measuring search algorithms: We compare strategies with four criteria. Completeness: is the algorithm guaranteed to find a solution when one exists (and to report failure when none exists)? Optimality, also called cost optimality: does it find a solution with the lowest path cost? Time complexity: how long does it take, measured as the number of nodes generated? Space complexity: how much memory does it need, measured as the maximum number of nodes stored at once?

The three letters b, d and m: Complexity in AI is measured with three quantities rather than the size of the whole graph, because the graph is often implicit and enormous. b is the branching factor: the maximum number of children of any node (successors). d is the depth of the shallowest goal: the number of steps along the shortest path from the root to a goal. m is the maximum length of any path in the state space, which can be infinite. For example, in the 8-puzzle b is at most 4 (average about 3), and a typical random puzzle needs d around 20 to 22 moves.

Search cost and total cost: The effectiveness of a search can be judged by search cost (the time and memory used to find a solution) and by the path cost of the solution found. Total cost combines both, for example "minutes of computing plus kilometres of driving". A map app that takes ten minutes to compute a route that saves one minute of driving is not useful. Real systems balance the two: sometimes a good-enough answer found quickly is better than the perfect answer found slowly.

Uninformed vs informed search, a preview: Uninformed (or blind) strategies know nothing about the problem beyond its definition; they can only generate children and recognise a goal. They differ only in the order of expansion: BFS, uniform-cost, DFS, depth-limited, iterative deepening and bidirectional search (lessons 6 and 7). Informed (heuristic) strategies have extra knowledge that estimates how close a state is to a goal, which lets them expand promising nodes first: greedy best-first and A* (lessons 8 and 9).

Real life example 1, finding your phone at home: You think "kitchen, bedroom, drawing room". You check the kitchen (expand it): under the table, near the fridge, on the counter become new places to check (children). Once you check a spot, you do not check it again, which is the explored set. If you always check the most recently thought-of spot first, you are doing depth-first; if you go room by room, level by level, you are doing breadth-first. Most people unknowingly switch strategies, which is why a good mental "explored list" saves so much time.

Real life example 2, a web crawler: Search engines use programs called crawlers that start from some known pages, download them, find links (children), and add new links to a queue (the frontier). They store a huge set of already-seen web addresses (the explored set), usually in hash-based structures, so that the same page is not downloaded again and again. Without that set, a crawler would loop forever between pages that link to each other.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often confuse a state with a node; remember that a node includes parent, action and path cost, and two nodes can hold the same state. Another error is thinking the search tree is the same as the state space; a finite graph can give an infinite tree. Also do not forget that time is counted in nodes generated and space in nodes stored. Typical exam questions: write the TREE-SEARCH or GRAPH-SEARCH pseudo-code, explain the explored set and why it is needed, define completeness, optimality, time and space complexity, and define b, d and m.

Recap: Search builds a tree from the initial state by expanding nodes. Nodes store state, parent, action and path cost. The frontier holds nodes waiting to be expanded, and its data structure decides the strategy. Graph search adds an explored set so that each state is expanded at most once. We judge algorithms by completeness, optimality, time and space, using b, d and m. Next, we meet the first two real strategies: breadth-first search and uniform-cost search.
key_points: A search tree grows from the initial state by expanding nodes into child nodes.
A finite state space can give an infinite search tree because of loops.
A node stores state, parent, action, path cost g(n) and depth.
The frontier holds leaf nodes waiting for expansion; FIFO, LIFO or priority queue decides the strategy.
Graph search adds an explored set so each state is expanded at most once.
Algorithms are compared by completeness, optimality, time and space complexity.
b = branching factor, d = depth of shallowest goal, m = maximum path length.
lessons.tip: When tracing any search algorithm on paper, draw two columns, "Frontier" and "Explored", and rewrite them after every single pop. Most marks in trace questions are lost by skipping a step in your head.
lessons.task: Draw the first three levels of the search tree for the practice map starting at Dhaka, without an explored set. Count how many nodes contain the state Dhaka. Then redo it with an explored set and compare.

quiz.q: What decides whether a search algorithm is breadth-first or depth-first?
options: The data structure used for the frontier (FIFO queue or LIFO stack)
The size of the explored set
quiz.explain: The order in which nodes leave the frontier is the only difference between many strategies.

quiz.q: Why can a finite state space produce an infinite search tree?
options: Because the goal test is wrong
Because the tree contains every path, including loops that go back and forth
quiz.explain: Dhaka-Cumilla-Dhaka-Cumilla... is a valid infinite path in the tree.

quiz.q: What is the explored set used for in graph search?
options: To avoid expanding the same state more than once
quiz.explain: It remembers expanded states so repeated and loopy paths are discarded.

quiz.q: In complexity analysis, what does d stand for?
options: The maximum depth of the state space
The depth of the shallowest goal node
quiz.explain: d is the number of steps on the shortest path to a goal; m is the maximum path length.

quiz.q: Which of these is part of a node but not part of a state?
options: The amount of water in a jug
The pointer to the parent node and the path cost so far
quiz.explain: A node is bookkeeping: state plus parent, action, path cost and depth.

lessons.title: Breadth-First Search and Uniform-Cost Search
lessons.content:
Drop a stone into a still pond in your village and watch the ripples. The first ring touches everything one step away, the next ring everything two steps away, and so on, in perfect circles. Breadth-first search explores a state space exactly like that ripple: first everything one action away, then everything two actions away, and so on. Uniform-cost search is a smarter ripple that grows according to cost instead of number of steps, like water spreading faster along cheap, smooth channels. These are the first two real strategies of the course, and both are the base of many famous algorithms.

Breadth-first search, the idea: Breadth-first search (BFS) expands the shallowest unexpanded node first. The root is expanded, then all its children, then all their children, level by level. It uses a FIFO queue as the frontier: new children join the back of the queue, and the next node to expand is taken from the front. BFS is an uninformed strategy: it does not know which direction the goal lies; it just checks every level completely before moving deeper.

BFS pseudo-code in words: Make a node for the initial state. If it is a goal, return it. Put it in a FIFO frontier and make an empty explored set. Loop: if the frontier is empty, return failure. Pop the front node and add its state to explored. For each action, make the child. If the child's state is not in explored and not in the frontier: if it is a goal, return the solution; otherwise add it to the back of the frontier. Notice the goal test is done when a child is generated. This early test is safe for BFS and saves one whole level of work.

BFS trace on the practice map: Recall the practice map: Dhaka-Cumilla 100, Dhaka-Chandpur 90, Cumilla-Feni 60, Chandpur-Noakhali 80, Noakhali-Feni 35, Feni-Chattogram 95, Chandpur-Chattogram 200. Start Dhaka, goal Chattogram. Frontier [Dhaka]. Pop Dhaka; children Cumilla and Chandpur, neither is the goal; frontier [Cumilla, Chandpur]. Pop Cumilla; child Feni (Dhaka is explored); frontier [Chandpur, Feni]. Pop Chandpur; children Noakhali and Chattogram; Chattogram is the goal, so stop. Solution: Dhaka, Chandpur, Chattogram, 2 steps, cost 290.

A second BFS trace on a tiny tree: Exams often use a letter tree. Let A be the root with children B and C; B has children D and E; C has children F and G; the goal is G. Frontier [A]. Pop A, add B and C: [B, C]. Pop B, add D and E: [C, D, E]. Pop C, generate F (not goal) and G (goal, stop). Expansion order: A, B, C. Nodes generated: B, C, D, E, F, G. Notice that D and E were generated but never expanded; with the early goal test, BFS stops as soon as G appears. If the question says "goal test on expansion", you would also pop D, E and F before G, so always read which version the question wants.

Implementation details: In code, the FIFO frontier is a normal queue, for example collections.deque in Python with append to add at the back and popleft to take from the front, both in constant time. Checking "is this state already in the frontier?" by scanning the queue would be slow, so programs keep a separate hash set of the states currently in the frontier, or one combined set called "reached" that holds every state ever generated. With that set, each membership test takes roughly constant time, and the whole BFS runs in time proportional to the number of states and edges it touches.

What BFS optimises: BFS found a path with the fewest steps, but its cost is 290, while Dhaka, Cumilla, Feni, Chattogram costs only 255. That is not a bug. BFS is optimal only when all step costs are equal (or, more generally, when path cost never decreases as depth increases). In puzzles like the 8-puzzle, where every move costs 1, BFS returns a shortest solution. On a road map with different distances, BFS can be wrong about cost.

Is BFS complete: Yes, if the branching factor b is finite. If a goal exists at depth d, BFS reaches depth d after finishing all shallower levels, and each level is finite. It will find the goal even if the state space is infinite, as long as each node has finitely many children.

BFS time and space: Suppose every node has b children and the shallowest goal is at depth d. The number of nodes generated is b + b^2 + b^3 + ... + b^d, which is O(b^d). Because every generated node stays in memory (either in the frontier or in explored), space is also O(b^d). For b = 2 and d = 3, that is 2 + 4 + 8 = 14 nodes, small. But exponential growth is brutal, as the next paragraph shows.

The numbers that scare everyone: Take b = 10, a computer that generates one million nodes per second, and 1 kilobyte of memory per node. Depth 6: about a million nodes, around one second, about 1 gigabyte. Depth 8: about 100 million nodes, around two minutes, about 100 gigabytes. Depth 12: about 10^12 nodes, around 13 days, about 1 petabyte. Depth 16: about 350 years. Two lessons come out of this table. First, memory runs out long before time does: a normal laptop has 8 or 16 GB of RAM. Second, exponential problems cannot be solved by uninformed search except for small depths.

Uniform-cost search, the idea: When step costs differ, we want the cheapest path, not the shortest. Uniform-cost search (UCS) expands the node n with the lowest path cost g(n). The frontier is a priority queue ordered by g. It is like spreading out from the start in rings of equal cost ("everything within 100 km, then within 150 km...") instead of rings of equal steps.

Two important changes from BFS: First, the goal test is applied when a node is selected for expansion, not when it is generated. The first goal node generated may sit on an expensive path, and a cheaper path to the same goal may still be found. Second, if a child's state is already in the frontier with a higher path cost, the frontier node is replaced by the cheaper one. Both rules are needed for UCS to be optimal.

UCS trace on the practice map: Frontier holds (town, g). Start: [(Dhaka, 0)]. Pop Dhaka 0; add Cumilla 100 and Chandpur 90. Pop the cheapest, Chandpur 90; add Noakhali 170 and Chattogram 290. Pop Cumilla 100; add Feni 160. Pop Feni 160; Chattogram via Feni costs 160 + 95 = 255, which is cheaper than 290, so replace it; Noakhali via Feni would cost 195, worse than 170, so ignore. Pop Noakhali 170; its neighbours are already explored. Pop Chattogram 255; it is the goal, return. Solution: Dhaka, Cumilla, Feni, Chattogram, cost 255, the optimal answer.

Why the late goal test mattered: Look again at the trace. Chattogram was first generated with cost 290 right after Chandpur was expanded. If UCS had tested the goal at generation, like BFS, it would have stopped and returned 290. By waiting until Chattogram was the cheapest node in the frontier, UCS guaranteed that no cheaper path existed. This is the most common trick question about UCS.

Why UCS is optimal: Whenever UCS pops a node for expansion, the path to that node is the cheapest possible. The reason: every other path to that state must leave the explored region through some frontier node, and every frontier node already costs at least as much (since UCS always pops the cheapest one), and step costs are non-negative, so continuing along that path can only add cost. So the first time a goal is popped, its cost is optimal.

Completeness and complexity of UCS: UCS is complete if every step cost is at least some small positive number epsilon. If there were zero-cost actions, UCS could loop forever along a zero-cost cycle (like a "NoOp" action). Its complexity is measured with C*, the cost of the optimal solution: time and space are O(b^(1 + floor(C*/epsilon))). This can be much worse than b^d, because UCS can explore many cheap little steps before trying one big useful step. When all step costs are equal, UCS behaves like BFS (it just finishes the goal's level instead of stopping early).

UCS and Dijkstra: You met Dijkstra's algorithm in the Algorithms course. UCS is essentially Dijkstra's algorithm with two practical changes: it starts with only the initial state in the queue instead of every vertex, and it stops as soon as it pops a goal. This matters for AI because state spaces are often huge or infinite; Dijkstra's usual form, which processes the whole graph, would never finish.

BFS and UCS side by side: Both explore outward from the start and both are complete under mild conditions. BFS measures distance in steps, UCS in cost. BFS uses a plain queue with constant-time operations; UCS uses a priority queue (usually a binary heap) where each insert or pop costs about log of the frontier size. BFS can test the goal early; UCS must test late. BFS is optimal only for equal costs; UCS is optimal for any non-negative costs with a positive minimum. Both store every node they generate, so both run out of memory on large problems, which is the weakness the next lesson attacks.

Real life example 1, friends of friends: Imagine a social app that wants to show how you are connected to someone. Treat people as states and friendships as actions, each of cost 1. BFS from you visits all your friends (level 1), then their friends (level 2), and so on. The first time the target person appears, you have the shortest chain of friends. Because levels grow so fast, real apps limit this to two or three levels, exactly as the exponential table warns.

Real life example 2, cheapest bus journey: Suppose you want to travel from Rangpur to Barishal and care only about ticket price. Each bus route between cities has a fare. UCS keeps a priority queue of "cheapest known total fare to each city". It always expands the cheapest city next, so the first time Barishal is popped from the queue, you have the lowest possible total fare, even if that route has more changes than another. BFS would instead find the route with the fewest buses.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often claim BFS is always optimal; correct this to "optimal when all step costs are equal". Another classic mistake is doing the goal test at generation in UCS. When tracing UCS, many forget to replace a frontier node when a cheaper path appears, or they pop by insertion order instead of by g. Exams usually give a small weighted graph and ask for the order of expansion and the path found by BFS and UCS, the frontier contents at each step, and the complexities O(b^d) and O(b^(1 + C*/epsilon)) with a one-line explanation of each.

Recap: BFS expands level by level with a FIFO queue; it is complete for finite b, optimal for equal step costs, and uses O(b^d) time and space, with memory as the real limit. UCS expands the cheapest node with a priority queue on g(n); it tests the goal at expansion, replaces worse frontier paths, and is complete and optimal when step costs are at least epsilon above zero. Next lesson we turn to strategies that use far less memory: depth-first search and its improved cousins.
key_points: BFS expands the shallowest node first using a FIFO queue.
BFS is complete when b is finite and optimal only when all step costs are equal.
BFS time and space are O(b^d); memory usually runs out first.
UCS expands the node with the lowest path cost g(n) using a priority queue.
