UCS must test the goal when a node is popped, not when it is generated, and must replace costlier frontier paths.
UCS is complete and optimal when every step cost is at least some epsilon > 0; complexity O(b^(1 + floor(C*/epsilon))).
UCS is Dijkstra's algorithm that starts from one state and stops at the goal.
lessons.tip: In any UCS trace, write the frontier sorted by cost after every pop, and circle a node only when it is popped. If you circle the goal when it is first generated, you have done BFS by mistake.
lessons.task: Draw the practice map on paper. Add one more road, Cumilla-Noakhali 50, and redo both the BFS and UCS traces from Dhaka to Chattogram. Does either answer change?

quiz.q: Which data structure does BFS use for its frontier?
options: A priority queue ordered by g(n)
quiz.explain: BFS takes nodes from the front and adds children at the back.

quiz.q: On the practice map, which path does BFS return from Dhaka to Chattogram?
quiz.explain: BFS finds the fewest-step path, which here is the 2-step route costing 290.

quiz.q: Why must UCS apply the goal test when a node is popped?
options: Because a cheaper path to the goal may still be found after the goal is first generated
Because the goal test is expensive
quiz.explain: On the practice map, Chattogram was first generated at 290; popping it later gave 255.

quiz.q: When is BFS guaranteed to find the cheapest path?
options: When the graph has no cycles
When all step costs are equal
quiz.explain: With equal costs, fewest steps means lowest cost.

quiz.q: With b = 10 and d = 12, what is usually the first problem for BFS?
options: Running out of memory, because about 10^12 nodes must be stored
quiz.explain: BFS keeps every generated node, so space O(b^d) explodes before time does.

lessons.title: Depth-First, Depth-Limited, Iterative Deepening and Bidirectional Search
lessons.content:
Remember exploring a big old house at your grandparents' village, the one with long corridors and many rooms. Some children explore it like this: go through the first door, then the first door inside that room, then the first door after that, deeper and deeper, until they hit a dead end; then they come back one step and try the next door. That is depth-first search. It needs very little memory, because you only remember the path behind you. But you might wander into a never-ending corridor and miss the room right next to the entrance. This lesson covers depth-first search, its weaknesses, and three clever fixes.

Depth-first search, the idea: Depth-first search (DFS) always expands the deepest node in the frontier. It uses a LIFO stack: the most recently generated child is expanded next. DFS goes straight down one branch until it reaches a node with no children (or a goal), then backs up to the deepest node that still has unexplored children, and continues. It can also be written very naturally as a recursive function: to search from a node, check it, then recursively search from each child in turn.

DFS trace on a letter tree: Root A has children B and C; B has D and E; C has F and G; goal G. Stack [A]. Pop A, push C then B (so B is on top). Pop B, push E then D. Pop D: no children, a dead end. Pop E: dead end. Pop C, push G then F. Pop F: dead end. Pop G: goal. Expansion order: A, B, D, E, C, F, G. Compare with BFS, which expanded A, B, C and found G at the next level. Here DFS was unlucky and explored the whole left half first.

DFS trace on the practice map: Use the practice map (Dhaka-Cumilla 100, Dhaka-Chandpur 90, Cumilla-Feni 60, Chandpur-Noakhali 80, Noakhali-Feni 35, Feni-Chattogram 95, Chandpur-Chattogram 200). Suppose neighbours are tried in this order: from Dhaka, Cumilla first; from Feni, Noakhali first; and we test the goal when a node is popped, skipping only explored states. Pop Dhaka, go to Cumilla, then Feni, then Noakhali, then Chandpur, then Chattogram. Path: Dhaka, Cumilla, Feni, Noakhali, Chandpur, Chattogram, cost 100 + 60 + 35 + 80 + 200 = 475. A correct path, but a very poor one. DFS simply takes the first route it stumbles into.

Is DFS complete: It depends. The graph-search version (with an explored set) is complete in finite state spaces, because it eventually visits every state. The tree-search version can loop forever: Dhaka, Cumilla, Dhaka, Cumilla... A cheap fix is to check that a new node's state is not already on the current path, which removes loops but not all redundant paths. In infinite state spaces both versions can fail, by running down an infinite branch that never contains a goal.

DFS as recursion: Because DFS always continues from the newest node, it fits recursion perfectly. In words: function DFS(node): if node is a goal, return the path; for each child of node, if the child is not on the current path, result = DFS(child), and if result is a solution, return it; after all children fail, return failure. The program's call stack does the work of the LIFO frontier. This is short and elegant, but on very deep searches the call stack itself can overflow, so large programs often write the loop with an explicit stack instead.

Is DFS optimal: No. As the trace showed, DFS returns the first solution it finds, which may be long and expensive, even when a much better one is close to the root.

Time and space of DFS: In the worst case DFS may generate all nodes up to the maximum depth m, so time is O(b^m), which can be far larger than b^d if m is much bigger than d, or infinite. The big advantage is space. The tree-search version only needs to store the current path from the root plus the unexpanded siblings of each node on that path. That is at most about b x m nodes, so space is O(bm), linear instead of exponential. A further variant called backtracking search generates one child at a time and remembers which child to try next, needing only O(m) memory.

How big is the memory saving: With b = 10, 1 KB per node and depth 16, BFS would need around 10 exabytes of memory (impossible), while DFS needs around 156 kilobytes, less than one photo on your phone. This dramatic difference is why DFS-style ideas are used in so many places, including constraint satisfaction, logic programming and game search, which we will see later.

Depth-limited search: To stop DFS from running down infinite branches, depth-limited search (DLS) gives it a depth limit l: nodes at depth l are treated as if they have no children. This solves the infinite-path problem but introduces new ones. If l is less than d, the shallowest goal is beyond the limit and DLS is incomplete. If l is greater than d, DLS can find a deeper, non-optimal goal. Time is O(b^l) and space O(bl). DLS has two kinds of failure: "failure" means no solution exists at all, and "cutoff" means no solution was found within the limit, but one might exist deeper.

Choosing a depth limit: Sometimes knowledge about the problem gives a good limit. On a map with 20 cities, any solution without repeated cities has at most 19 steps, so l = 19 works. Even better is the diameter of the state space: the largest number of steps needed to get from any state to any other. On our six-town practice map, every town can reach every other town in at most 2 steps, so l = 2 is enough. But for most problems we do not know such a limit in advance, which leads to the next idea.

Iterative deepening search: Iterative deepening search (IDS) runs depth-limited search again and again with limits 0, 1, 2, 3, ... until a goal is found. Pseudo-code: for depth = 0 to infinity: result = DLS(problem, depth); if result is not cutoff, return result. It combines the best of both worlds: like DFS, it uses only O(bd) memory; like BFS, it is complete when b is finite and optimal when all step costs are equal, because it finds the goal at the shallowest depth first.

IDS trace on the letter tree: Limit 0: expand only A; not a goal; cutoff. Limit 1: A, then B and C at depth 1; no goal; cutoff. Limit 2: A, B, D, E, C, F, G; goal found at depth 2. Total nodes visited across all iterations: 1 + 3 + 7 = 11, compared with 7 for one full pass. The repeated work looks wasteful at first glance.

Why the repeated work is cheap: In a tree with branching factor b, most nodes are at the bottom level. In IDS, nodes at depth d are generated once, those at depth d - 1 twice, and so on, with the root's children generated d times. Total: N(IDS) = d x b + (d - 1) x b^2 + ... + 1 x b^d, which is still O(b^d). For b = 10 and d = 5: N(IDS) = 50 + 400 + 3,000 + 20,000 + 100,000 = 123,450, while BFS generates 10 + 100 + 1,000 + 10,000 + 100,000 = 111,110. Only about 11 percent more work, with exponentially less memory. That is why IDS is the preferred uninformed method when the search space is large and the depth of the solution is unknown.

Bidirectional search: Another idea is to run two searches at the same time: one forward from the initial state, one backward from the goal, and stop when the two frontiers meet. The motivation is pure arithmetic: b^(d/2) + b^(d/2) is far smaller than b^d. With b = 10 and d = 6, a single BFS generates about 1,111,110 nodes, while two BFS searches meeting in the middle generate about 2,220. The check "does this new node appear in the other search's frontier?" is done with a hash table.

Limits of bidirectional search: It needs a way to search backwards: we must be able to compute predecessors of a state, which is easy on a two-way road map but hard when actions are not reversible. It also needs an explicit goal state. If the goal is a description like "checkmate", there are many goal positions and searching backwards from all of them is impractical. Memory is still O(b^(d/2)) because at least one side must keep its frontier for the meeting test. And for optimal answers with different step costs, the stopping rule must be designed carefully; the first meeting is not always the best path.

Comparing the uninformed strategies: BFS: complete if b is finite; optimal if step costs are equal; time and space O(b^d). UCS: complete and optimal if costs are at least epsilon; time and space O(b^(1 + floor(C*/epsilon))). DFS: not complete in infinite spaces; not optimal; time O(b^m); space O(bm). DLS: complete only if l is at least d; not optimal; time O(b^l); space O(bl). IDS: complete if b is finite; optimal if costs are equal; time O(b^d); space O(bd). Bidirectional: complete and optimal (with BFS on both sides and equal costs); time and space O(b^(d/2)).

Real life example 1, solving a maze puzzle: In a newspaper maze, most people trace one path with a pencil until they hit a wall, then go back to the last junction and try another branch. That is DFS with backtracking. It works well on paper because a printed maze is finite and you remember where you have been by the pencil marks, which play the role of the explored set. If the maze had an endless corridor, pure DFS could follow it forever.

Real life example 2, chess engines and route planners: Game-playing programs, including chess engines, widely use iterative deepening: they search to depth 1, then 2, then 3, and so on, until their thinking time runs out, and always have the best move from the last completed depth ready to play. Route-planning systems for road networks have also used bidirectional versions of Dijkstra's algorithm, growing one search from your location and one from your destination until they meet, to answer queries faster.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Many students say DFS needs O(b^m) space; the correct answer is O(bm), linear, while time is O(b^m). Many also think IDS is too slow because it repeats work; remember the 123,450 versus 111,110 calculation. Do not forget that DLS can return cutoff, which is different from failure. Exams typically ask: trace DFS, DLS and IDS on a given tree; compute N(IDS) for given b and d; fill in the comparison table of completeness, optimality, time and space; and explain why bidirectional search is faster and when it cannot be used.

Recap: DFS uses a stack, goes deep first, needs only O(bm) memory, but is neither optimal nor always complete. Depth-limited search adds a depth cutoff. Iterative deepening repeats depth-limited search with growing limits, getting completeness and optimality like BFS with memory like DFS, at only a small extra cost. Bidirectional search meets in the middle and cuts b^d down to about 2 b^(d/2), when backward search is possible. Next we give search some knowledge about the goal: heuristics.
key_points: DFS expands the deepest node first using a LIFO stack.
DFS is not optimal and can fail in infinite spaces or loops; time O(b^m), space only O(bm).
Depth-limited search stops at depth l; it can return failure or cutoff, and is incomplete if l < d.
Iterative deepening runs DLS with limits 0, 1, 2, ... ; complete and optimal like BFS, space O(bd) like DFS.
The repeated work of IDS is small: for b = 10, d = 5, about 123,450 nodes versus 111,110 for BFS.
Bidirectional search runs forward and backward searches; about 2 b^(d/2) nodes instead of b^d.
Bidirectional search needs computable predecessors and an explicit goal state.
lessons.tip: Memorise the uninformed-search comparison as a 6-row by 4-column table (BFS, UCS, DFS, DLS, IDS, bidirectional against complete, optimal, time, space). Draw it from memory once a day for a week; it appears in almost every AI exam.
lessons.task: Draw a tree of depth 3 where every node has 2 children (15 nodes, label them A to O level by level). Choose O as the goal. Write the order of nodes visited by BFS, DFS and IDS, and count how many node visits each needed.

quiz.q: What is the space complexity of tree-search DFS?
quiz.explain: DFS stores only the current path plus unexpanded siblings, so memory grows linearly.

quiz.q: What does "cutoff" mean in depth-limited search?
options: No solution was found within the depth limit, but one may exist deeper
The goal was found exactly at the limit
quiz.explain: Failure means no solution at all; cutoff means the limit stopped the search.

quiz.q: Why is iterative deepening preferred over BFS for large problems with unknown depth?
options: It is always faster than BFS
It finds cheaper paths when costs differ
It is complete and (for equal costs) optimal like BFS but uses only O(bd) memory
quiz.explain: IDS keeps BFS's guarantees with DFS's tiny memory, at only a small extra time cost.

quiz.q: With b = 10 and d = 6, roughly how many nodes do two BFS searches meeting in the middle generate?
quiz.explain: 2 x b^(d/2) is about 2 x 1,110, far less than b^d.

quiz.q: What does bidirectional search require that the other uninformed searches do not?
options: A way to compute predecessors and an explicit goal state
quiz.explain: The backward search must step from the goal to its predecessors.

lessons.title: Heuristics and Greedy Best-First Search
lessons.content:
You are new in Chattogram city and want to reach the Patenga sea beach. You do not have a map, but you can see the direction of the sea and feel the wind from it. At every crossing you take the road that seems to point most towards the sea. Most of the time this "rule of thumb" brings you close quickly, even without a map. Sometimes it fools you: the road that points to the sea ends at a canal, and you have to come back. That rule of thumb is a heuristic. In this lesson we give search algorithms heuristics, and look at the simplest way to use them, greedy best-first search.

Informed search: The uninformed methods of the last two lessons treat every direction as equally promising. Informed (heuristic) search uses problem-specific knowledge to guess which nodes are closer to a goal and expands those first. The general pattern is called best-first search: it is the same graph-search loop as before, but the frontier is a priority queue ordered by an evaluation function f(n), and the node with the lowest f is expanded next. Different choices of f give different algorithms. Uniform-cost search is in fact best-first search with f(n) = g(n).

The heuristic function: Most best-first algorithms include a heuristic function h(n) in f. h(n) is the estimated cost of the cheapest path from the state at node n to a goal state. Two simple rules: h(goal) = 0, and h depends only on the state, not on the path used to reach it. A heuristic does not need to be exact; it is an educated guess that is cheap to compute. A perfect heuristic would make search trivial, but computing it usually costs as much as solving the problem.

Straight-line distance: For route finding, the classic heuristic is the straight-line (as the crow flies) distance from a town to the destination. Roads bend around rivers and hills, so road distance is almost always longer than straight-line distance, but the straight line is a good hint of which towns are "towards" the goal. For our practice map, here are made-up straight-line estimates to Chattogram: Dhaka 200, Cumilla 130, Chandpur 120, Noakhali 90, Feni 80, Chattogram 0. Remember the roads: Dhaka-Cumilla 100, Dhaka-Chandpur 90, Cumilla-Feni 60, Chandpur-Noakhali 80, Noakhali-Feni 35, Feni-Chattogram 95, Chandpur-Chattogram 200.

Greedy best-first search: Greedy best-first search expands the node that appears closest to the goal, using f(n) = h(n). It completely ignores how much it has already spent (g). It is "greedy" because at each step it grabs what looks best right now, without thinking about the total.

Greedy trace on the practice map: Frontier ordered by h. Start [Dhaka 200]. Pop Dhaka; add Cumilla (h 130) and Chandpur (h 120). Pop Chandpur, the smallest h; add Noakhali (h 90) and Chattogram (h 0). Pop Chattogram, h 0; it is the goal. Path: Dhaka, Chandpur, Chattogram, total road cost 90 + 200 = 290. Only three expansions, very fast. But the optimal path, Dhaka, Cumilla, Feni, Chattogram, costs 255. Greedy was fooled because Chandpur looks slightly closer in a straight line, yet the only direct road from Chandpur to Chattogram is very long.

Greedy is not optimal: The trace shows the main weakness: greedy search ignores the path cost so far and the true road cost ahead, so it can return a poor solution. It is like always taking the road pointing to the sea, even if it is a muddy detour. Greedy search is useful when you need a solution fast and quality is less important.

Is greedy complete: The tree-search version is not even complete in finite spaces: it can oscillate between two states forever if each one makes the other look closer. A famous textbook example on the map of Romania goes from Iasi towards Fagaras: the heuristic prefers Neamt, a dead end, and tree-search greedy keeps going back and forth between Iasi and Neamt. The graph-search version, with an explored set, is complete in finite state spaces, but not in infinite ones. Worst-case time and space are O(b^m), but with a good heuristic the actual work is often tiny.

Greedy versus uniform-cost, two extremes: It helps to see greedy and UCS as two ends of a scale. UCS looks only backwards, at g(n), the cost already paid; it is careful and optimal but blind about direction, so it spreads out in all directions, even away from the goal. Greedy looks only forwards, at h(n), the estimated cost still to pay; it rushes towards the goal but forgets what the trip has already cost. Neither alone is satisfying. The natural idea is to add the two numbers together, so that each node is judged by the estimated total cost of a complete trip through it. That idea is exactly A*, the star of the next lesson.

Where good heuristics come from: For the 8-puzzle there are no straight lines, so we need other ideas. Two classic heuristics. h1 = the number of misplaced tiles (not counting the blank). h2 = the sum of the Manhattan distances of the tiles from their goal positions, where Manhattan distance is the number of horizontal plus vertical squares between where a tile is and where it should be (named after the grid-like streets of Manhattan; tiles cannot move diagonally).

Worked example for the 8-puzzle: Start state, row by row: 7 2 4 / 5 blank 6 / 8 3 1. Goal state: blank 1 2 / 3 4 5 / 6 7 8. h1: all eight tiles are in the wrong place, so h1 = 8. h2: tile 1 is 3 moves away, tile 2 is 1, tile 3 is 2, tile 4 is 2, tile 5 is 2, tile 6 is 3, tile 7 is 3, tile 8 is 2. Sum: 3 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 2 = 18. The true optimal solution for this start needs 26 moves. Both heuristics underestimate, which is good (as lesson 9 explains), and h2 is closer to the truth.

Never overestimating: Notice why both h1 and h2 can never be more than the true number of moves. Every misplaced tile must move at least once, so the real cost is at least h1. Every tile must travel at least its Manhattan distance, one square per move, so the real cost is at least h2. A heuristic that never overestimates is called admissible. Admissibility is the key property that makes A* optimal, and it is the main topic of the next lesson.

Relaxed problems, a recipe for heuristics: How did anyone invent h1 and h2? Both come from relaxing the rules of the puzzle. The real rule is: a tile can move from square A to square B if A is adjacent to B and B is blank. Drop "B is blank": a tile can move to any adjacent square; the exact solution cost of this easier puzzle is h2. Drop both conditions: a tile can jump anywhere in one move; the exact cost is h1. In general, the cost of an optimal solution to a relaxed problem is an admissible heuristic for the original problem, because the relaxed problem has extra shortcuts, so its solutions can only be cheaper or equal.

Why relaxed heuristics are admissible and quick: Because every move allowed in the original puzzle is also allowed in the relaxed one, every real solution is also a relaxed solution. So the best relaxed solution costs at most as much as the best real one. For this trick to be useful, the relaxed problem must be solvable fast, ideally without search, as with h1 and h2, which are just simple counts.

Dominance: If h2(n) is greater than or equal to h1(n) for every node n, and both are admissible, we say h2 dominates h1. A dominating heuristic is always at least as good for A*: it never expands more nodes (apart from ties). Since a tile out of place has Manhattan distance at least 1, h2 is always at least h1, so h2 dominates h1. The general rule: prefer the larger heuristic, as long as it is still admissible and cheap to compute.

Combining heuristics: If you have several admissible heuristics h1, h2, ..., hk and none dominates the others, take h(n) = max of all of them. The maximum of admissible heuristics is still admissible (each one is at most the true cost, so the biggest one is too) and it dominates every one of them. The price is computing all of them at each node.

Other sources of heuristics: Pattern databases store the exact solution cost for a sub-problem, for example placing just tiles 1, 2, 3 and 4 correctly, for every possible arrangement of those tiles; at search time, a quick table lookup gives an admissible estimate. Heuristics can also be learned from experience: solve many random instances, record features of each state (like h1 and h2) and the true cost, and fit a formula. Learned heuristics may lose the guarantee of admissibility, so they trade optimality for speed.

Real life example 1, a delivery app: A food delivery app might want to suggest the next order a rider should pick up. A greedy rule, "always go to the nearest pending pickup by straight-line distance", is fast and usually decent. But in Dhaka a nearby restaurant may be across a canal or a one-way road, so the greedy choice can lead to a long detour. Smart systems use the straight-line distance only as a quick estimate and then check real road travel times for the best candidates.

Real life example 2, a game character finding a path: In many video games, characters walk around obstacles on a grid map. A heuristic like the Manhattan distance (if the character moves only up, down, left and right) or the straight-line distance (if it can move in any direction) guides the search toward the target. Using greedy search makes characters react instantly but sometimes walk into dead-end rooms; using A* with the same heuristic, as we will see next, gives shortest paths.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students sometimes add g in greedy search; greedy uses only h. Another mistake is calculating Manhattan distance including the blank; the blank is not a tile and is never counted. Some think a bigger heuristic is always better; it is better only while it stays admissible. Exam favourites: compute h1 and h2 for a given 8-puzzle state; trace greedy best-first on a map with a heuristic table and show it is not optimal; explain relaxed problems; define dominance and say which of two heuristics is better.

Recap: Informed search uses a heuristic h(n), an estimate of the cost from n to a goal, inside best-first search. Greedy best-first uses f(n) = h(n): it is fast but not optimal, and incomplete in tree-search form. For the 8-puzzle, misplaced tiles (h1) and Manhattan distance (h2) are classic admissible heuristics that come from relaxed problems, and h2 dominates h1. The max of admissible heuristics is admissible. Next lesson: A*, which combines g and h to get the best of uniform-cost and greedy search.
key_points: Best-first search expands the node with the lowest evaluation function f(n) from a priority queue.
A heuristic h(n) estimates the cost from n to the nearest goal; h(goal) = 0.
Greedy best-first search uses f(n) = h(n); it is fast but not optimal.
On the practice map greedy returns Dhaka, Chandpur, Chattogram (290) instead of the optimal 255.
8-puzzle heuristics: h1 = misplaced tiles, h2 = sum of Manhattan distances; for the textbook start, h1 = 8, h2 = 18, true cost 26.
The exact cost of a relaxed problem is an admissible heuristic for the original problem.
If h2(n) >= h1(n) everywhere and both are admissible, h2 dominates h1 and is better; max of admissible heuristics is admissible.
lessons.tip: For Manhattan distance questions, draw the goal board next to the start board and compute each tile's distance in a small row of numbers, 1 to 8. Add them only at the end. This avoids the most common slip: counting the blank.
lessons.task: Write down this 8-puzzle start: 1 2 3 / 4 blank 6 / 7 5 8, with goal 1 2 3 / 4 5 6 / 7 8 blank. Compute h1 and h2. Then find the actual solution by hand and check that both heuristics are less than or equal to the true number of moves.

quiz.q: Which evaluation function does greedy best-first search use?
quiz.explain: Greedy looks only at the estimated distance to the goal and ignores the cost so far.

quiz.q: For start 7 2 4 / 5 _ 6 / 8 3 1 and goal _ 1 2 / 3 4 5 / 6 7 8, what is the Manhattan distance heuristic h2?
quiz.explain: Tile distances 3, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 2 add up to 18.

quiz.q: Why is a heuristic obtained from a relaxed problem admissible?
options: Every real solution is also a relaxed solution, so the relaxed optimum cannot cost more than the real optimum
It is computed by uniform-cost search
quiz.explain: Relaxation only adds shortcuts, so its optimal cost is a lower bound on the true cost.

quiz.q: h2 dominates h1 means:
options: h1 and h2 are always equal
h2(n) >= h1(n) for every node, with both admissible
quiz.explain: A dominating admissible heuristic is closer to the true cost and never expands more nodes in A*.

quiz.q: You have three admissible heuristics and none dominates the others. What is a good combined heuristic?
quiz.explain: The max is still admissible and dominates each one; the sum may overestimate.

lessons.title: A* Search: Optimal Search with a Good Guess
lessons.content:
Imagine two friends planning a trip from Dhaka to Chattogram. One only looks back: "We have spent 100 km so far, that is cheap, let's continue from here." The other only looks forward: "This town looks close to Chattogram, let's go there." Both make mistakes. A third friend says: "For each town, add what we have already travelled to what we still expect to travel. Go through the town where this total is smallest." That third friend is thinking like A*, the most famous search algorithm in AI. A* (pronounced "A-star") is used in maps, games and robots, and it is the heart of this lesson.

The A* idea: A* is best-first search with the evaluation function f(n) = g(n) + h(n). Here g(n) is the actual cost of the path from the start to node n, and h(n) is the heuristic estimate of the cheapest cost from n to a goal. So f(n) is the estimated cost of the cheapest complete solution that passes through n. A* always expands the node with the smallest f. It uses a priority queue, tests the goal when a node is popped (like UCS), and replaces a frontier node when a cheaper path to the same state is found.

The practice map again: Roads: Dhaka-Cumilla 100, Dhaka-Chandpur 90, Cumilla-Feni 60, Chandpur-Noakhali 80, Noakhali-Feni 35, Feni-Chattogram 95, Chandpur-Chattogram 200. Heuristic h (made-up straight-line estimates to Chattogram): Dhaka 200, Cumilla 130, Chandpur 120, Noakhali 90, Feni 80, Chattogram 0. Last lesson, greedy search, using only h, returned the 290 path.

A* trace, step 1 and 2: Start: Dhaka with g = 0, h = 200, f = 200. Pop Dhaka. Children: Cumilla with g = 100, f = 100 + 130 = 230; Chandpur with g = 90, f = 90 + 120 = 210. Frontier: Chandpur 210, Cumilla 230. Pop Chandpur (smallest f). Children: Noakhali with g = 90 + 80 = 170, f = 170 + 90 = 260; Chattogram with g = 90 + 200 = 290, f = 290 + 0 = 290. Frontier: Cumilla 230, Noakhali 260, Chattogram 290.

A* trace, step 3 to the end: Pop Cumilla (230). Child: Feni with g = 160, f = 160 + 80 = 240. Frontier: Feni 240, Noakhali 260, Chattogram 290. Pop Feni (240). Children: Chattogram via Feni with g = 255, f = 255, which is better than the 290 in the frontier, so replace it; Noakhali via Feni would have g = 195, worse than 170, so ignore. Frontier: Chattogram 255, Noakhali 260. Pop Chattogram (255): it is the goal. Solution: Dhaka, Cumilla, Feni, Chattogram, cost 255, the optimal path.

What A* saved: Compare with uniform-cost search from lesson 6. UCS expanded Dhaka, Chandpur, Cumilla, Feni, Noakhali and then Chattogram. A* expanded Dhaka, Chandpur, Cumilla, Feni and Chattogram; it never expanded Noakhali, because Noakhali's f value (260) was higher than the cost of the solution (255). On a six-town map that saves one step; on a map of all of Bangladesh, a good heuristic stops A* from exploring towns in the wrong direction, like Rangpur or Sylhet, saving enormous work.

Admissible heuristics: A heuristic is admissible if it never overestimates the true cost to reach the goal: h(n) <= h*(n) for every node n, where h*(n) is the real cheapest cost. Straight-line distance is admissible because no road can be shorter than a straight line. Check our map: the true cheapest cost from Chandpur to Chattogram is 200 (direct road) and h(Chandpur) = 120, fine; from Dhaka the true cost is 255 and h = 200, fine; from Noakhali the true cost is 130 (via Feni) and h = 90, fine. An admissible heuristic is optimistic: it always thinks the goal is at least as close as it really is.

Why admissible means optimal (tree search): Suppose a worse goal node G2 with cost g(G2) > C* (the optimal cost) is sitting in the frontier. Somewhere on the optimal path there is a node n that is also in the frontier (by the separation property). Because h is admissible, f(n) = g(n) + h(n) <= C*. And f(G2) = g(G2) + 0 > C*. So f(n) < f(G2), and A* will always pop n before G2. Following this argument along the optimal path, A* reaches the optimal goal before it ever pops G2. So with an admissible heuristic, the tree-search version of A* is optimal.

Consistent heuristics: For the graph-search version (with an explored set), we usually need a slightly stronger property called consistency (or monotonicity). h is consistent if, for every node n and every successor n' reached by action a, h(n) <= c(n, a, n') + h(n'). This is a triangle inequality: the estimate from n should not be more than the cost of one step plus the estimate from the next node. Check one edge: Dhaka to Chandpur: 200 <= 90 + 120 = 210, true. Dhaka to Cumilla: 200 <= 100 + 130 = 230, true. Every edge of our map passes this test, so our heuristic is consistent.

Why consistency matters: With a consistent heuristic, f values never decrease along any path: f(n') = g(n) + c + h(n') >= g(n) + h(n) = f(n). That means the sequence of nodes A* pops has non-decreasing f, and the first time A* pops any state, it has already found the cheapest path to it. So A* never needs to reopen an explored state. Every consistent heuristic is also admissible (but a few admissible ones are not consistent). In practice, most natural admissible heuristics, like straight-line distance and Manhattan distance, are consistent.

Contours: A nice picture: with a consistent heuristic, A* expands nodes in bands of increasing f, like contour lines on a hill map. First everything with f below 210, then below 230, and so on, until the contour reaches the goal's cost C*. A* expands all nodes with f(n) < C*, possibly some with f(n) = C*, and none with f(n) > C*. With h = 0 everywhere, the contours become circles around the start, and A* becomes uniform-cost search. The better the heuristic, the more the contours stretch towards the goal.

Ties and how to break them: Often two frontier nodes have the same f value. Any choice keeps A* optimal, but the choice changes how much work is done. A common rule is to prefer the node with the larger g (equivalently, the smaller h), because it is further along its path and probably closer to the goal. On a grid with many equal-cost routes, good tie-breaking can cut the number of expanded nodes a lot. In exam traces, if the question does not say how to break ties, state your rule (for example "alphabetical") in one line before you start.

Properties of A*: A* is complete as long as the branching factor is finite and every step cost is at least some positive epsilon. With an admissible heuristic (tree search) or a consistent heuristic (graph search), A* is cost-optimal. It is also optimally efficient: among optimal algorithms that extend paths from the start and use the same heuristic, none is guaranteed to expand fewer nodes than A* (apart from tie-breaking), because any algorithm that skipped a node with f(n) < C* could miss a better solution.

The catch, memory: A* keeps every generated node in memory, so on large problems it usually runs out of memory long before it runs out of time. Its time and space depend on the heuristic error; with a poor heuristic, the number of nodes is still exponential in the solution depth. For large puzzles A* alone is not practical.

Memory-bounded variants: Iterative deepening A* (IDA*) applies the idea of iterative deepening to f: each iteration is a depth-first search that cuts off any node whose f exceeds the current limit; the next limit is the smallest f that was cut off. IDA* uses memory linear in the solution depth and is optimal with an admissible heuristic, and it is a standard method for puzzles like the 15-puzzle. Recursive best-first search (RBFS) and simplified memory-bounded A* (SMA*) are other variants that use limited memory.

Weighted A*: Sometimes a good answer quickly is better than the best answer slowly. Weighted A* uses f(n) = g(n) + W x h(n) with W > 1. It trusts the heuristic more and expands fewer nodes. The price: the solution may not be optimal, but with an admissible h its cost is at most W times the optimal cost. For example, with W = 1.5, the path is at most 50 percent longer than the best one, and often much closer.

Effective branching factor: How do we measure a heuristic's quality in experiments? If A* generates N nodes to find a solution at depth d, the effective branching factor b* is the branching factor that a uniform tree of depth d would need to contain N + 1 nodes: N + 1 = 1 + b* + (b*)^2 + ... + (b*)^d. For example, if a solution at depth 5 needed 52 nodes, b* is about 1.92. A good heuristic gives b* close to 1. In the textbook's experiments on random 8-puzzles of solution length 12, iterative deepening generated millions of nodes, while A* with misplaced tiles needed a few hundred and A* with Manhattan distance less than a hundred.

Real life example 1, video game path finding: In strategy and adventure games, when you click a spot on the map, your character must walk there around walls, rivers and buildings. A* on a grid of tiles, with Manhattan or straight-line distance as the heuristic, has been the standard tool for this for decades. Game developers often use weighted A* or simplified maps to keep it fast when hundreds of characters move at once.

Real life example 2, a warehouse robot: Picture an e-commerce warehouse near Dhaka where small robots carry shelves to packing stations. The floor is a grid, some cells are blocked by shelves, and robots must reach a target cell quickly. A* with Manhattan distance gives each robot a shortest path. When many robots share the floor, planners combine A*-style search with rules for avoiding collisions, but A* remains the basic building block.

Common mistakes and exam questions: The biggest mistake in traces is forgetting to replace a frontier node when a cheaper path appears, or stopping when the goal is first generated. Another is mixing up admissible and consistent; remember consistent is the triangle rule on every edge, and it implies admissible. Some students believe A* is optimal with any heuristic; it needs admissibility (or consistency for graph search). Typical questions: trace A* on a given graph with an h table, showing g, h and f at each step; check whether a heuristic is admissible or consistent; prove A* optimality with admissible h; and explain IDA* or weighted A*.

Recap: A* expands the node with the lowest f(n) = g(n) + h(n). It is complete, and optimal when h is admissible (tree search) or consistent (graph search). It is optimally efficient among such algorithms, but its memory use is its weakness, which IDA*, RBFS and SMA* address. Weighted A* trades a bounded amount of optimality for speed. Good heuristics push the effective branching factor towards 1. Next, we leave paths behind and look at local search, where only the final state matters.
key_points: A* expands the node with the smallest f(n) = g(n) + h(n), the estimated total cost through n.
On the practice map A* finds the optimal 255 path and never expands Noakhali (f = 260).
Admissible: h(n) never overestimates the true cost; this makes tree-search A* optimal.
Consistent: h(n) <= c(n, a, n') + h(n') for every edge; this makes graph-search A* optimal, and implies admissibility.
A* expands every node with f < C*; with h = 0 it becomes uniform-cost search.
A* is complete and optimally efficient, but stores all nodes, so memory is its weakness.
IDA* uses an f-cost cutoff with depth-first search; weighted A* uses g + W x h for faster, bounded-suboptimal answers.
lessons.tip: In every A* trace, write each frontier entry as "Town (g + h = f)". Writing g and h separately makes replacement decisions obvious and lets the examiner give you marks even if you slip once.
lessons.task: Add a new road to the practice map: Cumilla-Noakhali 40. Check whether the heuristic table is still consistent on that edge, then redo the A* trace from Dhaka to Chattogram. Does the answer or the order of expansion change?

quiz.q: What does f(n) represent in A*?
options: The cost from the start to n only
The estimated cost from n to the goal only
The estimated cost of the cheapest complete solution through n
quiz.explain: f(n) = g(n) + h(n): cost already paid plus estimated cost still to pay.

quiz.q: A heuristic is admissible if:
options: It never overestimates the true cost to reach the goal
It always equals the true cost
It is larger than the true cost
It is zero everywhere except the goal
quiz.explain: Admissible heuristics are optimistic: h(n) <= h*(n).

quiz.q: Which condition is the consistency (triangle) rule?
options: h(n) <= c(n, a, n') + h(n') for every successor n'
quiz.explain: The estimate from n must not exceed one step's cost plus the estimate from the next node.

quiz.q: On the practice map, why does A* never expand Noakhali?
options: Noakhali was in the explored set from the start
Its f value (260) is higher than the optimal solution cost (255)
quiz.explain: A* expands only nodes with f below the optimal cost (and maybe some equal to it).

quiz.q: What does weighted A* with W = 2 guarantee when h is admissible?
options: A solution costing at most twice the optimal cost
A solution with at most 2 steps
quiz.explain: Weighted A* is bounded-suboptimal: cost at most W times the optimum.

lessons.title: Local Search and Hill Climbing
lessons.content:
Imagine you are dropped at night somewhere in the hills of Bandarban with a weak torch, and you want to reach the highest peak. You cannot see the whole landscape. All you can do is feel the ground around your feet and step in the direction that goes up most steeply. Step by step you climb, and when every direction goes down, you stop. You may be on the real summit, or only on a small hilltop, with the true peak hidden in the dark across a valley. That is hill climbing, the simplest local search algorithm, and its strength and weakness are both in this picture.

When the path does not matter: In the search problems so far, the answer was a path: a sequence of actions from start to goal. But in many problems only the final state matters. In 8-queens we only care about the final board, not the order in which queens were placed. In an exam timetable we want a good routine, not the history of how we built it. Other examples: placing components on a chip, designing a factory floor, scheduling buses, tuning the settings of a machine. For these, keeping a search tree full of paths wastes memory.

Local search: Local search algorithms keep only one current state (or a few), and repeatedly move to a neighbouring state. They do not remember paths. This gives two big advantages: they use very little memory, usually a constant amount, and they can find reasonable solutions in huge or even infinite (continuous) state spaces where systematic search is hopeless. They are also natural for optimisation problems, where the goal is to find the best state according to an objective function, not just any goal state.

The state-space landscape: A helpful picture is the landscape. Put every state along the ground (location) and draw its objective value as the height (elevation). If we want to maximise the value, we look for the highest peak, the global maximum. If the value is a cost to minimise, we look for the lowest valley, the global minimum; the two views are the same with the sign flipped. A complete local search algorithm always finds a goal if one exists; an optimal one always finds the global best.

Hill climbing: Hill climbing (steepest-ascent version) is a loop: look at all neighbours of the current state; if the best neighbour is not better than the current state, stop and return the current state; otherwise move to the best neighbour. In pseudo-code: current = initial state; loop: neighbour = highest-valued successor of current; if value(neighbour) <= value(current) then return current; current = neighbour. It is sometimes called greedy local search, because it grabs the best immediate neighbour without thinking ahead.

A tiny landscape trace: Let states be the numbers 0 to 9, neighbours are x - 1 and x + 1, and the values are: x = 0 gives 2, 1 gives 4, 2 gives 6, 3 gives 5, 4 gives 3, 5 gives 4, 6 gives 7, 7 gives 9, 8 gives 8, 9 gives 5. Start at x = 0 (value 2). Best neighbour is 1 (value 4): move. From 1, best neighbour is 2 (value 6): move. From 2, neighbours are 1 (4) and 3 (5), both worse: stop at x = 2 with value 6. But the global maximum is x = 7 with value 9. Hill climbing got stuck on a local maximum.

8-queens as local search: Use a complete-state formulation: every state has 8 queens on the board, one per column. A move takes one queen and moves it to another square in the same column, so each state has 8 x 7 = 56 neighbours. The cost h is the number of pairs of queens that attack each other, directly or diagonally. A solution has h = 0. Hill climbing (descending on h) looks at all 56 neighbours, picks one with the lowest h, and repeats. The space has 8^8, about 16.8 million, states, but hill climbing looks at only a tiny part of it.

Counting h on a small board: Practise on 4 queens, one per column, rows numbered 1 to 4 from the top. Write a state as the row of the queen in each column. The state (1, 2, 3, 4) puts all queens on one diagonal, so every pair attacks: 4 queens make 4 x 3 / 2 = 6 pairs, and h = 6. Two queens attack diagonally when the difference of their rows equals the difference of their columns. The state (2, 4, 1, 3) has h = 0: check column 1 and column 2, rows 2 and 4 differ by 2 while columns differ by 1, so no attack, and every other pair passes the same test. That state is a solution. Hill climbing tries to move from boards like the first towards boards like the second, one queen move at a time.

How well does it do on 8-queens: The textbook reports that, starting from a random board, steepest-ascent hill climbing gets stuck about 86 percent of the time and solves only about 14 percent of instances. But it is very fast: about 4 steps on average when it succeeds and about 3 when it gets stuck. Fast but often stuck: that is the typical behaviour.

Why it gets stuck, local maxima: A local maximum is a peak that is higher than each of its neighbours but lower than the global maximum. Hill climbing that reaches the neighbourhood of a local maximum is pulled up to it and stops, as in the tiny trace above. In 8-queens, there are boards where every single queen move increases the number of attacking pairs, yet h is not zero.

Why it gets stuck, ridges: A ridge is a sequence of local maxima that rises slowly in a direction that no single move follows. Imagine a narrow mountain path running diagonally while you are only allowed to step north, south, east or west: every allowed step goes downhill, even though the ridge itself keeps rising. Ridges are very hard for hill climbing.

Why it gets stuck, plateaus: A plateau is a flat area where neighbours have the same value. It can be a flat local maximum, from which no uphill exit exists, or a shoulder, a flat area from which progress is possible further along. On a plateau, hill climbing has no direction to follow and stops (the strict version requires a better neighbour).

Sideways moves: One fix for shoulders is to allow sideways moves: if no neighbour is better, move to one with an equal value. But this can loop forever on a flat local maximum, so we put a limit, for example at most 100 sideways moves in a row. In the textbook's 8-queens experiment, this raises the success rate from about 14 percent to about 94 percent. The cost: successful runs take about 21 steps on average, and failures about 64.

Stochastic and first-choice hill climbing: Stochastic hill climbing chooses randomly among the uphill moves, with steeper moves more likely. It usually converges more slowly but sometimes finds better solutions. First-choice hill climbing generates neighbours randomly one at a time and moves to the first one that is better than the current state. This is useful when a state has thousands of neighbours and checking them all would be slow.

Random-restart hill climbing: The most powerful simple fix is: if you get stuck, start again from a new random state. Random-restart hill climbing runs hill climbing many times from random initial states until a goal is found. If each run succeeds with probability p, the expected number of runs is 1/p. For 8-queens without sideways moves, p is about 0.14, so about 7 runs are needed on average, each only a few steps. With sideways moves, p is about 0.94 and you rarely need a second run. The textbook notes that, for 8-queens, this approach is very effective even for millions of queens. Its practical motto: "If at first you do not succeed, try, try again."

When hill climbing works well or badly: Success depends on the shape of the landscape. If there are few local maxima and plateaus, random-restart hill climbing finds a good solution very quickly. Many real problems have a landscape that looks like a hedgehog's back, full of small spikes; there, hill climbing finds a reasonable local maximum quickly but rarely the global one. This motivates the smarter methods of the next lesson.

Continuous spaces, a brief note: If the state is a set of real numbers, such as the positions of three airports to minimise travel distance for a city's people, there are infinitely many neighbours. Then we use the gradient, the direction of steepest increase, computed by calculus: x = x + alpha x gradient f(x), where alpha is a small step size. This is gradient ascent (or gradient descent when minimising). The same idea, on a giant scale, is how neural networks are trained, as you will see in lesson 24.

Real life example 1, an exam hall seating plan: A college in Khulna wants to seat 120 students so that no two students from the same section sit side by side. Start with a random seating, count the "bad pairs" (same-section neighbours), and repeatedly swap two students if the swap lowers the count. This is hill climbing on a cost function. If it gets stuck at, say, 3 bad pairs, restart from a new random seating or allow a few sideways swaps. Usually a plan with zero bad pairs appears quickly.

Real life example 2, placing mobile towers: A telecom company wants to place new towers in a district to cover as many villages as possible. The state is a set of tower positions, the objective is the number of people covered, and a move shifts one tower to a nearby site. Hill climbing improves coverage step by step. Because different starting layouts lead to different local maxima, engineers run several starts and compare, which is random restart in real life.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students sometimes think hill climbing is complete or optimal; it is neither, it stops at the first peak it reaches. Another error is confusing a shoulder (escape possible with sideways moves) with a flat local maximum (no escape). Do not mix up the cost view (minimise h) and the objective view (maximise value); just keep the direction consistent. Typical questions: write the hill-climbing pseudo-code; define local maximum, ridge, plateau and shoulder with a sketch; compute h for a given 8-queens board; explain random restart and why its expected number of runs is 1/p.

Recap: Local search keeps only the current state and moves to neighbours, using little memory and working for optimisation and huge spaces. Hill climbing always takes the best uphill move and stops at a peak, so it gets stuck at local maxima, ridges and plateaus. Sideways moves, stochastic and first-choice variants, and especially random restarts improve it greatly. Next lesson, we let the search take some downhill steps on purpose (simulated annealing) and borrow ideas from evolution (genetic algorithms).
key_points: Local search keeps only the current state and moves to neighbours; useful when only the final state matters.
Local search uses very little memory and suits optimisation problems with an objective function.
Steepest-ascent hill climbing moves to the best neighbour and stops when no neighbour is better.
8-queens: each state has 56 neighbours; h = number of attacking pairs; hill climbing solves only about 14% of random starts.
Hill climbing gets stuck at local maxima, ridges and plateaus (flat local maxima or shoulders).
Allowing up to 100 sideways moves raises 8-queens success to about 94%.
Random-restart hill climbing needs about 1/p runs on average, where p is the success chance of one run.
lessons.tip: When a question gives you a landscape picture, label every feature (global maximum, local maximum, shoulder, flat local maximum) before writing anything. Most hill-climbing theory questions are answered by pointing to the right part of that sketch.
lessons.task: Draw an 8x8 board and place 8 queens one per column at random (roll a die twice or use your phone's random number for each column). Count the attacking pairs h. Then try moving one queen within its column to reduce h, and repeat until you are stuck. Record how many moves you made and the final h.

quiz.q: What does local search store while it runs?
options: Only the current state (or a few states)
The explored set of every state
quiz.explain: Local search does not keep paths, so it uses very little memory.

quiz.q: In the tiny landscape trace (values 2, 4, 6, 5, 3, 4, 7, 9, 8, 5), where does hill climbing from x = 0 stop?
quiz.explain: From x = 2 both neighbours are worse, so it stops at a local maximum.

quiz.q: In the 8-queens formulation where each queen moves within its column, how many neighbours does each state have?
quiz.explain: Each of 8 queens can move to 7 other squares in its column: 8 x 7 = 56.

quiz.q: A flat area from which uphill progress is possible further along is called:
quiz.explain: A shoulder is a plateau with an uphill exit; sideways moves can help escape it.

quiz.q: If one hill-climbing run succeeds with probability p = 0.25, about how many random restarts are expected?
quiz.explain: The expected number of runs is 1/p = 4.

lessons.title: Simulated Annealing, Local Beam Search and Genetic Algorithms
lessons.content:
A blacksmith in a village bazaar heats a piece of iron until it glows, then lets it cool slowly while shaping it. If he cools it too fast, by dropping it in cold water, the metal becomes brittle and cracks easily. Cooled slowly, its tiny crystals have time to settle into a strong, low-energy arrangement. Strangely, this old craft gave AI one of its best search methods. In this lesson we learn three ways to escape the traps of hill climbing: simulated annealing (inspired by cooling metal), local beam search (many climbers sharing information) and genetic algorithms (inspired by evolution).

The problem we are solving: Hill climbing never goes downhill, so it gets stuck at local maxima. A purely random walk, moving to a random neighbour every time, will eventually wander everywhere and find the global maximum, but it is incredibly slow. The idea of simulated annealing is to combine the two: mostly go uphill, but sometimes, on purpose, accept a downhill move, especially early on, to escape local traps.

Simulated annealing, the algorithm: At each step, pick a random neighbour (not the best one). Compute delta E = value(neighbour) - value(current). If delta E is positive (the move is better), always accept it. If delta E is negative (worse), accept it only with probability e^(delta E / T), where T is a number called the temperature. Then lower T a little according to a schedule. When T reaches (nearly) zero, stop and return the current state. In pseudo-code: for t = 1, 2, 3, ...: T = schedule(t); if T = 0 return current; next = random neighbour; delta E = value(next) - value(current); if delta E > 0 then current = next, else current = next only with probability e^(delta E / T).

Feeling the formula with numbers: Suppose a move makes things worse by 2 (delta E = -2). At a high temperature T = 10, the acceptance probability is e^(-0.2), about 0.82, so bad moves are accepted most of the time. At T = 1, it is e^(-2), about 0.14. At T = 0.1, it is e^(-20), about 0.000000002, practically never. Also, a slightly bad move is accepted more often than a very bad one: at T = 10, delta E = -1 is accepted with probability about 0.90, but delta E = -5 only about 0.61, and at T = 1, delta E = -5 drops to about 0.007.

What temperature does: At the start, T is high, so the search wanders widely, jumping out of small valleys and exploring the landscape. As T falls, bad moves become rarer, and the search behaves more and more like hill climbing, settling into the best peak in the region it has reached. This is exactly like the blacksmith's metal: hot atoms move around freely; as it cools they settle into a strong, low-energy state.

The schedule and its guarantee: The cooling schedule decides how fast T falls. A common choice is geometric cooling: T = T x 0.95 after each step or batch of steps. Theory says that if the temperature is lowered slowly enough, simulated annealing finds a global optimum with probability approaching 1. The catch is that "slowly enough" can be extremely slow, so in practice we pick a schedule by experiment: fast enough to finish in reasonable time, slow enough to give good answers.

Where simulated annealing has been used: It became popular in the 1980s for VLSI layout, the problem of placing millions of components on a chip to keep wires short. It has also been widely used in scheduling problems, such as factory and airline scheduling, and other large optimisation problems where the landscape is bumpy and exact methods are too slow.

Local beam search: Instead of one current state, local beam search keeps k states. It starts with k random states. At each step it generates all successors of all k states. If any is a goal, it stops. Otherwise it selects the k best successors from the whole pool and repeats. For example, with k = 3, if each state has 10 successors, it looks at 30 candidates and keeps the best 3.

Beam search is not just k restarts: In random-restart hill climbing, the k runs are independent; each one has no idea what the others are doing. In local beam search the k states share information: if one state finds a great region, many of the best successors will come from it, and the search effectively says "come over here, the hills are higher". Unpromising searches are abandoned and their effort moves to promising areas.

The weakness and the fix: Local beam search can quickly lose diversity: all k states may end up crowded on the same small hill, so it becomes an expensive version of hill climbing. Stochastic beam search fixes this by choosing the k successors randomly, with the probability of choosing a successor increasing with its value. Good states are more likely to survive, but weaker ones sometimes survive too, keeping variety. This looks a lot like natural selection, which leads us to genetic algorithms.

Genetic algorithms, the idea: A genetic algorithm (GA) is a stochastic beam search in which new states are made by combining two parent states, instead of changing one state. It starts with a population of k random states. Each state is written as a string, often of digits or bits, called an individual. A fitness function scores each individual, higher is better. Then new generations are produced by three operations: selection, crossover and mutation.

Encoding 8-queens: An 8-queens board can be written as 8 digits, where the i-th digit is the row (1 to 8) of the queen in column i. For example, 24748552 means the column 1 queen is in row 2, column 2 in row 4, and so on. A good fitness function is the number of non-attacking pairs of queens. With 8 queens there are 8 x 7 / 2 = 28 pairs, so a solution has fitness 28.

Selection: Suppose the population has four individuals: 24748552 with fitness 24, 32752411 with fitness 23, 24415124 with fitness 20 and 32543213 with fitness 11. Total fitness is 78. In fitness-proportional selection, the chance of being picked as a parent is fitness divided by total: about 31 percent, 29 percent, 26 percent and 14 percent. We pick pairs of parents randomly with these chances, so fit individuals often get picked (sometimes twice) and weak ones rarely. Other schemes, such as tournament selection (pick a few at random, keep the best), are also common.

Crossover: For each pair of parents, choose a random crossover point and swap the tails. Take parents 32752411 and 24748552, with the crossover point after the third digit. Child 1 takes 327 from the first parent and 48552 from the second: 32748552. Child 2 takes 247 from the second parent and 52411 from the first: 24752411. Checking with the fitness function, these children score 23 and 22. On a board, crossover means the left part of one board is joined with the right part of another, so good "chunks" from different parents can be combined.

Mutation: Finally, each digit of each child is changed to a random value with a small probability, for example 1 in 100. Mutation keeps diversity and can create something no parent had, just as random mutations do in nature. Without mutation, a digit value that disappears from the population can never come back. Some GAs also use elitism: copy the best one or two individuals unchanged into the next generation, so the best solution found so far is never lost.

Why and when GAs work: Crossover helps when the problem has building blocks: useful substrings that are good on their own and stay good when combined. In 8-queens, a good arrangement of the first three columns is valuable no matter what is to the right. If the encoding scatters related information randomly, crossover just mixes noise. GAs are widely applied to design and scheduling problems, but it is honest to say they are not magic; on many problems a well-tuned simulated annealing or hill climbing with restarts does just as well. The art is in choosing the encoding, fitness function and operators.

Choosing among the methods: All three methods are stochastic, so two runs on the same problem may give different answers; it is normal to run them several times and keep the best. Simulated annealing needs only one state and a neighbour function, so it is simple to add to any hill-climbing program, but its schedule must be tuned. Local beam search needs k times the memory and work per step, and pays off when information sharing helps. Genetic algorithms need an encoding where crossover makes sense, plus several parameters (population size, mutation rate, selection scheme). A sensible order in practice: try random-restart hill climbing first, then simulated annealing, and reach for a GA when solutions naturally combine from good parts.

Real life example 1, a class routine: A school in Sylhet must build a weekly routine: each teacher teaches certain classes, no teacher can be in two rooms at once, the science lab is free only some periods, and teachers prefer not to have five periods in a row. Simulated annealing can start from a random routine, swap two periods at random, and accept worse routines sometimes early on. As the temperature drops, it settles on a routine with very few clashes.

Real life example 2, designing a delivery route mix: A courier company in Dhaka wants to decide which areas each van covers each day. Each candidate plan is encoded as a string: the van number assigned to each area. Fitness is the total parcels delivered on time minus fuel costs. A genetic algorithm keeps a population of plans, combines good halves of different plans, adds small mutations, and over many generations finds plans better than the ones people wrote by hand.

Common mistakes and exam questions: In simulated annealing, students often accept worse moves with probability e^(delta E / T) but forget that better moves are always accepted. Some write e^(T / delta E) or forget the minus sign; check with numbers that bad moves become less likely as T falls. In GAs, students forget mutation, or mix up crossover (combining two parents) with mutation (random change to one). Typical questions: write the simulated annealing pseudo-code and explain the role of T; compute an acceptance probability; compare local beam search with random restarts; and do one GA generation for 8-queens with given fitness values, including selection percentages and crossover.

Recap: Simulated annealing picks random moves, always accepts improvements, and accepts worse moves with probability e^(delta E / T) while the temperature T is slowly lowered. Local beam search keeps k states and lets them share information; stochastic beam search keeps diversity. Genetic algorithms evolve a population of strings using fitness-based selection, crossover and mutation. Next, we add an opponent to the search problem and study games with minimax.
key_points: Simulated annealing picks a random neighbour, always accepts better moves and accepts worse ones with probability e^(delta E / T).
High temperature means wide exploration; as T falls, the search behaves like hill climbing.
With a slow enough cooling schedule, simulated annealing finds a global optimum with probability approaching 1.
Local beam search keeps the k best states from all successors; the states share information, unlike independent restarts.
Stochastic beam search picks successors randomly in proportion to value to keep diversity.
Genetic algorithms use a population, a fitness function, selection, crossover and mutation.
For 8-queens, fitness = non-attacking pairs (max 28); fitnesses 24, 23, 20, 11 give selection chances of about 31%, 29%, 26%, 14%.
lessons.tip: For any simulated annealing question, make a small table of e^(delta E / T) for two temperatures and two values of delta E. Seeing the numbers shrink as T falls makes the explanation easy to write and hard to get wrong.
lessons.task: Take the GA example parents 24415124 and 32543213. Choose a crossover point after the fifth digit and write the two children. Then count each child's non-attacking pairs on an 8x8 board drawn on paper. Did either child beat both parents?

quiz.q: In simulated annealing, a move that improves the value is:
options: Accepted with probability e^(delta E / T)
quiz.explain: Improvements are always taken; only worse moves are accepted with probability e^(delta E / T).

quiz.q: A worse move has delta E = -2. Roughly what is its acceptance probability at T = 1?
quiz.explain: e^(-2) is about 0.135.

quiz.q: How does local beam search differ from k independent random restarts?
options: Its k states share information because the best k successors are chosen from the whole pool
It always finds the global optimum
quiz.explain: Effort moves to the most promising regions found by any of the k states.

quiz.q: In a genetic algorithm for 8-queens, what is a good fitness function?
options: The number of queens on the board
The number of non-attacking pairs of queens, with 28 meaning a solution
The sum of the digits of the string
quiz.explain: More non-attacking pairs is better; 28 pairs means no queen attacks another.

quiz.q: Parents 32752411 and 24748552 are crossed after the third digit. What is the child that starts with 327?
quiz.explain: Take 327 from the first parent and 48552 from the second.

lessons.title: Adversarial Search and the Minimax Algorithm
lessons.content:
When you play tic-tac-toe (many of us called it kata-kuti in school) with your cousin, you do not just think "where is a good square for me?". You think "if I play here, where will she play, and then what can I do?". You imagine her doing her best against you. That is the big difference between a puzzle and a game. In a puzzle, the world does not fight back. In a game, there is an opponent whose goal is the opposite of yours. In this lesson we learn how an agent can search in such a world, using the minimax algorithm.

Adversarial search: Search in a multi-agent, competitive environment where the agents' goals conflict is called adversarial search, and these problems are usually called games. AI research has focused most on a specific type: two players, taking turns, deterministic (no dice), perfect information (both see the whole board), and zero-sum. Chess, checkers, Go, tic-tac-toe and Othello are all of this type. Games with dice, like Ludo or backgammon, add chance, and games like poker add hidden information; we touch on these at the end of the next lesson.

Kinds of games: It helps to sort games along two questions: is there chance, and can every player see everything? Deterministic with perfect information: chess, checkers, Go, Othello, tic-tac-toe. Chance with perfect information: backgammon, Ludo and snakes and ladders, where dice add randomness but the board is visible. Deterministic with imperfect information: games like Battleship, where you cannot see the other side's ships. Chance with imperfect information: poker, bridge and most card games, where cards are both hidden and shuffled. Minimax as described here fits the first group exactly; the others need extensions.

Zero-sum: In a zero-sum game, what one player wins the other loses; the total payoff is constant. In chess, the outcome is win (1), loss (0) or draw (1/2) for each player, and the two players' results always add up to 1, which is constant, so chess counts as zero-sum (some books prefer the phrase "constant-sum"). This means there is no reason to cooperate: what is good for one player is exactly bad for the other.

MAX and MIN: We call the two players MAX and MIN. MAX moves first, and the agent we are building is usually MAX. MAX wants the final outcome to have the highest possible value; MIN wants it to be as low as possible. The two take turns until the game ends. One move by one player is called a ply; two plies, one by each player, make one full move in chess terms.

Formal definition of a game: A game can be defined as a search problem with these parts. S0: the initial state (the starting board). TO-MOVE(s): which player moves in state s. ACTIONS(s): the legal moves in s. RESULT(s, a): the state after move a. IS-TERMINAL(s): true when the game is over (win, loss or draw). UTILITY(s, p): the final numeric value of terminal state s for player p, for example +1 for a MAX win, -1 for a MIN win and 0 for a draw.

The game tree: The initial state, actions and result function define a game tree: nodes are game states and edges are moves, with levels alternating between MAX and MIN. For tic-tac-toe, the root has 9 possible first moves, each of those has 8 replies, and so on. The tree has fewer than 9! = 362,880 terminal nodes, and only 5,478 distinct positions. For chess the average branching factor is about 35 and games often last dozens of moves for each side, so the full tree has far more than 10^100 nodes. Nobody can draw or search it fully.

What is an optimal strategy: In a normal search problem, a solution is a sequence of actions. In a game, MAX cannot fix all its moves in advance, because MIN's replies are unknown. MAX needs a strategy: a move for the initial state, then a move for every possible reply by MIN, and so on. An optimal strategy gives the best possible result against an opponent who also plays perfectly.

Minimax values: The key idea is the minimax value of each node: the utility (for MAX) of reaching that node, assuming both players play optimally from there to the end. It is defined recursively. For a terminal state, MINIMAX(s) = UTILITY(s). If it is MAX's turn, MINIMAX(s) = the maximum of the minimax values of its children. If it is MIN's turn, MINIMAX(s) = the minimum of the minimax values of its children. So MAX picks the move to the child with the highest value, assuming MIN will then pick replies that give the lowest.

Worked example, a two-ply tree: The root A is a MAX node with three moves, a1, a2 and a3, leading to MIN nodes B, C and D. Each MIN node has three replies leading to terminal states with these utilities: under B: 3, 12, 8; under C: 2, 4, 6; under D: 14, 5, 2. MIN at B chooses the smallest: 3. MIN at C chooses 2. MIN at D chooses 2. MAX at A chooses the largest of 3, 2 and 2, which is 3. So the minimax value of the root is 3, and MAX's best move is a1. Notice that D contains the biggest number, 14, but a sensible MIN would never allow it; choosing a3 hoping for 14 is wishful thinking.

Choosing utilities: The utility function decides what "winning" means to the agent. Simple games use +1, -1 and 0. But if the margin of victory matters, as in a game scored by points, utilities can be the final score difference, so the agent prefers a big win to a narrow one. Utilities must be written from MAX's point of view everywhere in the tree; MIN simply tries to make that same number small. Mixing points of view, for example writing MIN's own score at MIN's leaves, is a classic source of wrong answers.

The minimax algorithm: The algorithm computes these values by a recursive depth-first search. In words: function MAX-VALUE(s): if s is terminal return UTILITY(s); v = minus infinity; for each action a: v = max(v, MIN-VALUE(RESULT(s, a))); return v. MIN-VALUE is the same with plus infinity and min. At the root, MAX chooses the action whose child has the highest MIN-VALUE. The recursion goes all the way down to the leaves, and the values are "backed up" through the tree as the recursion returns.

Following the recursion: In the worked example, the depth-first order is: go to B, see leaf 3, then 12, then 8, return 3 to A. Go to C, see 2, 4, 6, return 2. Go to D, see 14, 5, 2, return 2. At any moment, only one path from the root plus a few sibling values is in memory. Notice something interesting: after A knows that B is worth 3, and C's first leaf turns out to be 2, C can be worth at most 2, since MIN will pick 2 or something smaller. So C's other leaves (4 and 6) cannot change MAX's decision. Spotting such useless work is exactly the idea behind alpha-beta pruning.

A complete small game: Consider a matchstick game. There are 4 sticks; players take turns removing 1 or 2 sticks; whoever takes the last stick wins. MAX moves first. Work from the end. With 1 or 2 sticks left, the player to move wins by taking them all. With 3 sticks left, the player to move loses: taking 1 leaves 2 for the opponent, taking 2 leaves 1, and either way the opponent takes the rest. With 4 sticks, MAX takes 1, leaving 3 for MIN, a losing position for MIN. So the minimax value of the start is a win for MAX, and the optimal first move is "take 1". The general rule this reveals: always leave your opponent a multiple of 3.

Properties of minimax: Minimax is complete if the tree is finite. It is optimal against an optimal opponent. Against a weaker opponent, MAX can sometimes do better with other strategies, but playing minimax still guarantees at least the minimax value, whatever MIN does. Because it is a depth-first search, the time complexity is O(b^m) and the space complexity is O(bm) (or O(m) if moves are generated one at a time), where b is the number of legal moves and m is the maximum depth.

Why plain minimax is not enough: For tic-tac-toe, b^m is small and minimax plays perfectly; it can show that perfect play from both sides ends in a draw. For chess, b is about 35 and m is large, so O(b^m) is completely impossible. Real game programs therefore need two improvements: pruning branches that cannot matter (alpha-beta, next lesson), and cutting the search off at some depth and estimating the value of the position with an evaluation function.

More than two players: Minimax can be extended to games with three or more players by replacing the single number at each node with a vector of utilities, one per player. At each node, the player to move picks the child whose vector is best for themselves. Such games bring new behaviour, like temporary alliances: two weaker players may "gang up" on the leader, which emerges naturally from each player maximising their own utility.

Real life example 1, a chess app's difficulty level: Phone chess apps let you choose easy, medium or hard. Many engines control strength partly by limiting how deep or how long they search, and sometimes by adding random weaker moves at low levels. A shallow search may miss a trap two moves later; a deeper search sees it. Every level is built on the same minimax idea: assume your opponent will answer with their best reply.

Real life example 2, kata-kuti at school: If you write out the minimax values for tic-tac-toe, a few practical rules appear: take the centre or a corner first, always block an opponent's two-in-a-row, and look for a fork (a move that creates two threats at once). These are simply the moves with the best minimax values in common positions. That is why two careful players almost always draw, exactly as minimax predicts.

Common mistakes and exam questions: The most common mistake is backing up the wrong function: at MIN nodes take the minimum, at MAX nodes the maximum, and always look at whose turn it is at that node. Another is choosing MAX's move by the largest leaf, as in the a3 trap above. Students also forget that minimax assumes an optimal opponent. Typical questions: compute minimax values for a given tree and state the best move; define the components of a game; give time and space complexity; and explain why minimax cannot be used directly for chess.

Recap: Games are adversarial search problems with an opponent. Two-player, turn-taking, deterministic, perfect-information, zero-sum games are modelled with MAX and MIN, a game tree and a utility function. Minimax values are backed up from the leaves: max at MAX nodes, min at MIN nodes. Minimax is optimal against an optimal opponent, with time O(b^m) and space O(bm), which is far too slow for chess. Next lesson, alpha-beta pruning makes minimax much faster without changing its answer.
key_points: Adversarial search handles competitive multi-agent environments, usually called games.
Classic AI games are two-player, turn-taking, deterministic, perfect-information and zero-sum.
A game has an initial state, TO-MOVE, ACTIONS, RESULT, IS-TERMINAL and UTILITY.
Minimax value: utility at terminals, max of children at MAX nodes, min of children at MIN nodes.
In the classic tree with leaves 3,12,8 / 2,4,6 / 14,5,2, the root value is 3 and MAX's best move is a1.
Minimax is optimal against an optimal opponent; time O(b^m), space O(bm).
Chess has a branching factor of about 35, so full minimax is impossible; real programs need pruning and evaluation functions.
lessons.tip: When computing minimax by hand, write MAX or MIN beside every internal node before you start, and back up values one level at a time from the bottom. Nearly all errors come from using max where min belongs.
lessons.task: Play the matchstick game with 7 sticks (take 1 or 2, last stick wins) against a friend or family member. Before playing, use the minimax idea to decide who should win with perfect play and what the first move should be. Then check your prediction in a few games.

quiz.q: In a zero-sum game:
options: One player's gain is exactly the other player's loss
quiz.explain: The total payoff is constant, so there is no reason to cooperate.

quiz.q: For the tree with MIN nodes B (3, 12, 8), C (2, 4, 6) and D (14, 5, 2) under a MAX root, what is the root's minimax value?
quiz.explain: MIN values are 3, 2 and 2; MAX takes the largest, 3.

quiz.q: What are the time and space complexity of minimax?
quiz.explain: Minimax is a depth-first search of the whole game tree.

quiz.q: Why can't plain minimax play chess?
options: The game tree is astronomically large (branching factor about 35 over many moves)
Minimax only works for one player
quiz.explain: O(b^m) is impossible for chess, so pruning and evaluation functions are needed.

quiz.q: In the 4-stick game (take 1 or 2, last stick wins), what should MAX do first?
options: It does not matter; MAX always loses
quiz.explain: Leaving 3 sticks puts MIN in a losing position.

lessons.title: Alpha-Beta Pruning and Real Game-Playing Programs
lessons.content:
Suppose you are choosing a mobile phone shop in Elephant Road, and the first shop already offers your phone for 20,000 taka. At the second shop, the very first price you hear is "at least 22,000". You walk out immediately. You do not need to hear their other offers, because you already know this shop cannot beat the first one. That simple "walk out early" idea, applied to a game tree, is alpha-beta pruning. It gives exactly the same answer as minimax while skipping huge parts of the tree.
