In this lesson we learn how it works, then see how real game programs combine it with depth limits, evaluation functions and other tricks.

The idea of pruning: In the last lesson's tree, the MAX root had MIN children B (leaves 3, 12, 8), C (leaves 2, 4, 6) and D (leaves 14, 5, 2), and the root value was 3. After evaluating B, MAX knows it can get at least 3. At C, the first leaf is 2, so MIN at C can force a value of 2 or less. C can never be better than 3 for MAX, so MAX will never choose C, no matter what the other leaves under C are. We can skip them. Pruning means not exploring branches that cannot affect the final decision.

Alpha and beta: The algorithm keeps two numbers as it searches. Alpha is the value of the best choice found so far for MAX along the current path: MAX is guaranteed at least alpha. Beta is the value of the best choice found so far for MIN along the current path: MIN can hold MAX to at most beta. They start at alpha = minus infinity and beta = plus infinity. As the search learns more, alpha only rises and beta only falls, and the window between them shrinks. When the window closes, the current node cannot matter and is pruned.

The pruning rules: At a MIN node, while looking at children, if the value v found so far becomes less than or equal to alpha, stop: MAX already has a better option elsewhere, so it will never let play reach this node. At a MAX node, if v becomes greater than or equal to beta, stop: MIN already has a better option elsewhere and will avoid this node. In pseudo-code, MAX-VALUE(s, alpha, beta): if terminal return utility; v = minus infinity; for each action: v = max(v, MIN-VALUE(result, alpha, beta)); if v >= beta return v; alpha = max(alpha, v); return v. MIN-VALUE is the mirror image: v = min(...); if v <= alpha return v; beta = min(beta, v).

Full trace, part 1: Start at root A with alpha = minus infinity, beta = plus infinity. Go to B (MIN), passing the same window. Leaf 3: v = 3, beta at B becomes 3. Leaf 12: v stays 3. Leaf 8: v stays 3. B returns 3. Back at A: v = 3, so alpha at A becomes 3. MAX now knows it can get at least 3.

Full trace, part 2: Go to C with alpha = 3, beta = plus infinity. First leaf 2: v = 2. Now v = 2 <= alpha = 3, so prune: C returns 2 at once, and leaves 4 and 6 are never looked at. Back at A: max(3, 2) is still 3. Go to D with alpha = 3. Leaf 14: v = 14, not <= 3, so beta at D becomes 14. Leaf 5: v = 5, still more than 3, beta becomes 5. Leaf 2: v = 2, now v <= 3, prune (but there are no leaves left anyway). D returns 2. Root value: max(3, 2, 2) = 3. Same answer as minimax, best move a1, and we skipped 2 of the 9 leaves.

The answer never changes: Alpha-beta pruning never changes the value at the root or the best move. It only skips work that minimax would have done for nothing. This is an important exam point: pruning is a pure speed-up, not an approximation. (The values returned for pruned nodes are bounds, not exact values, but they are enough to make the right decision.)

Move ordering matters a lot: In the trace, D's leaves came in the order 14, 5, 2. If the 2 had come first, D would have been pruned immediately after one leaf, skipping 14 and 5 too. How much alpha-beta saves depends on examining good moves first. With perfect ordering, alpha-beta examines about O(b^(m/2)) nodes instead of O(b^m). That means the effective branching factor drops from b to about the square root of b: for chess, from about 35 to about 6. In other words, in the same time, alpha-beta can search roughly twice as deep as minimax. With random ordering, the cost is roughly O(b^(3m/4)) for moderate b.

How programs get good ordering: Programs use simple tricks. In chess, try captures first, then threats, then forward moves, then backward moves. Use killer moves: moves that caused a cutoff at the same depth elsewhere in the tree are tried first. Use iterative deepening: search to depth 1, then 2, then 3, and use the best moves from the previous iteration to order the next one. A transposition table, a hash table of positions already evaluated, avoids re-searching the same position reached by a different move order, which happens very often in chess.

Cutting off the search: Even with alpha-beta, chess trees are far too big to search to the end. So real programs stop at a depth limit (or when time runs out) and estimate the value there. Minimax becomes heuristic minimax: if the cutoff test says stop (for example, depth = 6), return EVAL(s) instead of a true utility. The rest of the algorithm is unchanged.

Evaluation functions: EVAL(s) estimates how good a position is for MAX. It must be fast and should agree with the true utility on terminal states. A common form is a weighted linear function: EVAL(s) = w1 x f1(s) + w2 x f2(s) + ... + wn x fn(s), where each f is a feature of the position. In chess, a classic feature is material: beginners' books value a pawn at 1, a knight at 3, a bishop at 3, a rook at 5 and a queen at 9. If White has a queen and a pawn more and Black has a rook more, the material score for White is 9 + 1 - 5 = 5. Other features include king safety, pawn structure and piece mobility. Modern programs often learn evaluation functions from data, including with neural networks.

The horizon effect and quiescence: A fixed depth cutoff has a danger. Suppose at depth 6 White has just captured Black's knight, so EVAL looks great, but at depth 7 Black recaptures the queen. The search cannot see past its "horizon", so it misjudges the position. The fix is quiescence search: only apply EVAL in quiet positions; if a position is in the middle of captures or checks, keep searching those moves a little deeper until things calm down. Another form of the horizon effect is delaying an unavoidable loss by playing useless moves that push it beyond the depth limit.

Forward pruning and lookup tables: Alpha-beta only prunes branches that provably cannot matter. Some programs also use forward pruning: they skip moves that look bad according to a quick check, without proof. This saves a lot of time but is risky, because a move that looks bad (like sacrificing a piece) might actually be brilliant. Programs also avoid search where they can simply look things up. An opening book stores good moves for the first part of the game, collected from expert play and analysis. Endgame tablebases store perfect results for positions with only a few pieces left, computed by searching backwards from all finished positions, so in those positions the program plays perfectly without any search at all.

Games of chance, expectiminimax: In games with dice, like backgammon or Ludo, the tree gets chance nodes between MAX and MIN nodes. The value of a chance node is the expected value: the sum over outcomes of probability x value. Example: a coin-flip chance node with outcomes worth 3 (probability 0.5) and 7 (probability 0.5) has value 0.5 x 3 + 0.5 x 7 = 5. This is the expectiminimax algorithm. Two side effects: the tree grows much faster because of the dice outcomes, so deep search is harder, and the evaluation function must be scaled carefully, because with averages, not only the order of positions matters but also how far apart their values are.

Monte Carlo tree search: For Go, with a branching factor of about 250 and no simple evaluation function, alpha-beta struggles. Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) takes a different approach. It repeats four steps many times: selection (walk down the tree choosing promising moves, balancing exploration and exploitation, for example with the UCB1 formula), expansion (add a new child node), simulation (play the rest of the game quickly, often randomly or with a simple policy, called a playout) and back-propagation (update win statistics along the path). The move with the most visits is played. AlphaGo combined MCTS with deep neural networks trained on games, and in 2016 beat Lee Sedol.

Real life example 1, Deep Blue: IBM's Deep Blue, which beat world champion Garry Kasparov in 1997, was built on alpha-beta search running on special-purpose chess hardware, with a carefully tuned evaluation function and an opening book. It examined a huge number of positions per second. It was not "thinking like a human"; it was very fast, well-pruned minimax with a good evaluation function, which shows how far these classic ideas can go.

Real life example 2, a Ludo bot: A Ludo app cannot use plain minimax because of the dice. A simple bot can do one level of expectiminimax: for each possible move with the current dice, compute the expected value over the opponent's next dice roll, using an evaluation function such as "pieces home x 10 + safe pieces x 3 - pieces in danger x 4". Even this shallow search plays much better than random moves.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often prune in the wrong direction; remember: at a MIN node prune when v <= alpha, at a MAX node prune when v >= beta. Another mistake is thinking alpha-beta can change the root value; it cannot. Some forget to pass the updated alpha and beta down to children. Exam favourites: trace alpha-beta on a given tree and mark the pruned branches; reorder the leaves to get maximum pruning; state the best-case complexity O(b^(m/2)); explain the horizon effect and quiescence search; and compute an expectiminimax value.

Recap: Alpha-beta pruning keeps alpha (best for MAX) and beta (best for MIN) and prunes nodes that cannot affect the decision, giving exactly the minimax answer. With good move ordering it searches about O(b^(m/2)) nodes, roughly twice as deep. Real programs add depth cutoffs with evaluation functions, quiescence search, transposition tables and iterative deepening. Chance games use expectiminimax, and games like Go use Monte Carlo tree search. Next we move to a new kind of problem: constraint satisfaction.
key_points: Alpha-beta pruning gives exactly the same root value and move as minimax but skips useless branches.
Alpha = best value for MAX so far on the path; beta = best value for MIN so far.
Prune at a MIN node when v <= alpha; prune at a MAX node when v >= beta.
In the classic tree, alpha-beta prunes leaves 4 and 6 under C after seeing the leaf 2.
With perfect move ordering alpha-beta needs about O(b^(m/2)) nodes, so it can search about twice as deep.
Real programs cut off at a depth and use an evaluation function, often a weighted sum of features like material.
Quiescence search fights the horizon effect; expectiminimax handles dice; MCTS uses playouts and statistics.
lessons.tip: In alpha-beta traces, write the window [alpha, beta] next to every node as you enter it, and update it as values come back. Pruning decisions then become a simple comparison you can see on the page.
lessons.task: Reorder the leaves of the classic tree (B: 3, 12, 8; C: 2, 4, 6; D: 14, 5, 2) to get as much pruning as possible without changing which leaves belong to which MIN node. Trace alpha-beta on your ordering and count how many leaves you skipped.

quiz.q: What does alpha represent in alpha-beta pruning?
options: The best value MIN can force so far
The best value MAX is guaranteed so far along the path
quiz.explain: Alpha is a lower bound for MAX; beta is an upper bound set by MIN.

quiz.q: At a MIN node, when can the remaining children be pruned?
quiz.explain: MAX already has an option worth alpha, so it will never let play reach this MIN node.

quiz.q: With perfect move ordering, alpha-beta examines about how many nodes?
quiz.explain: The effective branching factor becomes about the square root of b.

quiz.q: What is the horizon effect?
options: A fixed depth cutoff hides an important event (like a recapture) just beyond the search depth
The tree is too wide to draw
The evaluation function is always zero
The opponent can see your moves
quiz.explain: Quiescence search reduces it by searching unstable positions deeper.

lessons.title: Constraint Satisfaction Problems
lessons.content:
Every year before the final exams, someone in your university's exam office faces a headache. There are sixty courses, ten exam days with two slots each, a few big halls, and hundreds of students taking different combinations of courses. No student may have two exams at the same time, the big courses need the big hall, and some teachers are away on certain days. Nobody cares about the order in which the routine was built; they only need a routine that breaks no rule. This kind of puzzle, "find values for many variables so that all the rules are satisfied", is a constraint satisfaction problem, or CSP, and it has its own powerful family of methods.

From black boxes to variables: In the search lessons, a state was a black box: the algorithm could only ask "what are your successors?" and "are you a goal?". In a CSP, a state has an inside: it is a set of variables, each with a value. This is the factored representation from lesson 3. Because the algorithm can see which variable breaks which rule, it can use general-purpose tricks that work for any CSP: removing impossible values early, choosing the hardest variable first, and so on. That is why CSP solvers can handle problems with thousands of variables.

The formal definition: A CSP has three parts. X is a set of variables {X1, ..., Xn}. D is a set of domains {D1, ..., Dn}, one for each variable, listing the values it may take. C is a set of constraints, each specifying allowed combinations of values for some variables. A constraint has a scope (the variables involved) and a relation (the allowed combinations). For example, if X1 and X2 both have domain {1, 2, 3}, the constraint "X1 > X2" can be written as the scope (X1, X2) with the allowed pairs {(2, 1), (3, 1), (3, 2)}.

Assignments and solutions: An assignment gives values to some or all variables, for example {X1 = 3, X2 = 1}. An assignment that violates no constraint is consistent (or legal). An assignment that gives a value to every variable is complete. A solution is a complete and consistent assignment. A partial assignment leaves some variables unassigned; partial assignments are what search algorithms work with on the way to a solution.

The classic example, colouring Australia: The textbook's favourite CSP is colouring a map of Australia's seven regions: Western Australia (WA), Northern Territory (NT), South Australia (SA), Queensland (Q), New South Wales (NSW), Victoria (V) and Tasmania (T). Each region must be red, green or blue, and neighbouring regions must have different colours. Variables: the seven regions. Domains: {red, green, blue} for each. Constraints: WA is not equal to NT, WA not equal to SA, NT not equal to SA, NT not equal to Q, SA not equal to Q, SA not equal to NSW, SA not equal to V, Q not equal to NSW, NSW not equal to V. Tasmania is an island with no neighbours, so it has no constraints. One solution: WA = red, NT = green, SA = blue, Q = red, NSW = green, V = red, T = red.

The constraint graph: A CSP can be drawn as a constraint graph: each variable is a node, and each binary constraint is an edge between the two variables it involves. For Australia, SA sits in the middle, connected to five others, and T floats alone. The graph's shape tells us a lot. Since T is not connected to anything, it is an independent sub-problem and can be coloured separately. Real solvers use such structure to split large problems into smaller ones.

How many colours are enough: Map colouring is a special case of graph colouring, which you met in Graph Theory. A famous result, the four colour theorem, says that any map drawn on a flat surface, where regions are connected areas and neighbours share a border line, can be coloured with at most four colours. It was proved in 1976 with the help of a computer, which was controversial at the time. Some maps, like Australia's, need only three. Deciding whether a general graph can be coloured with three colours is NP-complete, which tells us that CSPs in general are hard problems, even though most practical instances are solved quickly.

Why CSP thinking saves work: Without constraints, the Australia problem has 3^7 = 2,187 complete assignments. But as soon as we choose SA = blue, none of its five neighbours can be blue, so they have only 2 choices each: 2^5 = 32 combinations instead of 3^5 = 243, a reduction of about 87 percent. A plain search algorithm would not notice this, because it cannot see inside states. A CSP solver notices immediately and cuts the domains. That is the core advantage.

Kinds of variables and domains: The simplest CSPs have discrete variables with finite domains, like colours or exam slots. Some have discrete but infinite domains, like integers for start times in a factory schedule, with constraints such as "StartJob1 + 5 <= StartJob3"; these need special constraint languages. Some have continuous domains, like the exact time a telescope observation starts; the best-known case is linear programming, where constraints are linear inequalities, which can be solved in time polynomial in the number of variables.

Kinds of constraints: A unary constraint involves one variable, for example "South Australia does not like green", written SA not equal to green. A binary constraint involves two variables, like SA not equal to NSW. A higher-order constraint involves three or more variables, for example "Y is between X and Z". A global constraint involves an arbitrary number of variables; the most common is Alldiff, meaning all the listed variables must have different values. Finally, preference constraints (soft constraints) say what is better rather than what is allowed, for example "Professor Rahman prefers morning classes". A CSP with preferences becomes a constraint optimisation problem.

Example, Sudoku: Sudoku is a perfect CSP. There are 81 variables, one per cell. Filled cells have a domain of one value; empty cells have domain {1, ..., 9}. There are 27 Alldiff constraints: one for each of the 9 rows, 9 columns and 9 boxes of 3x3. Every newspaper Sudoku is designed to have exactly one solution, and the reasoning people use ("this cell can only be 7, because 1 to 6 and 8 and 9 already appear in its row, column or box") is exactly constraint propagation, which we formalise next lesson. CSP solvers solve typical puzzles in a fraction of a second.

Example, cryptarithmetic: In TWO + TWO = FOUR, each letter stands for a different digit, and leading letters (T and F) cannot be zero. Variables: F, T, U, W, R, O, plus carry variables C1, C2, C3 for the units, tens and hundreds columns. Constraints: Alldiff(F, T, U, W, R, O); O + O = R + 10 x C1; C1 + W + W = U + 10 x C2; C2 + T + T = O + 10 x C3; C3 = F; and T and F are not zero. One solution is 734 + 734 = 1468, so T = 7, W = 3, O = 4, F = 1, U = 6, R = 8. These constraints involve several variables at once, so the picture is a constraint hypergraph.

Example, scheduling a job: Building a small house involves tasks with durations: foundation 3 days, walls 5 days, roof 2 days, wiring 2 days, painting 3 days. Variables: the start day of each task. Precedence constraints: walls start after the foundation ends (StartWalls >= StartFoundation + 3), the roof after the walls, wiring after the walls, painting after both roof and wiring. Plus a goal that everything ends within, say, 15 days. This is how real construction and factory schedules are modelled, often with resource constraints too (only one crane, only two electricians).

Example, 8-queens as a CSP: Let Qi be the row of the queen in column i, for i = 1 to 8, each with domain {1, ..., 8}. Constraints: for every pair i and j, Qi is not equal to Qj (different rows), and the absolute difference of Qi and Qj is not equal to the absolute difference of i and j (different diagonals). One-per-column is built into the formulation. You have now seen 8-queens solved as incremental search (lesson 4), as local search (lesson 10) and as a CSP: same problem, three different views.

Three ways to attack a CSP: There are three main families of methods, and the next lesson covers all three. Search: assign variables one at a time and back up when a constraint is broken (backtracking search). Inference, also called constraint propagation: use the constraints to remove values from domains that can never be part of a solution, sometimes solving the whole problem without any search, as in easy Sudokus. Local search: start with a complete assignment that breaks some constraints and repair it step by step, like the min-conflicts method. Real solvers usually mix search and inference: propagate, choose a variable, propagate again.

Real life example 1, exam timetabling: Back to the exam office. Variables: the 60 courses. Domain: the 20 slots (10 days x 2 slots). Constraints: any two courses that share at least one student must be in different slots, which is exactly graph colouring, with slots as colours. Unary constraints: a course whose teacher is abroad on Tuesday cannot be on Tuesday. Capacity constraints: the total students in one slot must fit the halls. Soft constraints: avoid a student having exams in both slots of the same day. Universities in Bangladesh and everywhere use software built on these ideas.

Real life example 2, a wedding seating plan: A family in Narayanganj is planning a wedding with 200 guests and 20 tables of 10. Variables: each guest's table. Domain: tables 1 to 20. Constraints: each table holds at most 10 people (a global capacity constraint); two uncles who are not on speaking terms must be at different tables; elderly guests must sit near the stage (a unary constraint); families should sit together where possible (soft constraints). Formulated this way, a computer can find a plan in seconds that would take a whole evening by hand.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often forget to state domains, or write constraints in vague words instead of precise relations. Another mistake is confusing a consistent assignment (breaks no rule) with a complete one (every variable has a value); a solution must be both. In cryptarithmetic, students forget the carry variables. Typical questions: define a CSP formally; formulate map colouring, Sudoku, cryptarithmetic or 8-queens as a CSP; draw the constraint graph; classify constraints as unary, binary, global or soft; and explain why CSPs can be solved more efficiently than plain state-space search.

Recap: A CSP has variables, domains and constraints, and a solution is a complete, consistent assignment. The factored representation lets algorithms see which constraints are broken and remove impossible values early. Constraints can be unary, binary, higher-order, global (like Alldiff) or soft preferences. Map colouring, Sudoku, cryptarithmetic, scheduling and 8-queens are classic CSPs, and exam timetabling is a real one. Next lesson: how to solve CSPs with backtracking, smart variable ordering, forward checking and arc consistency.
key_points: A CSP is defined by variables X, domains D and constraints C.
A solution is a complete (all variables assigned) and consistent (no constraint broken) assignment.
The constraint graph has variables as nodes and binary constraints as edges; independent parts can be solved separately.
In the Australia map, fixing SA = blue cuts its neighbours' combinations from 243 to 32.
Constraints can be unary, binary, higher-order, global (Alldiff) or soft preferences.
Sudoku has 81 variables and 27 Alldiff constraints; cryptarithmetic needs carry variables.
Exam timetabling is graph colouring: courses sharing students need different slots.
lessons.tip: For any CSP formulation question, write three labelled lines (Variables, Domains, Constraints) and then draw the constraint graph. The drawing often reveals mistakes, like a constraint you forgot or a variable with no connections.
lessons.task: Find a printed or online map of Bangladesh's eight divisions. Make a list of which divisions share a land border. Formulate it as a CSP with three colours, draw the constraint graph, and try to find a solution with three colours. Can you do it with fewer?

quiz.q: What is a solution to a CSP?
options: An assignment with at least one variable
quiz.explain: Every variable must have a value and no constraint may be violated.

quiz.q: Which of these is a global constraint?
options: SA is not equal to green
quiz.explain: Alldiff involves any number of variables and says all must differ.

quiz.q: In the Australia map, why can Tasmania be coloured independently?
options: It has no constraints connecting it to other regions
It has only one possible colour
quiz.explain: An unconnected node in the constraint graph is an independent sub-problem.

quiz.q: How many Alldiff constraints does a standard Sudoku have?
quiz.explain: 9 rows + 9 columns + 9 boxes = 27.

quiz.q: In TWO + TWO = FOUR, why do we add variables C1, C2 and C3?
options: To represent the letters T, W and O
To represent the carries between columns
quiz.explain: Column constraints like O + O = R + 10 x C1 need carry variables.

lessons.title: Solving CSPs: Backtracking, Heuristics and Propagation
lessons.content:
Watch an expert Sudoku solver at a tea stall reading the morning paper. She does not try random digits in every empty cell. She looks for the cell with the fewest possibilities, fills it, and immediately crosses out that digit from the cell's row, column and box. When she is stuck, she makes a careful guess, and if the guess leads to a contradiction she goes back and tries something else. Without knowing the names, she is using the three main tools of this lesson: backtracking search, smart ordering heuristics and constraint propagation.

Why plain search is wasteful: We could solve a CSP with ordinary search: start with an empty assignment, and let each action assign any value to any unassigned variable. With n variables and d values, the first level has n x d branches, the next (n - 1) x d, and so on, giving n! x d^n leaves, even though there are only d^n complete assignments. The waste comes from ignoring commutativity: assigning WA = red then NT = green gives the same result as NT = green then WA = red. So we fix the order: at each level of the tree, assign just one chosen variable. Now there are d^n leaves.

Backtracking search: Backtracking search is depth-first search that assigns one variable at a time and backs up as soon as a variable has no legal value left. In words: function BACKTRACK(assignment): if the assignment is complete, return it; choose an unassigned variable X; for each value v in X's domain (in some order): if v is consistent with the assignment, add X = v, (optionally run inference), result = BACKTRACK(assignment), and if result is not failure, return it; otherwise remove X = v; after all values fail, return failure.

A trace with a poor variable order: Colour Australia with variables in the order WA, NSW, NT, Q, SA, V, T, trying red, green, blue in that order. WA = red. NSW = red (no constraint with WA). NT = green. Q must differ from NT and NSW, so Q = blue. Now SA neighbours WA (red), NT (green), NSW (red) and Q (blue): no colour left, so SA fails. Back up: Q has no other value, so back up to NT: NT = blue, Q = green, and SA fails again. NT is exhausted, so back up to NSW: NSW = green, then NT = green, Q = red, SA = blue, V = red, T = red. Solved, but only after two dead ends caused by an early bad choice (NSW = red) that was discovered much later.

Three questions that improve backtracking: Backtracking becomes far faster by answering three questions cleverly. Which variable should be assigned next? In what order should its values be tried? What can we infer after each assignment to detect failure early? These need no knowledge of the particular problem; they work for any CSP.

Minimum remaining values (MRV): Choose the variable with the fewest legal values left. This is also called the "most constrained variable" or "fail-first" heuristic. If a variable has only one value left, assign it now; if it has zero, fail now instead of discovering it later. Example: after WA = red and NT = green, SA has only blue left, so MRV picks SA next. MRV usually beats a fixed or random order by a large factor.

Degree heuristic: MRV does not help at the start, when every domain is full. The degree heuristic breaks ties by choosing the variable involved in the most constraints with other unassigned variables. In Australia, SA has degree 5, the highest, so it is chosen first. Then NT, Q, NSW and others follow, and the map can be coloured with no backtracking at all.

Least constraining value (LCV): Once a variable is chosen, try first the value that rules out the fewest choices for neighbouring variables. Example: WA = red and NT = green, and we are choosing for Q. If Q = blue, SA (which neighbours WA and NT) loses its last value, blue. If Q = red, SA keeps blue. So LCV tries red first. Note the logic: for variables we want to fail first (to prune quickly), but for values we want to succeed first (since we only need one solution).

Forward checking: The simplest form of inference: whenever X is assigned, look at each unassigned neighbour Y and delete from Y's domain any value inconsistent with X's value. Example: WA = red removes red from NT and SA. Then Q = green removes green from NT, SA and NSW. Now NT and SA both have only {blue}. If we then assign V = blue, SA loses blue and its domain becomes empty, so forward checking detects failure immediately and backtracks, before ever trying to assign SA. Forward checking combines very naturally with MRV, since it keeps the domain sizes up to date.

What forward checking misses: In the same situation, after WA = red and Q = green, both NT and SA have only {blue}. But NT and SA are neighbours, so they cannot both be blue. Forward checking does not notice, because it only looks from the assigned variable to its neighbours, not between two unassigned variables. A stronger method is needed.

Arc consistency: A variable X is arc-consistent with respect to another variable Y if for every value x in X's domain there is at least one value y in Y's domain that satisfies the constraint between them. The directed pair (X, Y) is called an arc. Making arc X to Y consistent means deleting values of X that have no support in Y. Example: X < Y with both domains {1, 2, 3}. For X = 3, no Y value is bigger, so delete 3 from X; X becomes {1, 2}. For arc Y to X, Y = 1 has no smaller X, so Y becomes {2, 3}.

The AC-3 algorithm: AC-3 makes a whole CSP arc-consistent. Put every arc in a queue. Repeatedly remove an arc (Xi, Xj) and revise Xi's domain against Xj. If Xi's domain became empty, the CSP has no solution. If Xi's domain shrank, add back to the queue every arc (Xk, Xi) where Xk is a neighbour of Xi (other than Xj), because Xk's support in Xi might have disappeared. Stop when the queue is empty. For binary CSPs with c constraints and domain size d, AC-3 runs in O(c x d^3) time in the worst case.

AC-3 worked example: Variables X, Y, Z with domains {1, 2, 3} and constraints X < Y and Y < Z. Revise X against Y: remove 3, X = {1, 2}. Revise Y against X: remove 1, Y = {2, 3}. Revise Y against Z: Y = 3 needs a bigger Z, impossible, so Y = {2}. Because Y shrank, re-check X against Y: X must be less than 2, so X = {1}. Revise Z against Y: Z must be more than 2, so Z = {3}. The answer X = 1, Y = 2, Z = 3 appears by propagation alone, without any search. Many easy Sudokus are solved the same way.

Limits of arc consistency: Arc consistency is not enough to solve every CSP. Take three mutually neighbouring regions, like WA, NT and SA, with only two colours, {red, blue}. Each arc is consistent (for any colour of one, the other can take the other colour), yet no solution exists, because three neighbours in a triangle need three colours. Stronger notions, such as path consistency (looking at triples of variables) and k-consistency, catch more failures but cost more. Practical solvers usually maintain arc consistency (an algorithm called MAC) inside backtracking: after each assignment, run AC-3 starting from the arcs into the assigned variable.

Smarter backtracking and structure: Plain backtracking always returns to the most recent variable. Conflict-directed backjumping instead jumps back to a variable that actually caused the failure, like jumping straight from SA back to NSW in our trace, skipping the innocent NT. Structure helps too: if the constraint graph is a tree, the CSP can be solved in time linear in the number of variables, O(n x d^2), with no backtracking. And independent parts, like Tasmania, are solved separately.

Local search for CSPs, min-conflicts: Another approach starts from a complete assignment that may break constraints and repairs it. Min-conflicts: pick a variable that is in conflict, and give it the value that causes the fewest conflicts with other variables; repeat. For n-queens, the textbook reports that min-conflicts solves even the million-queens problem in an average of about 50 steps after the initial assignment. It was also used to schedule observations for the Hubble Space Telescope, cutting the time to schedule a week of observations from about three weeks to about ten minutes. Local search is especially good when the problem changes a little, for example when one teacher falls ill and the routine needs a quick repair.

Real life example 1, a Sudoku app's hint button: When you press "hint" in a Sudoku app, it can run constraint propagation from your current grid: it removes candidates using rows, columns and boxes, and finds a cell with only one possible digit (a "naked single"). It shows you that cell. If propagation is not enough, the solver behind the app uses backtracking with MRV, choosing the cell with the fewest candidates first, exactly as the tea-stall expert does.

Real life example 2, repairing a class routine: A school in Barishal has a finished weekly routine, but on Sunday a maths teacher is transferred. Rebuilding from scratch would change everything and confuse students. Instead, min-conflicts starts from the old routine, marks the classes that now have no teacher as conflicts, and moves only a few periods to fix them. The new routine looks almost like the old one, which everyone prefers.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students mix up MRV (choose the variable with fewest values) and LCV (choose the value that leaves the most options for others). Another error: thinking forward checking makes the CSP arc-consistent; it does not, it only checks arcs from the assigned variable. In AC-3, many forget to re-add neighbouring arcs after a domain shrinks. Typical questions: write the backtracking pseudo-code; apply MRV, degree and LCV on the Australia map; show forward checking step by step in a domain table; run AC-3 on a small CSP; and explain min-conflicts for n-queens.

Recap: Backtracking search assigns one variable per level and backs up on dead ends. MRV and the degree heuristic choose which variable next; LCV chooses which value first. Forward checking prunes neighbours' domains after each assignment; arc consistency (AC-3) propagates further and can sometimes solve a problem alone, though not always. Backjumping and tree structure help more, and min-conflicts local search is excellent for large problems and quick repairs. Next we turn to knowledge and logic: agents that reason.
key_points: Backtracking search is DFS that assigns one variable per level and backs up when a variable has no legal value.
MRV chooses the variable with the fewest legal values (fail-first); the degree heuristic breaks ties by most constraints.
LCV tries first the value that rules out the fewest values for neighbours.
Forward checking removes inconsistent values from neighbours of the just-assigned variable.
Arc X to Y is consistent if every value of X has some supporting value in Y; AC-3 enforces this for all arcs in O(c d^3).
Arc consistency can solve some CSPs alone (X < Y < Z example) but cannot detect every failure (two-colour triangle).
Min-conflicts local search repairs complete assignments and works very well on n-queens and scheduling.
lessons.tip: Trace forward checking and AC-3 with a domain table: one row per variable, one column per step, crossing out values as they are removed. Examiners like this format, and it makes empty domains obvious.
lessons.task: Solve one easy newspaper or app Sudoku using only constraint propagation: for each empty cell, write the small list of possible digits, and repeatedly fill cells with a single candidate. Note whether you ever needed to guess (backtrack).

quiz.q: Which heuristic chooses the variable with the fewest legal values left?
quiz.explain: MRV is the fail-first heuristic: it exposes dead ends early.

quiz.q: In Australia with all domains full, which variable does the degree heuristic choose first?
quiz.explain: SA is involved in constraints with 5 other regions, the most of any.

quiz.q: After WA = red and Q = green, forward checking leaves NT and SA with only {blue}. What does it fail to notice?
options: That NT and SA are neighbours and cannot both be blue

lessons.title: Knowledge-Based Agents and Propositional Logic
lessons.content:
Think of a good detective in a Bangla mystery story. He does not search every house in the city. He collects small facts ("the gate was locked from inside", "the dog did not bark"), combines them with general knowledge ("a dog barks at strangers"), and concludes new facts ("the visitor was someone the dog knew"). He reasons. So far our agents have searched through states; now we build agents that store knowledge as sentences and reason with it to decide what to do. This lesson introduces knowledge-based agents and the simplest logic they use, propositional logic.

Knowledge base: The central part of a knowledge-based agent is its knowledge base (KB): a set of sentences written in a knowledge representation language. Each sentence states something the agent believes about the world, like "there is no pit in square [1,1]" or "if a square is breezy, a neighbouring square has a pit". Some sentences are given at the start (background knowledge); others are added as the agent perceives the world.

TELL and ASK: A knowledge-based agent uses two standard operations. TELL adds a new sentence to the KB. ASK queries the KB about what is true. When we ASK, the answer must follow from what has been TELLed, through a process called inference. The agent program, in words, at each time step t: TELL the KB what it perceives now; ASK the KB what action it should do; TELL the KB which action it chose; then do the action and increase t. The details of reasoning are hidden inside TELL and ASK.

The declarative approach: You can build such an agent by simply telling it what it needs to know, starting from an empty KB, instead of writing code for every behaviour. This is called the declarative approach, in contrast to the procedural approach, where desired behaviours are coded directly. Real systems usually combine both. The big advantage of the declarative approach is that the same reasoning engine works for many problems; only the knowledge changes.

The wumpus world: The textbook's test world is a cave of 4 x 4 rooms, written [column, row], with the agent starting at [1,1] in the bottom-left. Somewhere is the wumpus, a beast that eats anyone entering its room; some rooms have bottomless pits; one room has gold. The agent senses: a stench in rooms next to the wumpus (not diagonally), a breeze in rooms next to a pit, a glitter in the gold's room, a bump when walking into a wall, and a scream when the wumpus is killed. Actions: Forward, TurnLeft, TurnRight, Grab, Shoot (one arrow only) and Climb (out, only from [1,1]). Performance: +1000 for climbing out with the gold, -1000 for dying, -1 for each action and -10 for using the arrow.

Classifying the wumpus world: Using the dimensions of lesson 3, the wumpus world is partially observable (the agent senses only its own room), deterministic (actions do exactly what they say), sequential (rewards come only after many actions), static (the wumpus and pits do not move), discrete and single-agent (the wumpus is part of the environment, not an opponent that plans). The main challenge is therefore not chance or opponents, but lack of information, which is exactly what logical reasoning helps with.

Reasoning in the wumpus world, step 1: At [1,1], the agent perceives no stench and no breeze. Since there is no breeze, neither neighbour, [1,2] nor [2,1], has a pit. Since there is no stench, neither has the wumpus. So both are safe. The agent moves right to [2,1] and feels a breeze. So there is a pit in [2,2] or [3,1] (not [1,1], which it came from safely). It does not know which, so it goes back and tries the other safe room.

Reasoning in the wumpus world, step 2: At [1,2], the agent smells a stench but feels no breeze. The stench means the wumpus is in [1,3] or [2,2] (not [1,1]). But at [2,1] there was no stench, so the wumpus is not in [2,2], which neighbours [2,1]. So the wumpus is in [1,3]. And no breeze at [1,2] means no pit in [2,2], so the pit noticed earlier must be in [3,1]. Now [2,2] is known to be safe. Pure reasoning from a handful of percepts has located a hidden danger. Our goal is to make a computer do this automatically.

Syntax and semantics: A logic has two parts. Syntax says which sentences are well formed, like grammar: "x + y = 4" is well formed in arithmetic, "x4y+ =" is not. Semantics defines the meaning: the truth of each sentence in each possible world. In logic, a possible world is called a model: a complete assignment of truth (or of values) to everything the sentences talk about. If sentence alpha is true in model m, we say m satisfies alpha, or m is a model of alpha. M(alpha) is the set of all models of alpha.

Entailment: The key idea of logical reasoning is entailment. KB entails alpha, written KB |= alpha, if and only if alpha is true in every model in which KB is true; in symbols, M(KB) is a subset of M(alpha). In plain words: whenever the knowledge base is true, alpha must also be true. For example, the sentence "x = 0" entails "x times y = 0", because in every model where x is zero, the product is zero.

Propositional logic, a recap: Propositional logic is the simplest logic, and you already know it from Discrete Mathematics, so we only recap. Atomic sentences are single symbols like P or W13 that are either true or false. Complex sentences are built with five connectives: not (written ~), and, or, implies (=>) and if and only if (<=>). Precedence from strongest: not, and, or, implies, iff. The only surprising truth-table row is implication: P => Q is false only when P is true and Q is false; when P is false, P => Q is true no matter what Q is.

Writing the wumpus world in propositional logic: Let P(x,y) mean "there is a pit in [x,y]" and B(x,y) mean "there is a breeze in [x,y]". The KB contains: R1: not P(1,1). R2: B(1,1) <=> (P(1,2) or P(2,1)). R3: B(2,1) <=> (P(1,1) or P(2,2) or P(3,1)). These general rules say exactly when a room is breezy. After the first two percepts, the agent adds R4: not B(1,1), and R5: B(2,1). Note the use of <=> rather than =>: a room is breezy if and only if a neighbour has a pit; with only => we could not conclude "no pit" from "no breeze".

Model checking with a truth table: How can the agent decide whether KB |= not P(1,2)? The direct method is model checking: list every model and check that, wherever the KB is true, the query is true too. Our KB uses seven symbols, B(1,1), B(2,1), P(1,1), P(1,2), P(2,1), P(2,2) and P(3,1), so there are 2^7 = 128 models. The KB (R1 to R5) is true in exactly three of them. In all three, P(1,2) is false, so KB |= not P(1,2): there is no pit in [1,2]. But P(2,2) is true in some of the three and false in another, so the KB does not entail either P(2,2) or not P(2,2); the agent cannot yet tell whether [2,2] has a pit.

The truth-table algorithm: The algorithm TT-ENTAILS(KB, alpha) enumerates all models recursively, assigning true and false to each symbol in turn, and checks alpha in every model where KB is true. It is sound (it only reports true entailments) and complete (it finds every entailment), because the number of models is finite. But with n symbols it takes O(2^n) time; space is only O(n), since it is a depth-first enumeration. With 50 symbols, 2^50 is about 10^15 models, already too many.

Sound and complete inference: More generally, an inference algorithm i derives alpha from KB, written KB |-i alpha. It is sound (truth-preserving) if it derives only sentences that are entailed; an unsound algorithm makes things up, like a gossip. It is complete if it can derive every sentence that is entailed. We want both. Also, if the KB is true in the real world, then anything derived by a sound procedure is also true in the real world; this connection is called grounding, and it depends on the agent's sensors and rules being correct.

Validity and satisfiability: A sentence is valid (a tautology) if it is true in all models, like "P or not P". A sentence is satisfiable if it is true in at least one model, and unsatisfiable if it is true in none, like "P and not P". Two facts link these to entailment. The deduction theorem: alpha |= beta if and only if (alpha => beta) is valid. And proof by contradiction: alpha |= beta if and only if (alpha and not beta) is unsatisfiable. This second fact is the basis of resolution in the next lesson. Checking satisfiability (the SAT problem) is NP-complete, yet modern SAT solvers handle problems with very many variables in practice.

Real life example 1, a smart home rule system: A smart home in Gulshan might store rules like "if the gas sensor is on, then danger" and "danger implies alarm and open window", and facts from sensors like "gas sensor is on". By inference, the system concludes "alarm" and "open window". Writing the knowledge as rules means an engineer can add a new rule ("if smoke and night, then call the guard") without rewriting the program.

Real life example 2, checking a class routine: The rules of a timetable can be written in propositional logic, with a symbol like MathSun1 meaning "the maths class is on Sunday, period 1". Constraints become sentences, like "not (MathSun1 and PhysicsSun1)" if one teacher teaches both. A SAT solver can then check whether a routine satisfying all sentences exists. Many industrial tools, for example in checking computer chip designs, translate problems into propositional logic for SAT solvers in exactly this way.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students confuse entailment (|=, about truth in models) with implication (=>, a connective inside a sentence) and with derivation (|-, about an algorithm). Another frequent error is the implication truth table when the left side is false. In the wumpus world, many write breeze rules with => only, which loses information. Typical questions: describe the wumpus world and its PEAS; reason by hand about which rooms are safe after given percepts; define model, entailment, soundness and completeness; check an entailment with a truth table; and define validity and satisfiability with examples.

Recap: A knowledge-based agent keeps a KB of sentences, adds percepts with TELL and gets actions with ASK. Logic gives sentences a syntax and a semantics in terms of models. KB |= alpha means alpha is true in every model of KB. Propositional logic can describe the wumpus world, and truth-table model checking decides entailment soundly and completely, but in O(2^n) time. Validity, satisfiability and the link "alpha |= beta iff alpha and not beta is unsatisfiable" prepare us for faster inference methods in the next lesson.
key_points: A knowledge-based agent stores sentences in a KB, uses TELL to add facts and ASK to query, with inference in between.
In the wumpus world, breezes signal pits and stenches signal the wumpus in adjacent rooms.
A model is a possible world; M(alpha) is the set of models where alpha is true.
KB |= alpha means alpha is true in every model where KB is true.
P => Q is false only when P is true and Q is false.
Truth-table model checking is sound and complete but takes O(2^n) time for n symbols.
alpha |= beta exactly when (alpha and not beta) is unsatisfiable; this is the basis of proof by contradiction.
lessons.tip: Keep three symbols apart in your notes: => is a connective inside a sentence, |= is entailment between sentences, and |- is what an inference algorithm derives. Writing a one-line example next to each removes most confusion.
lessons.task: Draw a 4 x 4 wumpus cave on paper. Ask a friend to secretly place one wumpus, two pits and the gold. Then ask only for percepts (stench, breeze, glitter) of rooms you choose to "enter", and use reasoning to avoid danger. Count how many moves you needed to find the gold safely.

lessons.title: Inference in Propositional Logic: Resolution and Chaining
lessons.content:
In a cricket match, the umpire does not watch replays of every possible way the ball could have travelled. He uses rules: "if the ball pitched in line, would have hit the stumps, and hit the pad first, then it is out". He chains facts and rules to reach a decision. Last lesson, our agent checked entailment by listing all possible worlds, which takes 2^n time. Today we learn to reason like the umpire: by applying rules of inference directly to sentences, producing a proof. We cover inference rules, the powerful resolution method, and the fast forward and backward chaining methods used in rule-based systems.

Theorem proving: Instead of enumerating models, theorem proving applies rules of inference to the sentences in the KB to build a chain of conclusions, called a proof, ending in the sentence we want. When there are many models but the proof is short, this is far more efficient. Two simple rules: Modus Ponens: from "alpha => beta" and "alpha", infer "beta". And-Elimination: from "alpha and beta", infer "alpha". We can also use any logical equivalence, such as De Morgan's laws, the contrapositive (alpha => beta is equivalent to not beta => not alpha), and biconditional elimination (alpha <=> beta is equivalent to (alpha => beta) and (beta => alpha)).

A proof in the wumpus world: From the KB of lesson 16 we prove that there is no pit in [1,2] or [2,1]. Start with R2: B(1,1) <=> (P(1,2) or P(2,1)). Biconditional elimination gives (B(1,1) => (P(1,2) or P(2,1))) and ((P(1,2) or P(2,1)) => B(1,1)). And-Elimination keeps the second part: (P(1,2) or P(2,1)) => B(1,1). Contrapositive: not B(1,1) => not (P(1,2) or P(2,1)). Modus Ponens with R4 (not B(1,1)) gives not (P(1,2) or P(2,1)). De Morgan: not P(1,2) and not P(2,1). Five short steps, and we never looked at the 128 models.

Monotonicity: Propositional logic is monotonic: adding new sentences to the KB can never remove a conclusion that was already entailed. If KB |= alpha, then KB plus beta |= alpha for any beta. This means an inference rule can be applied whenever its premises are found in the KB, without worrying about what else is there. (Human common-sense reasoning is often not monotonic, which is one reason it is hard to formalise.)

Searching for proofs: Finding a proof is itself a search problem: the initial state is the KB, the actions are applications of inference rules, the result adds the conclusion, and the goal is a state containing the query. But with many rules, which one to apply? We would like one single rule that, combined with a complete search, is complete on its own. That rule is resolution.

The resolution rule: Resolution works on clauses, which are disjunctions (ORs) of literals, where a literal is a symbol or its negation. The rule: from two clauses that contain complementary literals, one with P and the other with not P, infer a new clause containing all the other literals of both. Example: from (A or B) and (not B or C), infer (A or C). Reason it out: B is either true or false; if B is false, the first clause gives A; if B is true, the second gives C; either way A or C holds. A special case, unit resolution: from (A or B) and not B, infer A. If the same literal appears twice in the result, we keep only one copy (factoring).

Conjunctive normal form: Resolution needs sentences in conjunctive normal form (CNF): a conjunction (AND) of clauses. Every propositional sentence can be converted to CNF in four steps. One: eliminate <=>, replacing alpha <=> beta by (alpha => beta) and (beta => alpha). Two: eliminate =>, replacing alpha => beta by not alpha or beta. Three: move "not" inwards using De Morgan's laws and double negation, so "not" appears only in front of symbols. Four: distribute "or" over "and", for example (A and B) or C becomes (A or C) and (B or C).

CNF worked example: Convert R2: B(1,1) <=> (P(1,2) or P(2,1)). Step one: (B(1,1) => (P(1,2) or P(2,1))) and ((P(1,2) or P(2,1)) => B(1,1)). Step two: (not B(1,1) or P(1,2) or P(2,1)) and (not (P(1,2) or P(2,1)) or B(1,1)). Step three: (not B(1,1) or P(1,2) or P(2,1)) and ((not P(1,2) and not P(2,1)) or B(1,1)). Step four: (not B(1,1) or P(1,2) or P(2,1)) and (not P(1,2) or B(1,1)) and (not P(2,1) or B(1,1)). Three clauses.

Resolution refutation: To show KB |= alpha, we use proof by contradiction: show that KB and not alpha is unsatisfiable. Convert KB and not alpha to CNF, then repeatedly resolve pairs of clauses and add the results. Two things can happen. If we derive the empty clause (a clause with no literals, which means a contradiction, as from P and not P), then KB |= alpha. If no new clauses can be added, then KB does not entail alpha.

Refutation example: Prove alpha = not P(1,2) from the clauses of R2 and R4 (not B(1,1)). Add the negated goal: P(1,2). Resolve (not P(1,2) or B(1,1)) with P(1,2): we get B(1,1). Resolve B(1,1) with not B(1,1): we get the empty clause. Contradiction! So the KB entails not P(1,2): no pit in [1,2]. Two resolution steps.

Soundness and completeness of resolution: Resolution is sound: every resolvent is entailed by its parents. And resolution is refutation-complete: the ground resolution theorem says that if a set of clauses is unsatisfiable, resolution will eventually derive the empty clause. So resolution alone, with a systematic search, can decide any entailment in propositional logic. In the worst case it can still take exponential time, which is expected, since SAT is NP-complete.

Horn clauses: Many real knowledge bases only need a restricted kind of clause. A Horn clause has at most one positive literal. A definite clause has exactly one positive literal; it can be written as a rule: (A and B and C) => D, where the left part is the body (premise) and D is the head (conclusion); a single positive symbol, like A, is a fact. A goal clause has no positive literal. Knowledge bases of definite clauses have a big advantage: entailment can be decided in time linear in the size of the KB, using forward or backward chaining, which people also find natural to follow.

Forward chaining: Forward chaining starts from known facts and fires any rule whose premises are all known, adding its conclusion as a new fact, until the query is added or nothing new can be found. Example KB: P => Q; (L and M) => P; (B and L) => M; (A and P) => L; (A and B) => L; facts A and B. Query: Q. Trace: A and B are known, so (A and B) => L fires: L. Now B and L are known, so (B and L) => M fires: M. Now L and M are known, so (L and M) => P fires: P. Now P => Q fires: Q. Query proved. Forward chaining is data-driven: it reacts to new facts, like a person who keeps noticing consequences of what they see.

Backward chaining: Backward chaining works from the query backwards. To prove Q, find a rule with Q as head: P => Q, so prove P. To prove P, use (L and M) => P, so prove L and M. To prove L: the rule (A and P) => L needs P, which we are already trying to prove, so skip it to avoid a loop; the rule (A and B) => L needs A and B, both facts, so L is proved. To prove M: (B and L) => M; B is a fact and L is proved, so M is proved. Hence P, hence Q. Backward chaining is goal-directed: it only touches facts and rules relevant to the question, so it often does much less work than forward chaining. Prolog, which we meet in lesson 19, uses backward chaining.

Comparing the two chaining styles on one question: Suppose the KB also had a hundred unrelated rules about the weather and traffic. Forward chaining would happily fire all of them whenever their facts were present, producing many conclusions nobody asked for, before or after reaching Q. Backward chaining would never look at them, because none has Q, P, L or M as its head. On the other hand, forward chaining is the right choice for a monitoring agent that must notice every consequence of new percepts, such as a fire-alarm system. Both are sound, and both are complete for definite clauses.

Efficient model checking, a short note: Model checking does not have to list all 2^n models blindly. The DPLL algorithm searches over models depth-first but prunes early: it stops a branch as soon as one clause is false, assigns "pure" symbols that appear with only one sign, and immediately assigns symbols that are forced by unit clauses. WalkSAT is a local search for satisfiability, like min-conflicts for CSPs. Modern SAT solvers, built on these ideas with many improvements, routinely handle problems with a very large number of variables in hardware and software verification.

Real life example 1, a medical rule system: A simple clinic support system in a district hospital could store rules like "(fever and rash) => suspect measles" and "(suspect measles and no vaccination record) => refer to specialist". When a nurse enters facts about a child, forward chaining fires the rules and shows all conclusions. If the doctor asks "should this child be referred?", backward chaining checks only the rules that can lead to a referral and asks for missing facts. Real systems also need uncertainty handling, which we study in lessons 22 and 23.

Real life example 2, an admission eligibility checker: A university website can check whether an applicant is eligible: "(SSC GPA at least 4 and HSC GPA at least 4 and science group) => eligible for engineering". Each condition is a fact from the form. Backward chaining from "eligible" asks only the needed questions, and the "explanation" is simply the chain of rules used, which makes the decision easy to check.

Common mistakes and exam questions: In CNF conversion, students often forget to eliminate <=> first, or distribute "and" over "or" in the wrong direction. In resolution, they resolve on two pairs of literals at once, which is not allowed: resolve on exactly one complementary pair. Many forget to negate the query before refutation. Typical questions: convert a sentence to CNF; prove a query by resolution refutation; define Horn and definite clauses; trace forward and backward chaining on a small rule set; and compare data-driven and goal-directed reasoning.

Recap: Theorem proving uses inference rules like Modus Ponens and And-Elimination plus logical equivalences to build proofs. Resolution, working on CNF clauses with proof by contradiction, is sound and refutation-complete. Horn and definite clause KBs allow linear-time inference by forward chaining (data-driven) or backward chaining (goal-directed). DPLL and WalkSAT make model checking practical. Next lesson, we move to a much more expressive language: first-order logic.
key_points: Modus Ponens: from alpha => beta and alpha, infer beta; And-Elimination: from alpha and beta, infer alpha.
Propositional logic is monotonic: adding sentences never removes old conclusions.
Resolution: from (A or B) and (not B or C), infer (A or C); it works on clauses in CNF.
CNF conversion: eliminate <=>, eliminate =>, move not inwards, distribute or over and.
Resolution refutation proves KB |= alpha by deriving the empty clause from KB and not alpha; it is sound and refutation-complete.
Definite clauses (exactly one positive literal) allow linear-time forward and backward chaining.
Forward chaining is data-driven; backward chaining is goal-directed and often does less work.
lessons.tip: In resolution proofs, number every clause and write each new clause as "(5) from (2) and (4)". It keeps long proofs readable and lets the examiner follow, and award marks for, each step.
lessons.task: Write five rules about your daily routine as definite clauses, for example "(raining and no umbrella) => take rickshaw". Add three facts for today. Run forward chaining by hand to see everything that follows, then pick one conclusion and prove it again by backward chaining.

quiz.q: What does the resolution rule infer from (A or B) and (not B or C)?
quiz.explain: The complementary pair B and not B cancels, leaving the other literals.

quiz.q: Which is the first step when converting a sentence to CNF?
quiz.explain: Order: eliminate <=>, then =>, then move not inwards, then distribute.

quiz.q: How does resolution refutation show that KB |= alpha?
options: By deriving alpha directly with Modus Ponens
By checking that alpha is valid
By deriving the empty clause from KB and not alpha
quiz.explain: An empty clause means KB and not alpha is unsatisfiable, so KB entails alpha.

quiz.q: What is a definite clause?
options: A clause with exactly one positive literal
A clause with only negative literals
quiz.explain: It can be written as a rule (body => head) or as a fact.

quiz.q: Which statement about forward and backward chaining is correct?
options: Forward chaining starts from the query
Forward chaining is data-driven; backward chaining is goal-directed
Both take exponential time on definite clauses
quiz.explain: Both run in linear time on definite clauses; they differ in direction.

lessons.title: First-Order Logic
lessons.content:
Imagine telling a robot the rules of your school using only propositional logic. You would need a separate symbol for every fact: "Rahim is a student", "Karim is a student", "Rahim passed maths", and a separate rule for every student: "if Rahim passed all subjects, Rahim gets promoted", "if Karim passed all subjects, Karim gets promoted", and so on for all 800 students. That is clumsy and silly. People simply say "every student who passes all subjects gets promoted". First-order logic lets a computer say it that way too. This lesson introduces first-order logic (FOL), also called predicate logic, the main language for representing knowledge in classic AI.

The limits of propositional logic: Propositional logic treats every fact as a single unbreakable symbol. It cannot talk about objects and their properties in general. In the wumpus world, we had to write the breeze rule separately for each of the 16 rooms: B(1,1) <=> (P(1,2) or P(2,1)), then B(2,1) <=> ..., and so on. There was no way to say "for every room, it is breezy if and only if some adjacent room has a pit". As the world grows, the number of sentences grows with it. Natural language, by contrast, is built around objects (people, rooms, numbers), relations between them and general statements about all or some of them.

What FOL assumes about the world: Every logic makes an ontological commitment: what it assumes exists. Propositional logic assumes the world consists of facts that are true or false. First-order logic assumes the world contains objects (Rahim, Dhaka, the number 3, room [2,1]), relations among objects (Brother, Adjacent, GreaterThan, and properties like Student, which are relations with one argument), and functions (FatherOf, LeftLeg, Plus) that map objects to other objects. Probability theory, which we study later, makes a different kind of commitment, about what the agent believes: degrees of belief between 0 and 1, rather than just true, false or unknown.

The building blocks of FOL syntax: Constant symbols name objects, like Rahim, Karim, Dhaka, AI. Predicate symbols name relations, like Student, Brother, Teaches, Adjacent. Function symbols name functions, like FatherOf, Age. A term is an expression that refers to an object: a constant (Rahim), a variable (x), or a function applied to terms (FatherOf(Rahim)). Note that FatherOf(Rahim) is not a new name; it is a way of referring to Rahim's father without knowing his name.

Atomic and complex sentences: An atomic sentence is a predicate applied to terms: Brother(Rahim, Karim) says Rahim and Karim are brothers. Married(FatherOf(Rahim), MotherOf(Rahim)) says Rahim's father is married to Rahim's mother. An atomic sentence is true in a model if the relation named by the predicate holds among the objects referred to by the terms. Complex sentences use the same connectives as propositional logic: not, and, or, =>, <=>. For example: Student(Rahim) and not Student(FatherOf(Rahim)).

Models in FOL: A model in FOL contains a domain, the set of objects that exist, which must be non-empty, and an interpretation that says which object each constant refers to, which tuples of objects are in each relation, and what each function returns. Because there can be any number of objects and countless interpretations, we can no longer check entailment by listing all models; in general there are infinitely many. That is one reason FOL inference needs the methods of the next lesson.

The universal quantifier: The universal quantifier, "for all" (written forall), states something about every object. "All students in this school are Bangladeshi" becomes: forall x Student(x) => Bangladeshi(x). Read it as: for every object x, if x is a student then x is Bangladeshi. The sentence is true if it holds for every possible value of x in the domain, including objects that are not students; for them the implication is true automatically, because its left side is false.

The existential quantifier: The existential quantifier, "there exists" (written exists), says that at least one object has a property. "Some student in the class plays cricket" becomes: exists x Student(x) and PlaysCricket(x). The sentence is true if at least one object in the domain makes the inside true.

The most common mistake with quantifiers: The natural connective with "forall" is "=>", and with "exists" it is "and". Swapping them gives wrong meanings. "forall x Student(x) and Bangladeshi(x)" says that everything in the whole world is a student and is Bangladeshi, including the classroom chairs. "exists x Student(x) => PlaysCricket(x)" is true as soon as there is any object that is not a student, like a chair, because then the implication is true; so it says almost nothing. Remember the pair: forall with =>, exists with and.

Nested quantifiers: Quantifiers can be combined. "Everybody loves somebody": forall x exists y Loves(x, y). "There is someone who is loved by everyone": exists y forall x Loves(x, y). The order matters a lot: the first says each person has someone they love, possibly different people; the second says a single person is loved by all. Consecutive quantifiers of the same type can be swapped: forall x forall y is the same as forall y forall x.

Connections between the quantifiers: The two quantifiers are linked by negation, just like De Morgan's laws. "Everyone dislikes bitter gourd" is the same as "there is nobody who likes bitter gourd": forall x not Likes(x, BitterGourd) is equivalent to not exists x Likes(x, BitterGourd). And "not everyone likes cricket" means "someone does not like cricket": not forall x Likes(x, Cricket) is equivalent to exists x not Likes(x, Cricket). You met these rules in Discrete Mathematics; in FOL they are used constantly.

Equality: FOL usually includes the equality symbol: Term1 = Term2 is true if both terms refer to the same object. FatherOf(Rahim) = Kamal says Kamal is Rahim's father. Equality lets us count: "Rahim has at least two brothers" is exists x, y Brother(x, Rahim) and Brother(y, Rahim) and not (x = y). Without the last part, x and y could be the same person.

Practice translations, step by step: "No one likes exams": there is no person who likes exams, so not exists x Person(x) and Likes(x, Exams), or equivalently forall x Person(x) => not Likes(x, Exams). "Every teacher teaches at least one course": forall t Teacher(t) => exists c Course(c) and Teaches(t, c); notice the inner exists uses and, while the outer forall uses =>. "Only students can borrow books from the library": forall x Borrows(x, Library) => Student(x); the word "only" turns the direction of the implication around, a favourite exam trap. Writing each sentence in both forms (with forall and with not exists) is a good self-check.

The kinship domain, writing definitions: Family relations are a classic example. Basic predicates: Parent, Female, Male. Definitions: forall m, c Mother(m, c) <=> Female(m) and Parent(m, c). forall g, c Grandparent(g, c) <=> exists p Parent(g, p) and Parent(p, c). forall x, y Sibling(x, y) <=> not (x = y) and exists p Parent(p, x) and Parent(p, y). With these few sentences, a KB that knows parents automatically knows all grandparents and siblings, for every family, with no extra rules.

The wumpus world in FOL: Now the breeze rule needs only one sentence: forall s Breezy(s) <=> exists r Adjacent(r, s) and Pit(r). Adjacency of rooms can also be defined once: forall x, y, a, b Adjacent([x, y], [a, b]) <=> (x = a and (y = b - 1 or y = b + 1)) or (y = b and (x = a - 1 or x = a + 1)). One general rule replaces sixteen specific ones, and works for a cave of any size.

Two ways to read names: In standard FOL semantics, two different constants may refer to the same object, and facts not stated are simply unknown. So if the KB says Brother(Karim, Rahim) and Brother(Sakib, Rahim), it does not follow that Rahim has two brothers: Karim and Sakib might be the same person, and there might be other brothers not mentioned. Databases usually assume the opposite: different names mean different objects (the unique-names assumption), and anything not stated is false (the closed-world assumption). Both readings are useful, but you must know which one a system uses before trusting its answers to counting questions.

Asking questions: With FOL we TELL the KB sentences, like TELL(KB, Student(Rahim)), and ASK questions, like ASK(KB, exists x Student(x)), which returns true. Often we want to know which object makes a query true. ASKVARS(KB, Student(x)) returns a substitution, a set of variable bindings such as {x/Rahim} and {x/Karim}. This is how a question like "who are the students?" is answered.

Knowledge engineering: Building a KB in FOL for a real domain is called knowledge engineering. A standard process: identify the questions the KB must answer; collect the relevant knowledge, often by talking to experts; decide a vocabulary of predicates, functions and constants (an ontology); write the general rules of the domain; describe the specific problem instance; pose queries and get answers; and debug, because a missing or wrong rule leads to missing or wrong answers. The textbook works through this for digital circuits: gates, wires and signals become objects, relations and rules, and the KB can then answer "what is the output for these inputs?".

Beyond first-order logic: FOL quantifies over objects, but not over relations or functions themselves. A statement like "for every relation R, if R is symmetric then..." needs higher-order logic, which is more expressive but has much weaker computational properties. FOL also has no built-in notion of time, belief or probability; those are added through special vocabularies, other logics, or probability theory. For most classic AI knowledge bases, FOL is a good balance between what it can say and what can be computed.

Real life example 1, a university rule base: A university can write rules like: forall s (Student(s) and Passed(s, AI) and Passed(s, Statistics)) => CanTake(s, MachineLearning). And: forall s, c (Enrolled(s, c) and not Paid(s)) => Blocked(s, c). With facts about each student, the system answers "which students can take Machine Learning?" for 5,000 students with two rules, not 10,000.

Real life example 2, a family tree app: Family-tree websites and apps store parent links and display uncles, cousins and in-laws. Behind the screen, relations like Cousin are defined from Parent and Sibling, exactly like the kinship definitions above: forall x, y Cousin(x, y) <=> exists p, q Parent(p, x) and Parent(q, y) and Sibling(p, q). A family in Cumilla can enter just parents and children, and every other relation follows by logic.

Common mistakes and exam questions: The top mistake is using "and" with forall or "=>" with exists. Others: confusing a function with a predicate (FatherOf(Rahim) is an object; Father(Kamal, Rahim) is a sentence that is true or false), forgetting "not (x = y)" when counting, and mixing up the order of nested quantifiers. Typical questions: translate English sentences into FOL (like "every student who passes AI is happy" or "no one likes exams"); translate FOL back into English; write kinship definitions; explain the difference between propositional and first-order logic; and use quantifier negation rules.

Recap: First-order logic describes a world of objects, relations and functions using constants, predicates, functions, variables, connectives, quantifiers and equality. Forall pairs naturally with =>, exists with and. Nested quantifiers depend on order, and negation swaps forall with exists. One FOL sentence can replace many propositional ones, as in the wumpus breeze rule. Next lesson, we learn how to reason in FOL: unification, chaining, resolution and Prolog.
key_points: Propositional logic cannot state general rules about all objects; FOL can.
FOL assumes the world has objects, relations and functions.
Terms refer to objects: constants, variables and function applications like FatherOf(Rahim).
Universal statements use forall with =>; existential statements use exists with and.
The order of nested quantifiers matters: forall x exists y differs from exists y forall x.
not forall x P is equivalent to exists x not P, and not exists x P to forall x not P.
Equality (=) lets us say two terms are the same object and count objects.
lessons.tip: Before translating an English sentence into FOL, underline the objects, circle the properties and relations, and mark words like "every", "some" and "no". Then pick forall with => or exists with and. This three-colour habit prevents most translation errors.
lessons.task: Translate these into FOL using predicates you invent: (1) Every student in your class owns a phone. (2) Some teacher teaches both AI and Graphics. (3) No one in your family likes bitter gourd. (4) Everyone has a mother. Then check each for the forall-with-and or exists-with-implies mistake.

quiz.q: What does first-order logic assume the world contains, beyond facts?
options: Objects, relations among them and functions
quiz.explain: FOL's ontological commitment is objects, relations and functions.

quiz.q: Which is the correct translation of "Every student is Bangladeshi"?
quiz.explain: Forall pairs with =>; using and would claim everything is a student.

quiz.q: What does exists y forall x Loves(x, y) mean?
options: There is someone whom everybody loves
quiz.explain: The single y is chosen first, then every x loves that y.

quiz.q: not forall x Likes(x, Cricket) is equivalent to:
quiz.explain: "Not everyone likes cricket" means "someone does not like cricket".

quiz.q: In FOL, FatherOf(Rahim) is:
options: A sentence that is true or false
A term that refers to an object (Rahim's father)
quiz.explain: A function applied to a term gives a term, not a sentence.

lessons.title: Inference in First-Order Logic and Prolog
lessons.content:
Your teacher says, "Anyone who scores above 80 in the final gets an A", and the result sheet shows "Nadia scored 86". You instantly conclude "Nadia gets an A". Notice what your brain did: it matched the general word "anyone" with the specific person "Nadia", and then applied the rule. That matching step is the heart of reasoning in first-order logic, and AI calls it unification. In this lesson we see how an agent reasons with FOL sentences: by turning them back into propositional logic, by unification and generalised Modus Ponens, by forward and backward chaining, by resolution, and in the logic programming language Prolog.

Universal instantiation: A sentence that starts with "forall" can be applied to any specific object. The rule of universal instantiation (UI) says: from forall x alpha, we can infer alpha with x replaced by any ground term (a term with no variables). From forall x Student(x) => HasID(x), we can infer Student(Nadia) => HasID(Nadia), or Student(FatherOf(Nadia)) => HasID(FatherOf(Nadia)). A substitution is written like {x/Nadia}, meaning "replace x by Nadia".

Existential instantiation: From exists x alpha, we may replace x with a brand-new constant that does not appear anywhere else in the KB. From exists x Crown(x) and OnHead(x, John), we infer Crown(C1) and OnHead(C1, John), where C1 is a new name for "the crown, whichever it is". Such a new constant is called a Skolem constant. It must be new; using an existing name like Rahim would claim something we do not know.

Propositionalisation and its limit: Using these two rules, we could turn a FOL KB into a propositional one by instantiating every universal sentence with every ground term, and then use the methods of lesson 17. With function symbols, however, there are infinitely many ground terms: Nadia, FatherOf(Nadia), FatherOf(FatherOf(Nadia)), and so on. A theorem by Herbrand guarantees that if a sentence is entailed, a proof exists using only finitely many of them, so we can try nesting depth 1, then 2, and so on. But if the sentence is not entailed, this may never stop. Entailment in FOL is therefore semidecidable: there are algorithms that say yes to every entailed sentence, but none that also says no to every non-entailed one.

Unification: Propositionalising everything is wasteful: why create rules for every object when we only care about Nadia? Instead, we find a substitution that makes two sentences look the same. UNIFY(p, q) returns a substitution theta that makes p and q identical, called a unifier, or fails if none exists. For example, UNIFY(Knows(John, x), Knows(John, Jane)) = {x/Jane}. UNIFY(Knows(John, x), Knows(y, Bill)) = {x/Bill, y/John}. UNIFY(Knows(John, x), Knows(y, Mother(y))) = {y/John, x/Mother(John)}: first y must be John, then x must be Mother(y), which is Mother(John).

When unification fails, and standardising apart: UNIFY(Knows(John, x), Knows(x, Elizabeth)) fails, because x cannot be both John and Elizabeth. But if these come from two different sentences, their x's are unrelated variables that happen to share a name. Renaming one of them, say to x17, fixes it: UNIFY(Knows(John, x), Knows(x17, Elizabeth)) = {x/Elizabeth, x17/John}. Renaming variables so that different sentences share none is called standardising apart. Another failure is the occur check: x cannot unify with F(x), because x would have to contain itself forever.

A unification walkthrough: Unify P(x, F(y)) with P(G(z), F(A)), where A is a constant. Compare argument by argument. First arguments: x and G(z); x is a variable, so bind x/G(z). Second arguments: F(y) and F(A); same function symbol, so unify inside: y and A, bind y/A. Result: {x/G(z), y/A}. Applying it to both sentences gives P(G(z), F(A)) in both cases, so the unifier is correct. If instead the second sentence were P(G(z), H(A)), unification would fail at the second argument, because F and H are different function symbols and can never be made equal.

Most general unifier: Often many unifiers exist. UNIFY(Knows(John, x), Knows(y, z)) could return {y/John, x/z}, or {y/John, x/John, z/John}. The first is more general: it makes the sentences equal while committing to as little as possible.
