For every unifiable pair, there is a single most general unifier (MGU), unique up to renaming of variables, and the unification algorithm returns it. Using the MGU keeps conclusions as general as possible.

Generalised Modus Ponens: Combining unification with Modus Ponens gives one powerful rule. If we have a rule (p1 and p2 and ... and pn) => q, and facts p1', ..., pn' such that one substitution theta makes each pi' equal to pi, then we infer q with theta applied. Example: rule King(x) and Greedy(x) => Evil(x); facts King(John) and Greedy(y) (everyone is greedy). Theta = {x/John, y/John} matches both premises, so we infer Evil(John). This lifted version of Modus Ponens works directly on sentences with variables, creating only the instances we need.

The crime example: A classic textbook problem. The law says it is a crime for an American to sell weapons to hostile nations. The country Nono, an enemy of America, has some missiles, and all of its missiles were sold to it by Colonel West, who is American. Prove West is a criminal. In FOL, as definite clauses: (1) American(x) and Weapon(y) and Sells(x, y, z) and Hostile(z) => Criminal(x). (2) Owns(Nono, M1) and (3) Missile(M1), with M1 a Skolem constant for "some missile". (4) Missile(x) and Owns(Nono, x) => Sells(West, x, Nono). (5) Missile(x) => Weapon(x). (6) Enemy(x, America) => Hostile(x). (7) American(West). (8) Enemy(Nono, America).

Forward chaining on the crime example: Start with the facts and fire every rule whose premises unify with known facts. Round 1: rule 4 with {x/M1} gives Sells(West, M1, Nono); rule 5 with {x/M1} gives Weapon(M1); rule 6 with {x/Nono} gives Hostile(Nono). Round 2: rule 1 with {x/West, y/M1, z/Nono} gives Criminal(West). Done in two rounds. When a KB has no function symbols (a Datalog KB), forward chaining always reaches a fixed point, where no new facts can be added, and it is complete. With function symbols it may run forever if the query is not entailed.

Backward chaining on the crime example: Start from the goal Criminal(West). Rule 1 unifies with {x/West}, creating sub-goals: American(West), Weapon(y), Sells(West, y, z), Hostile(z). American(West) is fact 7. Weapon(y): rule 5 gives sub-goal Missile(y), which fact 3 satisfies with {y/M1}. Sells(West, M1, z): rule 4 with z = Nono needs Missile(M1) and Owns(Nono, M1), both facts. Hostile(Nono): rule 6 needs Enemy(Nono, America), fact 8. Every sub-goal succeeds, so Criminal(West) is proved. Notice how the substitutions found for one sub-goal (y = M1) are passed on to the next.

Making chaining efficient: Naive forward chaining re-checks every rule against every fact on every round, which wastes time. Incremental forward chaining only looks at rules whose premises include a fact added in the previous round, since nothing else can produce anything new. Backward chaining has a different problem: it may prove the same sub-goal again and again, for example the same Weapon(M1) inside many branches. Storing results of sub-goals already solved (called memoisation, or tabling in logic programming) avoids this repeated work, and also helps stop some infinite loops.

Prolog: Prolog ("programming in logic") is a language built on backward chaining over definite clauses. A rule is written head first: criminal(X) :- american(X), weapon(Y), sells(X, Y, Z), hostile(Z). Variables start with capital letters, constants with small letters, and ":-" means "if". A family example: parent(rahim, karim). parent(karim, nadia). grandparent(X, Z) :- parent(X, Y), parent(Y, Z). Asking ?- grandparent(rahim, W). makes Prolog unify, search depth-first and answer W = nadia. Prolog has been used for expert systems, language processing and teaching logic.

Prolog's practical shortcuts: For speed, Prolog makes choices that differ from pure logic. It searches depth-first, trying clauses top to bottom and sub-goals left to right, so a badly ordered rule like path(X, Z) :- path(X, Y), link(Y, Z). can loop forever, while path(X, Z) :- link(X, Y), path(Y, Z). works on graphs without cycles (on graphs with cycles, even this order can loop). Most Prolog systems skip the occur check by default, for speed. And Prolog uses negation as failure: "not P" succeeds if P cannot be proved, which is the closed-world assumption from lesson 18. Programmers must know these points to write correct Prolog.

Resolution in first-order logic: Resolution also lifts to FOL. Convert every sentence to CNF: eliminate implications, move "not" inwards (also through quantifiers), standardise variables apart, Skolemise (replace existential variables by Skolem constants or, when inside a forall, by Skolem functions of the universal variables), drop the forall symbols, and distribute or over and. Then resolve clauses using unification: two literals are complementary if one unifies with the negation of the other. Adding the negated goal and deriving the empty clause proves the goal. FOL resolution is sound and refutation-complete, and it is the basis of many automated theorem provers, which have been used to check designs of hardware and to help prove mathematical theorems.

Real life example 1, a course prerequisite checker: A university registration system can store facts like prerequisite(ai, discrete_math) and passed(nadia, discrete_math), and two rules in Making chaining efficient: Naive forward chaining re-checks every rule against every fact on every round, which wastes time. Incremental forward chaining only looks at rules whose premises include a fact added in the previous round, since nothing else can produce anything new. Backward chaining has a different problem: it may prove the same sub-goal again and again, for example the same Weapon(M1) inside many branches. Storing results of sub-goals already solved (called memoisation, or tabling in logic programming) avoids this repeated work, and also helps stop some infinite loops.

Prolog: missing(S, C) :- prerequisite(C, P), \+ passed(S, P). and canTake(S, C) :- course(C), \+ missing(S, C). Here \+ is Prolog's negation as failure: a student can take a course if no prerequisite is missing. Asking ?- canTake(nadia, ai). runs backward chaining with unification, and the chain of rules used becomes an explanation shown to the student.

Real life example 2, a fraud alert rule engine: A mobile banking company might write rules like: suspicious(T) :- transaction(T, Account, Amount), Amount > 50000, newDevice(Account). Each new transaction is a fact; forward chaining with unification fires rules immediately and raises alerts. Rule engines used in industry work on this principle, often with efficient matching algorithms such as Rete, which avoid re-checking every rule against every fact each time.

Common mistakes and exam questions: In existential instantiation, students reuse an existing constant; always use a new one. In unification, they forget to apply earlier bindings (in Knows(John, x) with Knows(y, Mother(y)), x is Mother(John), not Mother(y)). Many forget standardising apart and declare unification failures that are not real. Typical questions: give the unifier for pairs of sentences; prove a query with forward chaining and backward chaining (the crime example is a favourite); write a small family program in Prolog; explain semidecidability; and list the steps of CNF conversion for FOL including Skolemisation.

Recap: Universal and existential instantiation can reduce FOL to propositional logic, but entailment is only semidecidable. Unification finds the most general substitution making two sentences identical, and generalised Modus Ponens uses it to apply rules directly. Forward chaining (data-driven) and backward chaining (goal-directed) work on definite clauses; the crime example proves Criminal(West) both ways. Prolog is backward chaining with practical shortcuts, and FOL resolution with Skolemisation is sound and refutation-complete. Next lesson, we look at how to organise large knowledge bases: ontologies, semantic networks, frames and expert systems.
key_points: Universal instantiation replaces a forall variable with any ground term; existential instantiation uses a new Skolem constant.
Entailment in FOL is semidecidable: entailed sentences can be proved, but non-entailment may never be detected.
UNIFY(p, q) finds a substitution making p and q identical; the most general unifier commits to as little as possible.
Standardising apart renames variables so different sentences do not share them; the occur check stops x unifying with F(x).
Generalised Modus Ponens applies a rule after unifying its premises with facts.
In the crime example, forward chaining derives Criminal(West) in two rounds; backward chaining proves it from the goal.
Prolog uses depth-first backward chaining, negation as failure and usually no occur check.
lessons.tip: When unifying, go argument by argument from left to right, and after each new binding, rewrite both sentences with it before moving on. This one habit prevents the classic "forgot to apply the earlier binding" error.
lessons.task: Write a tiny family knowledge base for three generations of your own family as Prolog-style facts (parent(a, b).) and rules for grandparent and sibling. Without a computer, answer the query grandparent(X, you) by hand using backward chaining, writing each substitution.

quiz.q: What is UNIFY(Knows(John, x), Knows(y, Bill))?
quiz.explain: y must be John and x must be Bill.

quiz.q: Why does UNIFY(Knows(John, x), Knows(x, Elizabeth)) fail, and how is it fixed?
options: Because John and Elizabeth are constants; replace them by variables
x would need to be both John and Elizabeth; standardise apart by renaming one x
Because of the occur check; remove the variables
quiz.explain: Variables from different sentences are independent, so renaming one solves it.

quiz.q: In existential instantiation, which constant should replace x in exists x Missile(x)?
options: Any constant already in the KB
A brand-new Skolem constant like M1
quiz.explain: Using an existing name would claim knowledge we do not have.

quiz.q: In the crime example, which facts does forward chaining derive in the first round?
options: Sells(West, M1, Nono), Weapon(M1) and Hostile(Nono)
quiz.explain: Rules 4, 5 and 6 fire first; rule 1 fires in round 2.

quiz.q: What does "semidecidable" mean for FOL entailment?
options: Algorithms can confirm every entailed sentence, but may run forever on non-entailed ones
Only half the sentences can be written
quiz.explain: Proofs exist for entailed sentences, but there is no general way to always say no.

lessons.title: Knowledge Representation and Expert Systems
lessons.content:
Walk into a big pharmacy in Dhaka and ask for "something for a headache". The pharmacist does not know every tablet individually by heart from scratch each time. He knows categories: paracetamol is a painkiller, painkillers are medicines, medicines have doses and side effects. Because he knows that "Napa is a brand of paracetamol", he immediately knows its dose, without anyone telling him about Napa specifically. Organising knowledge into categories, properties and links, so that a lot can be known from a little, is called knowledge representation. In this lesson we see how AI organises large bodies of knowledge, and how expert systems used it to give advice like a human specialist.

Why representation matters: Lessons 16 to 19 gave us languages (propositional and first-order logic) and ways to reason with them. But a language is not enough. To build a useful KB about a real domain, such as medicine, law or a university, we must decide which things exist, how to group them, and which general facts hold. A good representation makes common questions easy to answer and the KB easy to extend. A poor one forces us to repeat facts, makes answers wrong when something changes, and hides knowledge in places where the reasoner cannot use it.

Ontologies: An ontology is an organised vocabulary of a domain: the kinds of things that exist, their properties and the relations between them. A general-purpose upper ontology describes the most general concepts, like physical objects, events, times, places and quantities, under which everything else fits. Domain ontologies cover one area in detail. In medicine, for example, large ontologies such as SNOMED CT give standard codes and relations for many thousands of clinical concepts, so that different hospital systems can mean the same thing by the same term. Agreeing on an ontology is often harder socially than technically, because different groups describe the same world differently.

Categories and objects: Much reasoning happens at the level of categories, not individual objects. A shopkeeper wants to buy "rice", not a specific grain. In FOL a category can be a predicate, Rice(x), or it can be treated as an object itself, Rice, with membership written Member(x, Rice) or x in Rice. Treating categories as objects lets us say things about the category, such as the number of known varieties. Categories are organised by subclass relations: Basmati is a subset of Rice, Rice is a subset of Grain, Grain is a subset of Food. The result is a taxonomy, a hierarchy like the biological classification of living things or the library classification of books.

Inheritance: The great power of a taxonomy is inheritance. If we state that all food is edible, and Basmati is a subclass of Rice, which is a subclass of Grain, which is a subclass of Food, then every bag of basmati inherits the property "edible" with no extra facts. In FOL: forall x x in Food => Edible(x), plus the subset links. Inheritance saves enormous effort: we state a property once, at the most general level where it holds, and it flows down to thousands of members. Categories can also be disjoint (no object is both a Mammal and a Bird), an exhaustive decomposition (every HSC student is in at least one of the listed groups), or a partition (both disjoint and exhaustive: every HSC student is in exactly one of Science, Humanities or Business Studies).

Other things to represent: Real domains need more than categories. Physical composition uses PartOf: Dhaka is part of the Dhaka Division, which is part of Bangladesh; PartOf is transitive. Measures, like weight, price or distance, are represented with units: Length(Padma Bridge) = Kilometres(6.15). Substances, like water or rice, behave differently from objects: half a glass of water is still water, but half a car is not a car. Events and time are handled by the event calculus, which states which facts hold at which times and which events start or end them. Mental objects, such as what an agent knows or believes, need special care. Each of these is a separate topic in advanced courses; here, it is enough to know that a serious KB must handle them.

Semantic networks: A semantic network draws knowledge as a graph: nodes for objects and categories, and labelled links for relations. A node "Mukta" has a MemberOf link to "Female Persons", which has a SubsetOf link to "Persons"; "Persons" might have a property link "Legs: 2". To find how many legs Mukta has, follow the links upward until a value is found: this is inheritance as graph traversal. Semantic networks are easy to read and draw, and their reasoning is efficient. A special case is when a member overrides the default: a node for a particular person with one leg can store "Legs: 1", and the more specific value wins. Semantic networks were proposed in the 1960s and influenced today's knowledge graphs.

Frames: A frame represents a stereotyped object or situation as a structure with named slots and values, a bit like a class with fields in object-oriented programming. A "Restaurant visit" frame might have slots for customer, restaurant, food ordered, bill and tip, with default values and procedures that run when a slot is filled or needed. A "Wedding" frame in Bangladesh might have slots for gaye holud, the main event and the reception, each with typical times and guests. Frames support inheritance (a "Biye" frame can be a kind of "Wedding" frame) and defaults. The idea, proposed by Marvin Minsky in the 1970s, is that understanding a situation means recognising which frame fits and filling its slots.

Default reasoning: Semantic networks and frames use default values, and defaults break monotonicity. We conclude that a bird flies, but if we later learn it is a penguin, we withdraw the conclusion. Pure FOL cannot do this, because adding facts never removes conclusions. Nonmonotonic logics, such as circumscription and default logic, try to formalise "assume normal unless told otherwise". Truth maintenance systems keep track of why each belief is held, so that when a premise is retracted, all beliefs based on it can be retracted too. Probability theory, in lesson 22, gives another, often better, way to handle exceptions.

Description logics: Description logics are a family of logics designed to make defining categories and checking subclass relations precise and efficient. A definition might say: a Bachelor is a Male who is an Adult and is not Married. The main inference tasks are subsumption (is every member of one category also in another?) and classification (where does an object belong?). Description logics give up some of FOL's power to keep these inferences decidable and reasonably fast. They are the logical basis of OWL, the Web Ontology Language, used to write ontologies on the web.

Knowledge graphs today: Modern search engines and digital assistants use very large knowledge graphs: networks of entities (people, places, organisations) and relations between them, like (Rabindranath Tagore, wrote, Amar Shonar Bangla). When you search for a famous person and see an information box with birth date and works, the data often comes from such a graph. Public examples include Wikidata. Knowledge graphs are a direct descendant of semantic networks, built at a much larger scale and usually filled partly by automatic extraction from text, which means they can contain errors.

Production rules: Another popular way to encode expert knowledge is production rules: IF conditions THEN action or conclusion. "IF the patient has fever AND the fever has lasted more than three days AND platelet count is low THEN suspect dengue." A rule-based system has three parts: a working memory holding current facts, a rule base, and an inference engine that matches rules to facts and decides which to fire, using forward chaining (lesson 17), backward chaining, or both. When several rules match at once, a conflict resolution strategy picks one, for example the most specific rule or the one using the most recent facts.

Expert systems: An expert system is a program that captures the knowledge of human specialists in a narrow domain and uses it to give advice. Its main parts: the knowledge base (facts and rules from experts), the inference engine, a user interface that asks questions and shows conclusions, an explanation facility that answers "why are you asking this?" and "how did you reach this conclusion?", and a knowledge acquisition component for adding and editing rules. Separating the knowledge base from the inference engine was a key idea: the same engine, called an expert system shell, could be reused for different domains by loading different rules.

MYCIN, a classic case: MYCIN, developed at Stanford in the 1970s, diagnosed bacterial blood infections and recommended antibiotics. It had a few hundred rules, used backward chaining from the goal "which organism is causing the infection?", asked the doctor questions, and handled uncertainty with certainty factors, numbers attached to rules showing how strongly evidence supported a conclusion. In a published evaluation, its recommendations were judged comparable to those of infectious disease experts and better than those of less specialised doctors. Yet MYCIN was never used in routine clinical practice, because of practical, legal and ethical issues, such as who is responsible for a wrong recommendation and how the system fits into hospital work.

Other expert systems: DENDRAL, from the 1960s, inferred molecular structures from mass spectrometry data and is often called the first expert system. XCON (also called R1), used by Digital Equipment Corporation in the 1980s, configured computer orders, and was reported to save the company millions of dollars per year. Expert systems became a major industry in the 1980s, and rule engines built on the same principles are still used today for tasks like insurance claim checking, loan eligibility and tax calculation, where the rules come from regulations and must be explainable.

Limits of expert systems: The biggest problem is the knowledge acquisition bottleneck: getting knowledge out of experts' heads and into rules is slow and expensive, and experts often cannot explain their intuition. Expert systems are brittle: outside their narrow domain, or when facing an unusual case, they fail badly rather than gracefully, because they lack common sense. Large rule bases are hard to maintain, as rules interact in unexpected ways. And handling uncertainty with ad hoc numbers like certainty factors can give inconsistent results. These limits led researchers towards probabilistic methods and machine learning, which learn from data rather than from hand-written rules.

Real life example 1, a crop advice system: Imagine an agriculture extension app for farmers in Rangpur. Its ontology has categories (crops, pests, diseases, fertilisers), subclass links (Aman rice is a kind of rice) and properties (season, water need). Rules encode advice from agronomists: IF crop is rice AND leaves show brown spots AND weather is humid THEN suspect brown spot disease AND suggest consulting the local agriculture officer. The explanation feature shows the farmer which observations led to the advice. Such a system would need careful testing with real experts before use, since wrong advice has real costs.

Real life example 2, a university course catalogue: A university can describe its programmes as an ontology: CSE courses are a subclass of Engineering courses; every course has credits, prerequisites and a semester. A frame for "AI course" fills these slots. A chatbot answering "which courses can a third-year CSE student take next semester?" uses inheritance (CSE courses inherit general registration rules) and production rules (IF prerequisites passed THEN eligible). Changing one general rule automatically updates the answer for every course.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students confuse MemberOf (an individual in a category) with SubsetOf (a category inside a category): Mukta is a member of Persons, but Female Persons is a subset of Persons. Another mistake is thinking expert systems learn by themselves; classic ones did not, their rules were written by people. Typical questions: define ontology and taxonomy; draw a semantic network for a given paragraph and answer a query by inheritance; describe a frame with slots; list the parts of an expert system; describe MYCIN; and discuss the knowledge acquisition bottleneck and other limits.

Recap: Knowledge representation organises a domain into an ontology of categories, objects, properties and relations. Taxonomies allow inheritance, so a property stated once applies to all members. Semantic networks draw this as a graph; frames package it as slots with defaults; description logics make it precise and efficient; knowledge graphs scale it up today. Production rules and inference engines power expert systems like MYCIN, DENDRAL and XCON, which worked well in narrow domains but suffered from the knowledge acquisition bottleneck and brittleness. Next lesson, we turn from knowing to doing: classical planning.
key_points: An ontology is an organised vocabulary of the kinds of things in a domain, their properties and relations.
Taxonomies of categories with subclass links allow inheritance: a property stated once applies to all members.
MemberOf links an individual to a category; SubsetOf links a category to a larger category.
Semantic networks represent knowledge as labelled graphs; frames represent stereotyped objects as slots with default values.
Default reasoning is nonmonotonic: conclusions can be withdrawn when exceptions are learned.
An expert system has a knowledge base, inference engine, user interface, explanation facility and knowledge acquisition component.
MYCIN used backward chaining and certainty factors; expert systems suffer from the knowledge acquisition bottleneck and brittleness.
lessons.tip: For any semantic network question, first draw the hierarchy from top (most general) to bottom (individuals), then attach each property at the highest node where it is true. Answer queries by walking upward from the individual and taking the first value you meet.
lessons.task: Draw a semantic network for the vehicles you see on Dhaka roads: Vehicle, Motor vehicle, Non-motor vehicle, Bus, CNG auto-rickshaw, Rickshaw, plus one specific rickshaw. Attach properties like number of wheels and fuel type at the right levels, add one exception, and answer "how many wheels does my rickshaw have?" by inheritance.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of inheritance in a taxonomy?
options: A property stated once for a category applies to all its subclasses and members
It removes the need for categories
It guarantees the KB has no errors
quiz.explain: Properties flow down the hierarchy, so facts are not repeated.

quiz.q: "Mukta is a female person" is best represented with which link?
options: SubsetOf from Mukta to Female Persons
PartOf from Mukta to Female Persons
MemberOf from Mukta to Female Persons
SubsetOf from Female Persons to Mukta
quiz.explain: An individual belongs to a category by membership, not as a subset.

quiz.q: Which part of an expert system answers "how did you reach this conclusion?"
quiz.explain: The explanation facility shows the rules and facts used.

quiz.q: Why is default reasoning called nonmonotonic?
options: Adding new information can remove an earlier conclusion
quiz.explain: Learning that a bird is a penguin withdraws "it flies".

quiz.q: What is the knowledge acquisition bottleneck?
options: The inference engine running too slowly
Too few categories in the ontology
The difficulty and cost of getting experts' knowledge into rules
The limit on the number of slots in a frame
quiz.explain: Experts' knowledge is slow and expensive to extract, and much is intuitive.

lessons.title: Classical Planning
lessons.content:
Before Eid, a family in Mirpur has a list of goals: new clothes bought, the house cleaned, the cow brought home, the bus tickets to the village booked. Each task has conditions: you cannot bring the cow before the haat opens, you cannot buy clothes without withdrawing money, and booking tickets uses some of that money. Nobody plans this by listing every possible state of the whole family's world. Instead, they think in terms of actions with preconditions and effects, and put them in a sensible order. Classical planning is the part of AI that does exactly this: given a description of actions, a start state and a goal, find a sequence of actions that reaches the goal.

Planning versus plain search: In lessons 4 to 7, a search agent treated states as black boxes: it could only ask "is this the goal?" and "what are the successors?". That works for route finding, but breaks down when states have many parts. If a house has 20 chores, each done or not, there are over a million states, and an uninformed search would wander among them blindly. A planner instead uses a factored representation: a state is a set of facts, and actions are described by which facts they need and which they change. This structure lets the planner reason about goals directly, ignore irrelevant actions, and build powerful heuristics automatically.

The classical assumptions: Classical planning assumes the environment is fully observable, deterministic, static and discrete, with a single agent. The agent knows the start state exactly, every action has one predictable outcome, and nothing changes except through the agent's actions. These are strong assumptions, but they make the problem clean, and many extensions (planning under uncertainty, with time and resources, or with several agents) build on the classical methods.

Representing states: In STRIPS-style planning, and in the modern standard language PDDL (Planning Domain Definition Language), a state is a conjunction of ground atomic facts, such as At(Truck, Dhaka) and At(Parcel, Dhaka) and Fuelled(Truck). Facts not listed are assumed false (the closed-world assumption from lesson 18). The goal is also a conjunction of facts, possibly with variables, like At(Parcel, Sylhet). Any state that contains all the goal facts satisfies the goal, so there are usually many goal states.

Action schemas: An action schema describes a family of actions with variables. It has a name with parameters, a precondition (facts that must be true before the action), and an effect, often split into an add list (facts that become true) and a delete list (facts that become false). Example: Drive(t, from, to). Precondition: Truck(t) and At(t, from) and Fuelled(t). Effect: At(t, to) and not At(t, from). Another: Load(p, t, c). Precondition: At(p, c) and At(t, c). Effect: In(p, t) and not At(p, c). An action is applicable in a state if its precondition holds; the result is the state minus the delete list plus the add list. Everything not mentioned stays the same, which neatly avoids the frame problem of listing what does not change.

The blocks world: The most famous planning domain is the blocks world: a few blocks on a table and a robot arm that can move one clear block (with nothing on top) at a time. Facts: On(x, y), OnTable(x), Clear(x). Action Move(b, x, y): move block b from x onto block y. Precondition: On(b, x) and Clear(b) and Clear(y). Effect: On(b, y) and Clear(x) and not On(b, x) and not Clear(y). A similar action MoveToTable(b, x) puts b on the table. The domain is simple to state but contains real planning difficulty.

A worked blocks example: Start: C is on A; A and B are on the table. So On(C, A), OnTable(A), OnTable(B), Clear(C), Clear(B). Goal: On(A, B) and On(B, C), a tower with A on top, B in the middle, C at the bottom. A plan: (1) MoveToTable(C, A): now A is clear. (2) Move(B, Table, C): B goes on C. (3) Move(A, Table, B): A goes on B. Three actions. Check each precondition: C was clear for step 1; B and C were clear for step 2; A and B were clear for step 3. The goal holds at the end.

Why this example is famous: This start and goal form the Sussman anomaly. A naive planner that solves one goal fully and then the next fails here. If it first achieves On(A, B), by moving C to the table and then A onto B, it must then undo that to put B on C. If it first achieves On(B, C), by putting B straight on C, the result is a tower B on C on A, and A is buried at the bottom; to put A on B it must take the whole tower apart again. Either order of solving the goals one by one forces undoing work. The optimal plan interleaves the steps for the two goals. The lesson: goals interact, and good planners must handle that.

Forward state-space planning: The simplest planner searches forward from the start state, applying applicable actions, like the search algorithms of lessons 5 to 9. Its weakness is that many actions are applicable but irrelevant. In a logistics problem with 10 airports, 50 planes and 200 parcels, there are thousands of possible actions at each step, most having nothing to do with the goal. Without a good heuristic, forward search drowns. With a good heuristic, it is today one of the most effective approaches.

Backward relevant-state search: Backward (regression) search starts from the goal and works towards the start, considering only relevant actions: those whose effects achieve some goal fact and do not undo another. To regress a goal through an action, remove the facts the action adds and add its preconditions. Example: goal At(Parcel, Sylhet). The relevant action Unload(Parcel, t, Sylhet) has the precondition In(Parcel, t) and At(t, Sylhet), which becomes the new sub-goal. Backward search usually has a smaller branching factor, but it works with sets of states, which makes heuristics harder to design.

Heuristics from relaxed problems: The key to modern planning is that a good heuristic can be computed automatically from the action schemas, using the idea of relaxed problems from lesson 8. The ignore-delete-lists relaxation pretends that actions never make any fact false. Then progress is never undone, and the length of a plan for this easier problem is a useful estimate of the real cost. The ignore-preconditions relaxation pretends every action can be applied at any time, so the estimate becomes roughly the number of unsatisfied goal facts. Planners like FF (Fast Forward) combine forward search with relaxed-plan heuristics and solve large problems quickly.

Planning graphs and GRAPHPLAN: A planning graph is a layered structure alternating levels of facts and actions: level 0 holds the start facts, then all actions applicable to them, then all facts they could produce, and so on. It also records mutual exclusion (mutex) links between actions or facts that cannot both hold at the same level. The level at which all goal facts first appear without mutexes is an admissible estimate of plan length, and the GRAPHPLAN algorithm extracts a plan from the graph by searching backwards through it. Planning graphs are built in polynomial time, which made them a breakthrough in the 1990s.

Planning as satisfiability: Another approach translates a planning problem with a fixed number of steps into a propositional sentence, with symbols like At(Truck, Sylhet) at time 3 and Drive action at time 2, and hands it to a SAT solver (lesson 17). If the sentence is satisfiable, the satisfying assignment gives a plan; if not, increase the number of steps and try again. This shows how the logic and search ideas of the course connect.

Partial-order planning: The planners above produce a strict sequence of actions. A partial-order planner instead builds a plan as a set of actions with only the ordering constraints that are needed, plus causal links recording which action provides which precondition for which other action. For example, "put on left sock" and "put on right sock" can happen in either order, but both must come before the matching shoe. The planner keeps fixing flaws: an open precondition (add an action or link to supply it) or a threat (an action that could undo a causal link; fix it by ordering the threatening action before or after the link). Partial-order plans are flexible and easy for people to understand, and the idea remains useful in scheduling and multi-agent tasks.

Hierarchical planning: People plan at several levels: "go to the village for Eid" breaks into "book tickets, pack, travel", and "travel" breaks into "rickshaw to Gabtoli, bus to Rangpur, van to the house". Hierarchical task network (HTN) planning uses such high-level actions and refinements, which reduces search enormously because the planner considers a few big steps first. Many practical planners, including ones used in games and in military logistics, are hierarchical.

Planning, time and resources: Classical plans say what to do and in what order, but not when or with how many resources. Real projects also need scheduling: each action has a duration, some actions use limited resources (two trucks, one crane, three workers), and there are deadlines. A common approach is "plan first, schedule later": find the actions with a planner, then assign start times with a scheduling method such as the critical path method, which finds the longest chain of dependent actions and so the earliest possible finish time. Construction of a bridge or a building is managed this way.

Real life example 1, delivery logistics: An e-commerce company delivering parcels from a warehouse in Tejgaon to customers across Dhaka faces a planning problem: trucks, routes, loading and unloading, time windows. Real systems combine planning ideas with optimisation methods, but the core representation, with facts like At(Parcel, Warehouse) and actions like Load and Drive with preconditions and effects, is exactly the classical one. Automatic heuristics let planners handle many parcels without hand-written rules for each case.

Real life example 2, space missions and robots: NASA has used automated planners for spacecraft: the Remote Agent experiment on the Deep Space 1 probe in 1999 planned and executed spacecraft operations on board, and planners have been used to schedule activities of Mars rovers. In factories and warehouses, robots use planners to decide the order of picking and placing items. Game characters in some video games use planners (goal-oriented action planning) to choose believable sequences of actions.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often forget the delete list, producing states where a block is on two things at once. Others write preconditions that do not include everything the action needs (like Clear(y) for Move). In regression, they forget to add the action's preconditions to the new goal. Typical questions: write STRIPS or PDDL schemas for a small domain; trace a plan in the blocks world and check each precondition; explain the Sussman anomaly; compare forward and backward planning; explain the ignore-delete-lists heuristic; and describe partial-order planning with causal links and threats.

Recap: Classical planning finds action sequences in fully observable, deterministic worlds using factored states (sets of facts) and action schemas with preconditions, add lists and delete lists, as in STRIPS and PDDL. Forward search with automatically derived heuristics, such as ignoring delete lists, is very effective; backward search considers only relevant actions. Planning graphs, SAT encoding, partial-order planning and hierarchical planning offer other views. The blocks world and the Sussman anomaly show that goals interact. Next lesson, we drop the assumption of certainty and learn to reason with probability.
key_points: Classical planning finds a sequence of actions from a start state to a goal in a fully observable, deterministic world.
States are sets of ground facts; facts not listed are false.
An action schema has a precondition and an effect, split into an add list and a delete list.
The Sussman anomaly shows that solving goals one at a time can fail because goals interact.
Forward planning searches from the start; backward planning regresses from the goal using only relevant actions.
Ignoring delete lists gives a relaxed problem whose plan length is a strong, automatically computed heuristic.
Partial-order planning keeps only necessary orderings, with causal links and threat resolution.
lessons.tip: When writing an action schema, test it on one concrete state: write the state, check the precondition, apply delete then add, and look at the result. If any impossible fact appears, like a block on two things, a delete is missing.
lessons.task: Write PDDL-style action schemas for making a cup of tea at home: actions like BoilWater, PutTeabag, PourWater, AddSugar, with preconditions and add and delete lists. Then write a start state and goal and find a plan by hand, checking each precondition. Which steps could be done in either order?

quiz.q: In a STRIPS action schema, what does the delete list contain?
options: Facts that must be true before the action
Facts that become false after the action
quiz.explain: The result is the state minus the delete list plus the add list.

quiz.q: In the blocks world, what is the precondition of Move(b, x, y)?
options: On(b, x) and Clear(b) and Clear(y)
quiz.explain: b must be on x and have nothing on top, and y must be clear to receive it.

quiz.q: What does the Sussman anomaly demonstrate?
options: Solving goals one by one can force undoing earlier work because goals interact
Blocks cannot be moved to the table
quiz.explain: The optimal plan interleaves steps for both goals.

quiz.q: What is the ignore-delete-lists heuristic?
options: The cost of a plan for a relaxed problem where actions never make facts false
The number of actions in the delete list
A heuristic that ignores the goal
The exact cost of the real plan
quiz.explain: Without deletes, progress is never undone, so the problem is easier to solve.

quiz.q: In partial-order planning, what is a threat?
options: A goal that cannot be achieved
An action that could undo a fact protected by a causal link
A cycle in the planning graph
quiz.explain: It is fixed by ordering the threatening action before or after the link.

lessons.title: Uncertainty, Probability and Bayes' Rule
lessons.content:
You plan to leave home in Uttara 90 minutes before your flight. Will you reach the airport on time? Logic would want a guarantee: "if I leave 90 minutes early, I will arrive on time". But no such guarantee exists. The road might be jammed, a rally might block it, the car might get a flat tyre. Leaving four hours early would be safer but would waste your day. What you actually do is reason with likelihoods: "90 minutes is very likely enough on a normal weekday". Real agents almost never have certain knowledge. This lesson introduces the tool AI uses to reason under uncertainty: probability theory, and in particular Bayes' rule.

Why logic alone fails: Consider a dental diagnosis rule: Toothache => Cavity. It is wrong, because toothaches can have other causes, such as gum disease or an abscess. We could try Toothache => Cavity or GumProblem or Abscess or ..., listing endless causes. The reverse, Cavity => Toothache, is also wrong, because not all cavities hurt. Logic fails here for three reasons: laziness (listing every exception and condition is too much work), theoretical ignorance (medicine has no complete theory of the domain), and practical ignorance (even with full rules, we do not have all the tests for this particular patient). The agent's knowledge can at best give a degree of belief.

Degrees of belief and rational decisions: Probability gives a number between 0 and 1 to each sentence, summarising the agent's uncertainty: P(Cavity) = 0.2 means that, given what the agent knows, there is a 20% chance of a cavity. This is not a claim that the world itself is partly true; the cavity is either there or not. It is a statement about the agent's knowledge, and it changes when new evidence arrives. To act, an agent combines probabilities with preferences, called utilities. Decision theory says: choose the action with the highest expected utility. A plan to leave 90 minutes early might have a 95% chance of success with low waiting time, which may beat a 99.9% plan that wastes four hours.

Basic language of probability: The set of all possible worlds is the sample space; each world has a probability between 0 and 1, and they sum to 1. Random variables describe parts of the world: Weather can take values sunny, rain, cloudy or storm; Cavity is Boolean, true or false. A proposition like Weather = rain or Cavity = true has a probability equal to the sum of the probabilities of the worlds where it holds. The unconditional or prior probability, like P(Cavity = true) = 0.2, is the belief before any evidence. A probability distribution lists the probabilities of all values of a variable, written in bold P: P(Weather) = (0.6, 0.1, 0.29, 0.01).

The axioms: Probability follows a few rules, called the Kolmogorov axioms. Every probability is between 0 and 1. The probabilities of all possible worlds add up to 1. And for any propositions a and b: P(a or b) = P(a) + P(b) - P(a and b), the inclusion-exclusion rule from discrete mathematics. From these follow facts like P(not a) = 1 - P(a). An important argument by de Finetti shows that an agent whose beliefs violate these axioms can be offered a set of bets it considers fair but that guarantee it loses money. So the axioms are not arbitrary; they are what consistent belief requires.

Conditional probability: Once evidence arrives, we use conditional or posterior probability. P(a | b), read "the probability of a given b", is the probability of a when all we know is b. Definition: P(a | b) = P(a and b) / P(b), when P(b) > 0. Example: P(Cavity | Toothache) = 0.6 means that if a patient has a toothache and we know nothing else, the chance of a cavity is 60%. Rearranging gives the product rule: P(a and b) = P(a | b) P(b). Note that P(Cavity | Toothache) = 0.6 does not mean "if toothache then cavity with 60%" in a logical sense; if we also learn the patient has gum disease, we must use P(Cavity | Toothache and GumDisease), which may be quite different.

The full joint distribution: The full joint distribution gives the probability of every combination of values of all variables. The textbook example uses three Boolean variables: Toothache, Cavity and Catch (the dentist's probe catches in the tooth). With cavity: toothache and catch 0.108, toothache and no catch 0.012, no toothache and catch 0.072, no toothache and no catch 0.008. Without cavity: 0.016, 0.064, 0.144 and 0.576. The eight numbers add up to 1. From this table, any probability can be computed: P(Cavity) = 0.108 + 0.012 + 0.072 + 0.008 = 0.2.

Marginalisation and inference by enumeration: Summing out the other variables to get the probability of one variable is called marginalisation. P(Toothache) = 0.108 + 0.012 + 0.016 + 0.064 = 0.2. A conditional probability comes from two sums: P(Cavity | Toothache) = P(Cavity and Toothache) / P(Toothache) = (0.108 + 0.012) / 0.2 = 0.6. Similarly P(not Cavity | Toothache) = (0.016 + 0.064) / 0.2 = 0.4. Notice that the two answers share the denominator P(Toothache), so we can compute the unnormalised values 0.12 and 0.08 and then scale them to sum to 1. This trick is called normalisation and is written with alpha: P(Cavity | toothache) = alpha (0.12, 0.08) = (0.6, 0.4).

The problem with the full joint: Inference by enumeration works, but the table for n Boolean variables has 2^n entries. For 30 symptoms and diseases, that is over a billion numbers, impossible to store or to estimate from data. We need a way to describe the same knowledge with far fewer numbers. The two key ideas are independence and conditional independence.

Independence: Two variables are independent if knowing one tells you nothing about the other: P(a | b) = P(a), or equivalently P(a and b) = P(a) P(b). Whether it rains in Sylhet today is independent of whether your tooth has a cavity. If we have four weather values and the eight-entry dental table, the joint table has 32 entries, but with independence we only need 4 + 8 = 12 numbers. Independence is usually a judgement from domain knowledge, not something computed. Full independence is rare among variables that matter in the same problem, though.

Bayes' rule: From the product rule written two ways, P(a and b) = P(a | b) P(b) = P(b | a) P(a), we get Bayes' rule: P(b | a) = P(a | b) P(b) / P(a). It looks simple but it is one of the most useful equations in AI. It lets us compute a diagnostic probability, P(cause | effect), from a causal probability, P(effect | cause), which is often easier to know and more stable. A doctor knows how often a disease causes a symptom; Bayes' rule turns this into how likely the disease is given the symptom.

A worked example, testing for a disease: Suppose 1% of people in a district have a certain disease. A test detects it in 90% of people who have it (sensitivity), but also gives a positive result for 5% of people who do not have it (false positives). A person tests positive. What is the chance they have the disease? By Bayes' rule, P(D | +) = P(+ | D) P(D) / P(+). P(+) = 0.9 x 0.01 + 0.05 x 0.99 = 0.009 + 0.0495 = 0.0585. So P(D | +) = 0.009 / 0.0585, about 0.154, only around 15%. Most positives are false positives, because healthy people far outnumber sick ones. Many people, including professionals, guess around 90%; ignoring the base rate (the 1% prior) is called the base rate fallacy.

What the example teaches: The result is not a reason to distrust tests; it is a reason to think about priors. If the same person had strong symptoms, the prior for them would be much higher than 1%, and a positive result would be far more convincing. Doctors often confirm a positive screening result with a second, more specific test, and Bayes' rule explains exactly why this works: the posterior after the first test becomes the prior for the second. Updating beliefs step by step as evidence arrives is the central pattern of probabilistic reasoning.

Combining evidence and conditional independence: Suppose the dentist sees both Toothache and Catch. We need P(Cavity | toothache and catch), which normally needs a table over all combinations of evidence. But toothache and catch are both caused by the cavity, and given whether there is a cavity, they do not affect each other: the probe does not care whether the tooth hurts. This is conditional independence: P(toothache and catch | Cavity) = P(toothache | Cavity) P(catch | Cavity). Then P(Cavity | toothache and catch) = alpha P(toothache | Cavity) P(catch | Cavity) P(Cavity). Conditional independence is far more common than full independence, and it is the key to making probabilistic reasoning scale.

Naive Bayes: When a single cause has many effects that are assumed conditionally independent given the cause, we get the naive Bayes model: P(Cause, Effect1, ..., Effectn) = P(Cause) multiplied by P(Effecti | Cause) for each i. The assumption is often not exactly true, which is why it is called naive, but the model works surprisingly well in practice and needs only a number of parameters that grows linearly with the number of effects. It is a standard first method for text classification.

Real life example 1, a spam filter: Suppose 40% of emails to a university address are spam. The word "free" appears in 30% of spam and 2% of normal mail; the word "offer" appears in 20% of spam and 5% of normal mail. An email contains both words. Naive Bayes: score for spam = 0.4 x 0.3 x 0.2 = 0.024; score for normal = 0.6 x 0.02 x 0.05 = 0.0006. Normalising, P(spam | free, offer) = 0.024 / 0.0246, about 0.976. The filter marks it as spam. Real filters use thousands of words and learn these probabilities from labelled emails, and are combined with other checks.

Real life example 2, weather forecasts: When the Bangladesh Meteorological Department or a weather app says "70% chance of rain in Chattogram tomorrow", it is giving a probability, not a promise. A well-calibrated forecaster is one for whom, over many days with a 70% forecast, it rains on about 70% of them. You use this number with your own utilities: a 30% chance of rain may be enough to carry an umbrella to class, but not enough to cancel a cricket match planned for weeks.

Common mistakes and exam questions: The most common mistake is confusing P(a | b) with P(b | a): the probability of a positive test given disease (90%) is not the probability of disease given a positive test (about 15%). Others: forgetting to normalise, assuming independence without justification, and treating probabilities above 1 or summing distributions that do not add to 1 as acceptable. Typical questions: compute marginal and conditional probabilities from a joint table; apply Bayes' rule to a medical test; explain why logic fails for uncertain domains; define independence and conditional independence; and classify a message with naive Bayes.

Recap: Agents face uncertainty because of laziness, theoretical ignorance and practical ignorance, so they use probability as a degree of belief and choose actions by expected utility. Probabilities obey the Kolmogorov axioms; conditional probability is P(a | b) = P(a and b) / P(b). The full joint distribution answers any question by enumeration and normalisation, but grows as 2^n. Independence and especially conditional independence shrink it. Bayes' rule turns causal knowledge into diagnosis, and the disease-test example shows why priors matter. Naive Bayes applies these ideas to spam filtering. Next lesson, Bayesian networks put conditional independence into a graph.
key_points: Agents use probability because of laziness, theoretical ignorance and practical ignorance.
A probability is a degree of belief given the agent's knowledge; rational agents maximise expected utility.
Conditional probability: P(a | b) = P(a and b) / P(b); product rule: P(a and b) = P(a | b) P(b).
The full joint distribution answers any query by summing entries, but has 2^n entries for n Boolean variables.
Bayes' rule: P(b | a) = P(a | b) P(b) / P(a), turning causal knowledge into diagnostic knowledge.
In the test example (1% prior, 90% sensitivity, 5% false positives), a positive result gives only about 15% chance of disease.
Conditional independence makes naive Bayes possible: P(Cause) times the product of P(Effect | Cause).
lessons.tip: For any Bayes' rule question, first draw a table of 1,000 imaginary people: how many have the disease, how many of those test positive, how many healthy people test positive. Counting people is much harder to get wrong than juggling formulas, and it shows the base rate clearly.
lessons.task: Take the dental joint table from this lesson and compute by hand: P(Catch), P(Cavity | Catch), and P(Cavity | toothache and catch). Then check whether Toothache and Catch are conditionally independent given Cavity by comparing P(toothache and catch | cavity) with P(toothache | cavity) x P(catch | cavity).

quiz.q: Why does a logical rule like Toothache => Cavity fail?
options: Because logic cannot use the word Cavity
Because toothaches have other causes and we cannot list every exception
quiz.explain: Laziness, theoretical ignorance and practical ignorance make exact rules impractical.

quiz.q: Using the dental table, what is P(Cavity | Toothache)?
What is Bayes' rule?
options: P(b | a) = P(a | b) P(b) / P(a)
quiz.explain: It follows from writing the product rule in two ways.

quiz.q: A disease affects 1% of people; a test has 90% sensitivity and 5% false positives. After a positive test, the chance of disease is about:
quiz.explain: 0.009 / 0.0585 is about 0.154; most positives come from the many healthy people.

quiz.q: What does naive Bayes assume?
options: Effects are conditionally independent given the cause
The cause has only one effect
quiz.explain: This lets the joint be written as P(Cause) times the product of P(Effect | Cause).

lessons.title: Bayesian Networks
lessons.content:
Your neighbour Jamal calls: "Your house alarm is ringing!" Should you rush home from the office in Motijheel? Maybe there is a burglar. But the alarm also goes off sometimes when there is a small earthquake, and Jamal sometimes confuses your alarm with a phone ringtone. Another neighbour, Mitu, usually calls too when she hears it, but she plays loud music and often misses it. Today Mitu also called. How worried should you be? Reasoning like this, with several causes and several pieces of noisy evidence, is exactly what Bayesian networks were built for. This lesson shows how a graph plus small tables can represent a full probability model compactly, and how to answer questions with it.

From the full joint to a network: Last lesson we saw that the full joint distribution answers every question but needs 2^n numbers, and that conditional independence can shrink it. A Bayesian network (also called a belief network or Bayes net) is a way to write down exactly which conditional independences hold, as a graph, and then to specify the model with a small number of local probabilities. It was developed largely by Judea Pearl in the 1980s, and it changed AI by making probabilistic reasoning practical.

The structure: A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Each node is a random variable. A directed arrow from X to Y means X has a direct influence on Y; X is called a parent of Y. Usually arrows go from causes to effects. Each node has a conditional probability table (CPT) that gives P(node | parents) for every combination of parent values. A node with no parents simply has a prior probability. The graph must have no directed cycles, so no variable can, through a chain of arrows, influence itself.

The burglary network: The classic textbook example has five Boolean variables: Burglary (B), Earthquake (E), Alarm (A), JohnCalls (J) and MaryCalls (M), which we can read as Jamal and Mitu. Arrows: B to A, E to A, A to J, A to M. The neighbours do not hear the burglar or feel the earthquake directly; they only react to the alarm. The CPTs, with the textbook's numbers: P(B) = 0.001, P(E) = 0.002. P(A | B, E) = 0.95, P(A | B, not E) = 0.94, P(A | not B, E) = 0.29, P(A | not B, not E) = 0.001. P(J | A) = 0.90, P(J | not A) = 0.05. P(M | A) = 0.70, P(M | not A) = 0.01.

Counting the numbers: For a Boolean node with k Boolean parents, the CPT needs 2^k numbers (we only store P(true); P(false) is one minus that). The burglary network needs 1 + 1 + 4 + 2 + 2 = 10 numbers. The full joint for five Boolean variables needs 2^5 - 1 = 31 numbers. The saving grows dramatically: if each of n variables has at most k parents, the network needs at most n times 2^k numbers, which grows linearly with n, while the full joint grows as 2^n. With 30 variables and at most 5 parents each, that is 960 numbers instead of over a billion.

The meaning: the chain rule: A Bayesian network defines the full joint distribution as the product of the local CPT entries: P(x1, ..., xn) = product over i of P(xi | parents(Xi)). This comes from the general chain rule of probability, P(x1, ..., xn) = product of P(xi | x1, ..., xi-1), together with the network's assumption that each variable, given its parents, is conditionally independent of its other predecessors. So the graph is not just a picture; it is a precise statement about the joint distribution.

Computing one joint entry: What is the probability that the alarm rings, both neighbours call, but there is neither a burglary nor an earthquake? P(j, m, a, not b, not e) = P(j | a) P(m | a) P(a | not b, not e) P(not b) P(not e) = 0.90 x 0.70 x 0.001 x 0.999 x 0.998, which is about 0.00063. Every entry of the full joint can be computed this way by multiplying five numbers, so the network contains all the information of the table.

Conditional independence in the network: The network's structure tells us which independences hold. The key rule: each node is conditionally independent of its non-descendants, given its parents. So JohnCalls is independent of Burglary and Earthquake given Alarm: once you know the alarm rang, learning there was a burglary does not change the chance Jamal calls. An equivalent, sometimes more useful rule: a node is conditionally independent of all other nodes given its Markov blanket, which is its parents, its children and its children's other parents.

Three basic patterns: Most reasoning about independence comes down to three patterns. A chain, X to Y to Z (Burglary to Alarm to JohnCalls): X and Z are dependent, but independent given Y. A common cause, Y to X and Y to Z (Alarm to JohnCalls and Alarm to MaryCalls): X and Z are dependent (if Jamal calls, Mitu is more likely to call too), but independent given Y. A common effect, X to Y and Z to Y (Burglary to Alarm and Earthquake to Alarm): X and Z are independent, but become dependent when Y is observed. That last one is surprising and deserves a closer look.

Explaining away: Burglaries and earthquakes are independent: one does not make the other more likely. But suppose you know the alarm rang. Now if you hear on the radio that there was an earthquake, the earthquake explains the alarm, and a burglary becomes less likely. Two independent causes become dependent once their common effect is observed. This is called explaining away, and people do it naturally: if your friend is late and you learn there was a huge jam on the Mohakhali flyover, you stop worrying that they forgot the meeting. Bayesian networks capture this pattern correctly, while many simple rule systems do not.

Building a network: To construct a network, choose an ordering of the variables, preferably with causes before effects. Add the variables one by one; for each, choose as parents the smallest set of earlier variables that it directly depends on, and fill its CPT. Causal orderings produce compact networks with numbers experts can estimate (how often does an earthquake trigger the alarm?). A bad ordering, for example adding MaryCalls, JohnCalls, Alarm, Burglary, Earthquake in that order, produces more arrows and needs probabilities that are hard to judge, like P(Earthquake | Burglary, Alarm), even though it represents the same distribution.

Inference by enumeration: The main task is computing a posterior, P(Query | evidence). Example: given that both Jamal and Mitu called, what is the probability of a burglary? P(B | j, m) = alpha times the sum over e and a of P(B) P(e) P(a | B, e) P(j | a) P(m | a). We sum over the hidden variables Earthquake and Alarm. Carrying out the calculation with the CPTs above gives unnormalised values of about 0.000592 for burglary and 0.001492 for no burglary, so P(b | j, m) is about 0.000592 / 0.002084, roughly 0.284. Even with two calls, the chance of a burglary is only about 28%, because burglaries are rare and false alarms and false calls happen.

Making inference faster: Enumeration repeats the same sub-calculations many times. Variable elimination does the sums from the inside out and stores intermediate results, called factors, so nothing is computed twice; it also drops variables that are irrelevant to the query, such as nodes with no observed descendants. For networks shaped like trees (polytrees, with at most one undirected path between any two nodes), exact inference takes time linear in the size of the network. For general networks, exact inference is NP-hard in the worst case, so for big networks we turn to approximation.

Approximate inference by sampling: Sampling methods generate many random worlds from the network and count. In direct (prior) sampling, sample each variable in topological order from its CPT given the already sampled parents. To estimate P(b | j, m), rejection sampling throws away samples that disagree with the evidence and counts burglaries among the rest; it is simple but wasteful when evidence is rare. Likelihood weighting fixes the evidence variables and weights each sample by how likely the evidence was. Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, such as Gibbs sampling, wander through states by resampling one variable at a time given its Markov blanket. With enough samples, the estimates approach the true probabilities.

Beyond the basics: Real networks often have continuous variables, like temperature or blood pressure, handled with distributions such as the Gaussian. Dynamic Bayesian networks repeat a network over time slices to model processes that change, and hidden Markov models, used for many years in speech recognition, are a simple special case. Bayesian networks can also be learned from data: both the CPT numbers and, with more effort, the structure. And adding decision and utility nodes gives decision networks, which choose actions with the highest expected utility.

Real life example 1, medical diagnosis: A network for respiratory illness might have nodes for Smoking, Air pollution (high in Dhaka winters), Tuberculosis, Lung cancer, Bronchitis, Cough, Shortness of breath and X-ray result. Doctors and data supply the CPTs. Entering a patient's symptoms and test results gives posterior probabilities for each disease, and explaining away works naturally: a positive TB test makes lung cancer a less likely explanation for an abnormal X-ray. Systems of this type have been studied extensively in medical research, alongside careful evaluation before any clinical use.

Real life example 2, troubleshooting: Technical support systems have used Bayesian networks to diagnose faults: printer problems, car engine faults, or network outages. For an internet provider in Chattogram, nodes might be Router fault, Fibre cut, Area power cut, Customer's light on, Neighbours affected. Observing "neighbours also offline" explains away a router fault and points towards a fibre cut or power cut, so the technician checks the right thing first.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often think an arrow must mean strict cause; it means direct dependence, though causal arrows give the best networks. Others forget that CPTs need one row per combination of parent values, or think two causes are dependent before the effect is observed. In enumeration, they forget to sum over hidden variables or to normalise. Typical questions: draw a network for a story and write its CPT sizes; compute a joint entry with the chain rule; compute a posterior like P(B | j, m) by enumeration; identify conditional independences; explain explaining away; and describe rejection sampling.

Recap: A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph with a CPT at each node, representing the full joint as the product of P(xi | parents(Xi)). It needs far fewer numbers than the full joint. Each node is independent of its non-descendants given its parents; chains and common causes are blocked by observing the middle node, while common effects create dependence (explaining away). Exact inference by enumeration or variable elimination, and approximate inference by sampling, answer queries like P(Burglary | both neighbours call), which is about 0.28. Next lesson, we look at how machines learn such models, and much more, from data.
key_points: A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph with a conditional probability table at each node.
The joint distribution is the product of P(xi | parents(Xi)) over all nodes.
The burglary network needs 10 numbers, compared with 31 for the full joint.
Each node is conditionally independent of its non-descendants given its parents.
Explaining away: two independent causes become dependent when their common effect is observed.
P(Burglary | Jamal and Mitu both call) is about 0.28, computed by summing over Earthquake and Alarm and normalising.
Exact inference is NP-hard in general; sampling methods like rejection sampling and likelihood weighting give approximations.
lessons.tip: When computing a posterior by enumeration, write the product of CPT terms first, then list the hidden variables to sum over, then compute the unnormalised value for each query value, and only at the end normalise. Doing the steps in this fixed order prevents most errors.
lessons.task: Draw a Bayesian network for being late to class: nodes Rain, Traffic jam, Bus late, Overslept, Late to class. Decide the arrows, write the CPT sizes, and invent reasonable numbers. Then explain in words how learning "there was a big traffic jam" changes your belief that you overslept, given that you were late.

quiz.q: What does an arrow from X to Y in a Bayesian network mean?
options: X directly influences Y; X is a parent of Y
quiz.explain: Each node's CPT gives P(node | parents), and arrows usually go from causes to effects.

quiz.q: How many numbers does the burglary network need, compared with the full joint of 31?
How is P(j, m, a, not b, not e) computed in the burglary network?
options: P(j) + P(m) + P(a) + P(not b) + P(not e)
P(a | j, m) times P(not b)
P(j | a) P(m | a) P(a | not b, not e) P(not b) P(not e)
quiz.explain: The chain rule multiplies each node's CPT entry given its parents.

quiz.q: What is explaining away?
options: A node becomes independent of its children
Evidence is ignored when computing a posterior
Two independent causes become dependent once their common effect is observed
quiz.explain: Learning of an earthquake makes a burglary a less likely explanation for the alarm.

quiz.q: After both neighbours call, P(Burglary) is about:
quiz.explain: The prior is so low that, even with two calls, a burglary is only about 28% likely.

lessons.title: Introduction to Machine Learning and Neural Networks
lessons.content:
How did you learn to tell a ripe mango from an unripe one? Nobody gave you a rulebook with exact colours and firmness values. You saw many mangoes, tasted some, were corrected by your grandmother at the bazaar, and slowly your brain built its own sense of "ripe". The expert systems of lesson 20 needed humans to write every rule, which was slow and brittle. Machine learning (ML) takes the other path: the program improves its performance at a task by learning from data and experience. This lesson is an introduction only; you will study ML properly in its own course later. Here we see the main types of learning, a few classic methods, and the basic idea of neural networks.

What learning means for an agent: An agent is learning if it improves its performance on future tasks after making observations about the world. Learning is needed when the designer cannot anticipate every situation (a robot in a new building), when conditions change over time (spam keeps evolving), or when nobody knows how to write the program at all (how exactly do you recognise your friend's face?). In ML, we give the computer examples and a way to measure how well it is doing, and the algorithm adjusts a model, a function with adjustable parts called parameters, to do better.

Three main kinds of learning: In supervised learning, each training example comes with the correct answer, called the label: emails marked spam or not spam, house descriptions with their prices. The goal is a function that predicts labels for new examples. When the label is a category, it is classification; when it is a number, it is regression. In unsupervised learning, there are no labels; the algorithm finds structure on its own, for example grouping customers of a shop into clusters with similar buying habits. In reinforcement learning, the agent acts in an environment and receives rewards or punishments, like a dog being given treats, and learns which actions lead to more reward over time.

Supervised learning more precisely: We have a training set of N example pairs (x1, y1), ..., (xN, yN), where each y was produced by some unknown function f, so that y = f(x). The task is to find a hypothesis h, from a chosen hypothesis space (all straight lines, all decision trees of some size, all networks of a certain shape), that approximates f well. "Well" means not just on the training examples but on new examples it has never seen. This ability is called generalisation, and it is the whole point.

Decision trees: A decision tree makes a prediction by asking a sequence of questions. Example, a tree for "will the customer wait for a table at a restaurant in Dhanmondi?": first ask "How many people are inside?"; if none, predict no; if some, predict yes; if full, ask "What is the estimated wait?", and so on. Each internal node tests an attribute, each branch is a possible value, and each leaf gives a prediction. Trees are easy for people to read and explain, which is a big advantage in fields like banking or medicine.

Learning a decision tree: The standard algorithm builds the tree top-down, greedily. At each node, choose the attribute that best separates the examples into pure groups (all yes or all no), split the examples by that attribute's values, and repeat on each branch. "Best" is measured by information gain, based on entropy: entropy measures how mixed a set is, being 0 bits for a pure set and 1 bit for a 50/50 mix of two classes. The attribute that reduces entropy the most gives the most information. Stop when a group is pure or no attributes are left.

Training, validation and test sets: How do we know if a learned model is good? Never judge it only on the data it learned from; it may simply have memorised it. The standard practice is to split data into a training set (to learn the parameters), a validation set (to choose settings like tree depth, called hyperparameters), and a test set (used once at the end to estimate real performance). When data is limited, k-fold cross-validation splits the data into k parts, trains on k minus 1 parts and tests on the remaining one, rotating k times and averaging. Using test data during development is a serious mistake, because the reported accuracy then becomes too optimistic.

Overfitting and underfitting: A model overfits when it fits the training data very closely, including its noise and accidents, and then performs poorly on new data. Think of a student who memorises last year's answers word for word and fails when the questions are rephrased. A model underfits when it is too simple to capture the real pattern, like predicting every house price with a single average. A good model sits between: complex enough to capture the pattern, simple enough to generalise. Remedies for overfitting include more data, simpler models, pruning decision trees, and regularisation, which adds a penalty for complexity to the learning objective.

Linear models: Another simple and very useful hypothesis is a straight line or flat plane. Linear regression predicts a number as a weighted sum of inputs: for a flat in Mirpur, price might be estimated as w0 + w1 times area + w2 times number of rooms. Learning means finding weights that minimise the average squared error on the training data, which can be done exactly with a formula or step by step with gradient descent: repeatedly nudge each weight in the direction that reduces the error. For classification, a linear classifier draws a line (or plane) separating the classes, and logistic regression outputs a probability with a smooth S-shaped curve.

The artificial neuron: Neural networks are loosely inspired by brain cells. A single artificial neuron, or unit, takes inputs x1, ..., xn, multiplies each by a weight, adds a bias b, and applies an activation function g: output = g(w1 x1 + ... + wn xn + b). If g is a step function (output 1 if the sum is above 0, otherwise 0), the unit is a perceptron, a linear classifier introduced by Frank Rosenblatt in the late 1950s. Common modern activation functions are the sigmoid, which squashes any number to between 0 and 1, and the ReLU, which outputs max(0, sum).

The perceptron learning rule: The perceptron learns by correcting its mistakes. For each training example, compute the output y; if it is wrong, change each weight by (target minus y) times the input: wi = wi + (t - y) xi, and similarly b = b + (t - y). If the output is right, change nothing. If the data can be separated by a line, this rule is guaranteed to find such a line in a finite number of steps.

A perceptron worked example, learning OR: Inputs (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1) with targets 0, 1, 1, 1. Start with w1 = w2 = 0, b = 0, step output 1 if the sum is above 0. Pass 1: (0,0) gives 0, correct. (0,1) gives 0 but target 1, so update: w2 = 1, b = 1. (1,0): sum 0 + 1 = 1, output 1, correct. (1,1): correct. Pass 2: (0,0): sum = 1, output 1, wrong; b becomes 0. (0,1): sum 1, correct. (1,0): sum 0, output 0, wrong; w1 = 1, b = 1. (1,1): correct. Pass 3: (0,0): sum 1, wrong; b = 0. The rest are correct with w = (1, 1), b = 0. Pass 4: all four correct, so learning stops. The final perceptron computes OR exactly.

The limit of one perceptron: A single perceptron can only learn patterns separable by a straight line. Minsky and Papert famously pointed out in 1969 that it cannot learn XOR (output 1 when exactly one input is 1), because no single line separates (0,1) and (1,0) from (0,0) and (1,1). This contributed to a period of reduced interest in neural networks. The fix is to stack units into layers: a network with one hidden layer can compute XOR easily.

Multilayer networks and backpropagation: A feedforward neural network has an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer, with each unit feeding the next layer. With enough hidden units, such networks can approximate a very wide range of functions. Training uses gradient descent on a loss function that measures error. The challenge is knowing how much each hidden weight contributed to the error. Backpropagation solves this: compute the output error, then pass it backwards layer by layer using the chain rule of calculus, giving the gradient for every weight efficiently. The idea was popularised in the mid-1980s and remains the core of training today.

Deep learning: Deep learning means using neural networks with many layers. Since around 2012, deep networks have made dramatic progress, helped by three things: large datasets, fast parallel hardware such as GPUs, and better training techniques. Special architectures suit special data: convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for images, which reuse the same small filters across the image; recurrent networks for sequences; and transformers, introduced in 2017, which use a mechanism called attention and now underlie most large language models. Deep networks often need a lot of data and computation, and their reasoning is hard to inspect, which raises the explainability issues of the next lesson.

Real life example 1, Bangla handwritten digit recognition: Researchers in Bangladesh have built datasets of handwritten Bangla digits and characters, collected from many writers, and trained CNNs to recognise them. Such systems can help digitise forms, postal codes and old records. A model trained only on neat writing from university students may do worse on writing from older people or children; this is overfitting to the kind of data seen, and it shows why diverse training data matters.

Real life example 2, credit scoring for mobile loans: A digital lending service might predict whether a borrower will repay, using features like transaction history and repayment of earlier small loans. A decision tree or logistic regression can be explained to customers and regulators ("rejected because of three missed payments"), while a deep network might be slightly more accurate but harder to justify. The choice of model is therefore not only about accuracy, but also about fairness and explanation.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students confuse classification with regression, or supervised with unsupervised learning. Many judge a model by training accuracy, missing overfitting. In the perceptron rule, they forget to update the bias, or update when the output is already correct. Typical questions: define the three types of learning with examples; build a small decision tree or choose the root attribute by information gain; explain overfitting and how to detect it with a validation set; trace the perceptron learning rule on AND or OR; explain why one perceptron cannot learn XOR; and describe backpropagation in words.

Recap: Machine learning builds models from data instead of hand-written rules. Supervised learning uses labelled examples, unsupervised learning finds structure, and reinforcement learning learns from rewards. Decision trees split data by the most informative attribute; linear models use weighted sums. Good models generalise, which we check with separate validation and test sets, guarding against overfitting. A perceptron learns linearly separable patterns like OR by correcting mistakes, but not XOR; multilayer networks trained by backpropagation, and deep learning, go much further. The final lesson looks at language, vision and the ethics of AI.
key_points: Machine learning improves performance at a task by learning from data rather than hand-written rules.
Supervised learning uses labelled examples (classification or regression); unsupervised finds structure; reinforcement learns from rewards.
Generalisation to unseen data is the goal; use separate training, validation and test sets.
Overfitting means fitting noise in training data and doing poorly on new data; underfitting means the model is too simple.
