Decision trees choose splits by information gain, based on entropy.
The perceptron rule updates wi = wi + (t - y) xi only on mistakes; it learns OR but cannot learn XOR.
Multilayer networks are trained by backpropagation and gradient descent; deep learning uses many layers.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see a model's accuracy, ask two questions: "Measured on which data?" and "Compared with what simple baseline?". A 95% accuracy is meaningless if 95% of the examples belong to one class and the model just always predicts it.
lessons.task: Trace the perceptron learning rule by hand for the AND function, starting with w1 = w2 = 0 and b = 0 and the same step function as in the lesson. Record the weights after every update and count how many passes it needs. Then try XOR for a few passes and describe what happens.

quiz.q: Grouping shop customers by buying habits without any labels is an example of:
quiz.explain: No labels are given; the algorithm finds clusters itself.

quiz.q: What is overfitting?
options: A model too simple to capture the pattern
A model that has not finished training
Fitting noise in the training data so that performance on new data is poor
quiz.explain: The model memorises accidents of the training set instead of the real pattern.

quiz.q: What is the perceptron learning rule for weight wi when the output is wrong?
quiz.explain: The weight moves in the direction that corrects the mistake; no change when correct.

quiz.q: Why can a single perceptron not learn XOR?
options: XOR's positive and negative examples cannot be separated by a straight line
quiz.explain: A single perceptron is a linear classifier; XOR needs a hidden layer.

quiz.q: What does backpropagation compute?
options: The gradient of the error with respect to every weight, layer by layer from the output back
quiz.explain: It applies the chain rule backwards so gradient descent can update hidden weights.

lessons.title: Language, Vision, AI Ethics and Course Wrap-Up
lessons.content:
Your aunt in Sylhet sends a voice message in Sylheti, your cousin replies in Banglish typed with English letters, and a shop sign in the photo they share mixes Bangla and English. A human reads all of this without effort. For a computer, every part is hard: understanding speech, handling a dialect, reading text written in two scripts, and recognising letters in a blurry photo. This final lesson gives an overview of two big application areas of AI, natural language processing and computer vision, then looks carefully at the ethical questions AI raises, and ends with a recap of the whole course.

Natural language processing: Natural language processing (NLP) is the part of AI that deals with human languages: understanding, generating and translating them. Common tasks include text classification (spam, sentiment, topic), information extraction (finding names, dates and places in news), machine translation, question answering, summarisation, speech recognition and speech synthesis. Language is hard for computers because it is ambiguous ("I saw the man with the telescope": who has the telescope?), depends on context and world knowledge, and keeps changing with new words and slang.

Classic approaches to language: Early NLP used hand-written grammars and rules, close to the logic-based methods of this course. Grammars describe how words combine into phrases and sentences, and parsing finds the structure of a sentence as a tree. From the 1990s, statistical methods became dominant: language models assign probabilities to word sequences, often using n-grams (the probability of a word given the previous one or two words), and naive Bayes and similar models classify text using word counts. These methods learn from large text collections instead of relying only on rules written by linguists.

Neural language models: Modern NLP mostly uses neural networks. Words are represented as vectors of numbers, called embeddings, learned so that words used in similar contexts get similar vectors. Transformer networks, introduced in 2017, process whole sequences using attention, which lets each word look at all other words to decide what matters. Large language models are transformers trained on enormous amounts of text to predict the next piece of text; after further training, they can answer questions, write and summarise. They are useful but have well-known limits: they can produce fluent but false statements, often called hallucinations; they reflect biases in their training data; and their abilities depend heavily on how much data exists for a language.

Challenges for Bangla: Bangla is one of the most spoken languages in the world, yet it has historically had far fewer digital resources (labelled datasets, tools, large clean text collections) than English, so it is often described as a low-resource language in NLP. Specific challenges include rich word forms (one root with many suffixes and inflections), compound characters (juktakkhor) and Unicode encoding issues, code-mixing with English and Banglish written in Latin letters, dialects such as Sylheti and Chittagonian, and fewer high-quality annotated datasets for tasks like named entity recognition. Researchers in Bangladesh and abroad have been building datasets and models for Bangla, and this is an area where local students can contribute a lot.

Speech and translation: Speech recognition turns audio into text, and speech synthesis turns text into natural-sounding audio; both are now mostly done with neural networks trained on many hours of recorded speech. Machine translation has moved from rule-based systems, through statistical systems that learned from aligned sentence pairs, to neural systems. Translation between Bangla and English has improved a lot, but it still struggles with idioms, dialect words, names and long sentences, so important documents, like legal papers or medical instructions, should still be checked by a fluent person.

Computer vision: Computer vision is the part of AI that extracts information from images and video. Core tasks include image classification (what is in this picture?), object detection (where are the objects, with boxes around them?), segmentation (which pixels belong to which object?), face recognition, optical character recognition (reading printed or handwritten text), and tracking objects through video. Vision is hard because the same object looks very different under different lighting, angles, distances and partial occlusion, while a photo is just a grid of numbers.

How vision systems work today: Classic vision used hand-designed features, such as edges and corners, with separate classifiers. Since around 2012, convolutional neural networks have become the standard approach: early layers learn simple patterns like edges, deeper layers combine them into textures, parts and whole objects. A widely cited turning point was the 2012 ImageNet competition, where a deep CNN greatly reduced the error rate compared with earlier methods. Today, transformer-based models are also used for vision, and some models handle both images and text together.

Vision applications around us: Phones unlock by recognising faces; apps translate signs by reading their text; cars in some countries use cameras to keep lanes and detect pedestrians; doctors use systems that help flag possible problems in X-rays and retinal scans; and farmers can photograph leaves to check for disease. In Bangladesh, possible uses include reading vehicle number plates in traffic systems, monitoring crops and rivers from satellite images, and digitising old Bangla documents. Each of these also raises the ethical questions we turn to now.

Limits of today's systems: It is important to be realistic. Current AI systems are powerful at specific tasks with plenty of data, but they can fail in surprising ways when inputs differ from their training data: a vision model may be fooled by small, carefully designed changes to an image (adversarial examples), and a language model may give different answers to the same question phrased slightly differently. They do not have the broad common sense, grounded understanding of the physical world or reliable reasoning that people often assume. Whether and when more general AI will be achieved is debated among experts, and confident predictions in either direction should be treated with care.

Why AI ethics matters: AI systems now influence who gets a loan, which job applicants are shortlisted, what news people see and how police allocate attention. Mistakes or unfairness can harm many people quickly, and harms are often hard to see from inside the system. Engineers who build AI therefore carry responsibility not only for accuracy, but also for fairness, privacy, transparency and safety. These questions are not only for philosophers; they shape design decisions every day.

Bias and fairness: A model learns from data, and data reflects the past, including past discrimination and uneven coverage. A widely reported example: some commercial face analysis systems were found to have much higher error rates on darker-skinned women than on lighter-skinned men, because training data and testing had not covered all groups well. A hiring model trained on past hiring decisions can learn to repeat past biases. Defining fairness is itself hard: equal accuracy across groups, equal approval rates and other definitions can conflict, so choices must be made openly. Good practice includes checking performance separately for different groups, such as rural and urban users, or speakers of different dialects.

Privacy and surveillance: AI works best with lots of data, and much of that data is about people: messages, locations, faces, purchases. Collecting and combining such data can reveal private facts, and face recognition makes large-scale surveillance technically easy. Responsible systems collect only the data they need, protect and anonymise it, ask for meaningful consent, and follow data protection laws where they exist. Techniques such as differential privacy and federated learning, which trains models without collecting raw data in one place, can help.

Explainability and accountability: When a deep network denies a loan, the person deserves a reason, and regulators need to check the system. Yet large networks are hard to interpret. Methods for explainable AI try to show which inputs mattered most for a decision, and in high-stakes areas simpler, interpretable models are sometimes preferred. Accountability asks who is responsible when an AI system causes harm: the developer, the company deploying it, or the user. Recall MYCIN from lesson 20: one reason it was not used routinely was exactly this question of responsibility, which remains important today.

Work, misinformation and safety: AI can automate some tasks, which may change or reduce some jobs while creating others; the effect on any particular country, including Bangladesh's large garment and service sectors, is debated and uncertain, so we should be cautious about confident predictions either way. Generative models can create realistic fake images, audio and text, which can be misused for scams and misinformation, especially around elections. Researchers also study AI safety: making sure systems reliably do what their designers intend, behave well in unexpected situations, and cannot easily be misused. These are active, open problems.

Guidelines and good practice: Many governments, companies and organisations have published principles for trustworthy AI, typically including fairness, transparency, privacy, safety, accountability and human oversight, and some regions have begun to pass laws regulating high-risk AI uses. For a student, practical habits matter most: know where your data came from, test on diverse users, document your model's limits, keep a human in the loop for important decisions, and ask "who could be harmed if this is wrong?" before deploying.

Real life example 1, a Bangla customer service chatbot: A telecom company wants a chatbot that answers customers in Bangla. The team must handle Banglish and dialect words, avoid confidently making up wrong information about tariffs, protect customer data in the logs, offer an easy way to reach a human, and test the bot with users from different districts and age groups, not only young city users. Each of these is both a technical and an ethical requirement.

Real life example 2, AI in exam proctoring: Some online exams use cameras and AI to flag suspicious behaviour. If the system was trained mostly on well-lit faces and quiet rooms, it may wrongly flag students in poorly lit homes or shared rooms, more often from poorer families. A fair deployment would test for such differences, let humans review every flag, explain the decision to students and allow appeals.

Course wrap-up, the big picture: We started with agents: an agent perceives and acts, and a rational agent does what is expected to maximise its performance measure (lessons 1 to 3). We learned to formulate problems and solve them by search: uninformed methods like BFS, UCS and IDS (lessons 4 to 7), and informed methods like greedy search and A* with admissible heuristics (8 and 9); local search for optimisation (10 and 11); adversarial search with minimax and alpha-beta for games (12 and 13); and constraint satisfaction with backtracking and arc consistency (14 and 15). We then represented knowledge in propositional and first-order logic and reasoned with resolution and chaining (16 to 19), organised it in ontologies and expert systems (20), and planned actions (21). Finally we handled uncertainty with probability, Bayes' rule and Bayesian networks (22 and 23), learned from data (24), and looked at language, vision and ethics today.

Where to go next: Machine learning, in its own course, deepens lesson 24. Courses on natural language processing, computer vision, robotics and reinforcement learning build on the search, logic and probability ideas here. Whatever you choose, the habits from this course remain useful: formulate the problem clearly, choose a representation, pick an algorithm whose guarantees you understand, test honestly, and think about the people your system affects.

lessons.tip: For any AI project, write a one-paragraph "limits" note before you finish: what data it was trained on, where it may fail, and who could be harmed if it is wrong. Examiners, employers and users all value an engineer who knows the limits of their own system.

quiz.q: Why is Bangla often called a low-resource language in NLP?
options: It has had far fewer digital datasets and tools than languages like English
quiz.explain: Despite many speakers, labelled data and tools have historically been limited.

quiz.q: What is a "hallucination" in a large language model?
options: A fluent but false statement produced by the model
A model that refuses to answer
A spelling mistake in the input
quiz.explain: The model can produce confident text that is not true.

quiz.q: Which task finds where objects are in an image by drawing boxes around them?
quiz.explain: Detection gives locations; classification only says what is present.

quiz.q: A face analysis system has much higher error rates for one group of people. This is mainly an issue of:
quiz.explain: Uneven training data and testing can make systems unfair to some groups.

quiz.q: Which practice best supports accountability for an AI system making important decisions?
options: Keeping a human in the loop, documenting limits and allowing appeals
Using only the largest available model
quiz.explain: People affected need explanations, review and a way to challenge decisions.
